en: The Pratāparudrīya composed by the illustrious Vidyānātha,
accompanied by the Ratnāpaṇa commentary written by the illustrious Kumārasvāmin; now begins the section on the Hero (Nāyaka).
I salute the goddess of speech, the moonlight for the night-lotus of knowledge, the crest-jewel of the Vedas, the wife of the Lotus-born Brahmā, and the mother of the three worlds;
for the prostrations at her lotus feet become the site for planting the seeds of the process of Sarasvatī’s grace for the virtuous, and serve as the sole life-force for the drama of poetry. (1.1)
With palms joined in respectful salutation toward the ancients such as Bhāmaha and others,
I shall correctly set forth this compendium of the entire essence of the science of poetics (*alaṅkāra-śāstra*).
After a long time, the *Kāvyālaṅkārasaṃgraha* has fulfilled its purpose, by which the fame of King Pratāparudradeva is made manifest. (1.3)
Wherein rasa is predominant, and wherein word, meaning, qualities, ornaments, styles, and diction [prevail]—this is the scope of the treatise and the path of poetry. (ViPrud 1.4)
Although this [poetic figure] has been properly defined by the ancients in their treatises,
nevertheless, no example of it has been provided that is commensurate with its leader (the *nāyaka*).
The life-story of the one of meritorious fame deserves to be cited as an example; no one such as he has been made an ornament for literary compositions by those of former times.
The description of the virtues of the leader who constitutes the subject matter is the very root of both the fame and the established status of compositions as well as their authors. (ViPrud 1.7)

Just as the description of Rāma’s virtues brought about the great establishment of the *Rāmāyaṇa* and its birth from Valmīki, so indeed does the composition of a literary work become conducive to spiritual welfare through the description of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Just as from the Vedas, the Śāstras, the Purāṇas, and so forth, there is the attainment of the beneficial and the cessation of the harmful, [so it is with such compositions].
Likewise, [this knowledge arises] even from poetry because it has a virtuous basis;
however, this much is the distinction: from poetry, the cognition that something ought to be done is full of aesthetic flavor (*sarasā*), whereas it is not so in other cases.
For instance:

We offer our longing to that splendor of poetry by which the wise man—who has long been instructed by the Veda, which is like a master and consists primarily of words; and who has been taught by the Purāṇas and similar texts, which are like a friend and incline toward meaning; and who has been made curious about what ought to be done by the beauty of poetry, which is like a beloved and imparts sweetness—is now rendered eager to compose. (ViP Rudra 1.8)
Therefore, poetry is highly useful because it produces both visible and invisible results.
This has been stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*:
"Poetry leads to fame, the attainment of wealth, proficiency in worldly conduct, and the destruction of that which is inauspicious."
It serves to bring about immediate supreme bliss, being taught in a manner as intimate as that of a beloved woman.
Thus it is said;
and this is well known in the great treatises:
"Knowledge increases, fame is acquired, and virtues are manifested."
Having heard the conduct of the Great Man, why would the established conventions of poetry not captivate one?
Consciousness increases, fame is acquired, virtues are earned, and the conduct of great men is heard; what is it that prevents poetic discourses from captivating us?
Furthermore, that poetry in which the deeds of the Supreme Person (uttamapuruṣa) are not composed should indeed be abandoned;
and this [work] is rooted in that.
The Smṛti states: "One should avoid poetic discourse.
This path belongs not only to poetry; rather, because it is the constant refuge even for the entire body of sacred scripture (śāstra), it commands great respect from the world.
Likewise, the Vaiśeṣika and other systems attain veneration by the world because they establish the existence of God;
similarly, even the Mahābhārata and other such works possess superiority over the entire universe precisely because they are devoted to the description of Great Beings.
What need is there for more? Even the Vedāntas are held to be supremely exalted because they expound upon Brahman.

By the great seer who composed the Sūtras, beginning with the words "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma," it was acknowledged that the very life-breath of the scripture is the description of the qualities of the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa) by means of the inquiry into Dharma— the highest quality inherent in man;
for even in this mass of compositions devoted to the exposition of various logical principles, the description of the qualities of the Great Person is the supreme fragrance of gold.
And therefore,
O virtuous ones, may this treatise on poetics (*alaṅkāraprabandha*), composed by relying upon the virtues of King Pratāparudradeva, be a feast for your ears. (ViPrud 1.9)
This work of Vidyānātha was composed to adorn the fame of the Kākatīya king; now it is being adorned by him himself.
As it was said by Daṇḍin: "The reflection of the fame of those first kings, having reached the mirror of literature, does not perish of its own accord even in their absence; behold!"
Thus,
the greatness of the composition is indeed well-established by the majesty of its subject matter.
As it was said by the ancient Bhāmaha:
“Due to the greatness of that which is to be praised, the excellences of poetry shine forth.
Thus it was stated by Udbhaṭa.
“Even when endowed with the beauty of poetic qualities and ornaments, a poem becomes exceedingly radiant through the excellence of its subject, just as the celestial tree is made so by Mount Meru.”
Thus it has been said by Rudrabhaṭṭa as well: "The foundation of a literary work is its noble character.
And this has been elaborated in the *Sāhityamīmāṃsā*: "Garlands of well-spoken verses, strung together with the virtues of the hero, adorn the virtuous until the end of the kalpa."
And it has been stated by King Bhoja:
"Even a slight utterance of a poet becomes an ear-ornament for the learned,
provided that the hero is described as possessing superhuman excellence."
Thus [ends the section on] the qualities of the Leader, such as noble lineage and so forth.
In this context, these are the qualities of the hero:
nobility of great lineage, brilliance, great fortune, magnanimity, majesty, cleverness, righteousness, and other such virtues. (ViPrud 1.11)
In accordance with previous treatises, these few qualities of King Pratāparudradeva have been described; yet they remain beyond the reach of words.
Now, their essential nature and examples:
therein,
[1.1.1] noble birth.
Noble lineage means being born into a great family;
for example:
"The Lotus-born [Brahmā] was long sought after by Indra and the hosts of gods, who, through the power of their fortune in that intermediate world, desired to sport upon the earth."
He founded the Kākatīya lineage, which surpassed the illustrious families of the sun and the moon; in that lineage, the Lord of Lakṣmī now awakens in the form of Vīrarudra.
[1.1.2 Radiance] Now, regarding radiance:
"Radiance is proclaimed to be the possession of a body endowed with beauty. (ViPrud 1.14)

"Just as he who was formerly born from Mahādeva upon the daughter of the ocean [Pārvatī]—that very Kāma, now embodied as Pratāpaśrī Rudra—is victorious through the abundance of the world’s good fortune; such is the thought of the deer-eyed women. (ViPrud 1.15)
[1.1.3 Great Fortune] Now, as for great fortune:
that which consists in sovereignty over the entire earth is called great fortune.
For example:

Having ascended the throne—the first path for the descent of the Goddess of Royal Fortune, and which is illuminated by the rays of the jewels shimmering on the crowns of prostrate kings—the King Śrī Vīrarudra, a treasury of virtues whose prowess is unmatched and whose speed is such that it leaps over the praises of rival monarchs, protects the earth with his incomparable exploits. (ViPrud 1.16)
[1.1.4 Magnanimity] Now, as for magnanimity: that which is the habitual practice of giving is declared to be magnanimity. (ViPrud 1.17)
For example:
"There is no other generous man equal to King Rudra in the three worlds—he whose fame has eclipsed that of Indra and Īśāna by the praise of his multitude of virtues;
for the courtyards of the jewel-houses of learned men are made fragrant on all sides by the scent of the rutting ichor of elephants emerging from him. (ViPrud 1.18)
[1.1.5 Brilliance] Now, regarding brilliance:
that which consists in being the illuminator of the world is called brilliance.
For example:

While the victorious lord of the Kākatis, the sun of splendor, ever shines—stealing away the pride of the darkness that is the tresses of the wives of rival kings—the manifestation of light occurs even in the western rocks of the boundary mountains, which were previously inaccessible to the sun and shrouded in ancient, unrestrained darkness. (ViPrud 1.19)
[1.1.6 Vaidagdhyam] Now, regarding *vaidagdhyam* (cleverness): skillfulness in matters to be accomplished is proclaimed as *vaidagdhyam*.

How can the cleverness of the illustrious Vīrarudra, that treasure-house of virtues, be described, wherein even the great splendors of mutually opposed speech and fortune possess such straightforwardness?
Moreover, that king, the conqueror of the quarters, maintains this earth— made charming by the graceful conduct of these two [qualities] alike— free from rivalry through such festivals.
[1.1.7 Righteousness] Now, regarding righteousness:
the state of having one's mind entirely dependent upon the Dharma is proclaimed as righteousness.
For example:
"The Lord of Kākatīya cannot tolerate impropriety even in jest, talk of another's wife even in a dream, or the attribution of faults even to an enemy. (ViPrud 1.22)
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," [qualities such as] great majesty, scholarship, and so forth are meant.
That great majesty would consist in being of the very nature of the deity.
[1.1.8 The nature of being the Great Earth] For example: Kausalyā was his first mother.
Devakī was the second mother of Viṣṇu, and thereafter the highly honored Mummaḍāmbā was the third;
he who became the Lord of the Raghus in the Tretā age and Śauri in the Dvāpara age, he now triumphs in the Kali age as the incarnation of Vīrarudra to protect the earth.
Here, by virtue of being the very essence of Garuḍa’s banner, his great majesty is described.
Now, regarding erudition (pāṇḍitya):
That which is superiority in all branches of knowledge is declared to be *pāṇḍitya* (erudition).
For example:
Delighting the assemblies of the wise with discourses on the boundaries of the six systems of philosophy, and pleasing the poets with well-spoken verses skilled in showing the path of true Sarasvatī;
Delighting the lute-players in the assembly with sequences of musical instruments that reveal the secrets of the Upaniṣads of music, the illustrious Kākatīndra king sports there.
Now, following the description of the qualities of the hero, the nature of the hero is defined:
"The hero is proclaimed to be one who is distinguished by fame and majesty, devoted to virtue, pleasure, and wealth, capable of bearing the burden [of leadership], and rich in virtues. (ViPrud 1.26)
Regarding fortune through fame and majesty— as for example, fortune:
The vast orb of fame of King Kākati Vīrarudra bears the sovereign glory of the triple world, raised aloft with the Dharma as its support;
this vault of heaven appears dark blue like a water-lily, as if it were his shadow, and therefore I believe that the sun of his majesty shines resplendently above it.
[1.2.2 Devotion to Dharma, Kāma,
and Artha] Devotion to dharma, kāma, and artha is as follows:
Dharma possesses the full splendor of artha, and artha is established like dharma.
Those two were like Kāma and Rudra, as it were, in the lord of men, Rudra.
[1.2.3 Bearing the Burden (dhurīṇakā)] An example of bearing the burden (*dhurīṇatā*):
Śeṣa rejoices in his own wives as they sing by nodding his head; the Lord of Tortoises pleases Lakṣmī today by revealing the expanse of his chest.
And as King Kākati Vīrarudra bears the entire earth upon his arm, the elephants of the quarters dispel their distress by following after him.
[1.2.4 Abundance of Qualities] Regarding abundance of qualities, for example:
If the serpent-king were to speak with a thousand mouths, and the sun-god were to write with a thousand hands;
And may Hari behold with a thousand eyes the virtues of the lord of Kākatīya Vīra in their proper place.
Now the specific types of heroes (nāyaka) are defined: The noble (udātta), the haughty (uddhata), the playful (lalita), and the tranquil (śānta)—
these four types of heroes are traditionally taught by the ancients as being preceded by the term "resolute" (dhīra).

In that regard, there are four types of heroes common to all aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*): the noble-steadfast (*dhīrodātta*), the haughty-steadfast (*dhīroddhata*), the playful-steadfast (*dhīralalita*), and the tranquil-steadfast (*dhīraśānta*).
Their essential nature and examples are as follows:
[1.3.1 *Dhīrodātta*]
A great being who is profoundly deep, compassionate,
free from boastfulness, steadfast like Pratāparudra, and noble-minded— he is considered *dhīrodātta*.
For example:

When his enemies were hesitant, King Śrī Vīrarudra—fortunate with a fame that transcends the three worlds—was gentle out of compassion; yet when he drew his sword to slay them for a moment, he felt ashamed before his bards who praised him for his love of heroic glory as they bowed their brows. He did not display even the slightest hint of facial expressions indicative of pleasure, anger, or joy. (ViPrud 1.33)
Abounding in pride and envy, fierce in conduct, boastful,
deceitful, and easily provoked to anger— he is called the "haughty hero" (dhīroddhata).
[1.3.2 The Noble and Haughty (dhīrodatta):
For example— "Hey there, Ghūrjara! You are shattered in battle; O Lampāka, why do you tremble? O Vaṅga, why do you flee in vain? O Balaraja, you are one-eyed; O Koṅkaṇa, why are you [afraid]?"
“Hūṇa, devote yourself to life! These warriors of the Andhra king, who have conquered the Mahārāṣṭra kingdom, overcome their enemies, thinking, ‘These are our foes. (ViPrud 1.35)
Herein lies the *dhīroddhata* (dignified and haughty) nature of the warriors;
[the *dhīralalita* (dignified and playful) is as follows:
"The sole source of celestial bliss."
This is an alternative reading:
"The *dhīralalita* is free from anxiety, devoted to the arts, happy, and gentle. *i*.
[An alternative reading is *sukhaikabhūḥ*. For example:
His heat of valor is unrestrained; all rival kings have been made to bow down; this lord, Śiva, the self-existent, possesses abundant devotion to his consort.
"This prince alone, being steadfast, bears the entire burden of the illustrious Vīrarudra"—thus the king, the illustrious Lord of Kākatīyas, rejoices at every moment.
[1.3.4 Dhīraśāntaḥ]:
One who is steadfast, peaceful, and serene in soul is called *dhīraśānta*, such as a twice-born (*dvija*) and others. *ViPrud* 1.37.
Just as—this multitude of wise men rejoices at the rise of the heroic jewel among kings, Rudra, like a fresh lotus-pond at the arrival of the sun;
having become the dwelling place for the sport of blossoming lotuses, it incessantly spreads joy to the entire world through its own expansions, eager for the end of the night. (ViPrud 1.38)
Herein lies the steadfast composure of the Brahmins.
Now, the heroes of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) are described;
these four types of heroes are the subjects of the erotic sentiment.
They are known as the Anukūla (favourable), the Dakṣiṇa (courteous), the Dhṛṣṭa (bold), and the Śaṭha (crafty).
Their essential nature and examples are as follows:
the *anukūla* (favourable) hero is one who is devoted exclusively to a single heroine; he is specifically attached to one heroine alone.
For example:
"O friend, what kind of penance has been performed by the Earth, that King Rudra is celebrated as her heroic husband? Where is such virtuous conduct on his part, that I might become his beloved?"
"Know this, O proud lady: do not despair. Having proclaimed your name before him, I shall make the king—who has the ocean for his girdle—eternally devoted to you."
Here, Pratāparudra’s special affection for the earth is manifested,
by which the proclamation of his love is made through the mention of her name as "the bride whose girdle is the ocean" (*ratnākaramekhalā*), signifying her stability.
[1.4.2 Dakṣiṇa]
The *dakṣiṇa* (straightforward) hero is equal toward many;
that is, the *nāyaka* who follows his affection without partiality toward several heroines.
For example:
By means of playful banter alone, I restrained a certain woman from her amorous pastimes; by a meaningful glance, I revealed my heart to someone else;
and to another, I sent a treasure of ornaments through the hand of a messenger.
While she was lost in thought as to where I might go, the night turned into dawn for the King.
And likewise: [he bestowed] speech with his mouth,
and prosperity with his two eyes.
And by supporting the earth with his arm,
Rudra, the lord of men, maintains equality with them.
[1.4.3 Dhṛṣṭaḥ] One who has gone openly and is free from fear is *dhṛṣṭa* (bold/impudent), as for example:
Beholding every limb of yours, which proclaims the enjoyment of royal splendor, what impropriety could there be? This very audacity has indeed been offered by me.
I know you to have many beloveds; what more need be said? We are but few, yet your love for her is greater—she who is named Vasumatī (the Earth). What is the use of further words?
[1.4.4 Śaṭha: One who acts unpleasantly in secret is a *śaṭha*. // ViPrud_1.44 //
The *śaṭha* (the rogue) is one who performs disagreeable acts known only to the heroine.
For example:

"With your gaze you look [at me] only with your eyes, not with your mind; you speak pleasant words with your voice, but not with your heart. You display your chest before me, but not your inner being."
O Lord of Kākatīya, it is known that the earth is merely a mockery for those like me who meditate upon your supreme mistress, the sovereign of your life; therefore,
enough with these futile external agitations.
In this context, by taking the Kākatīya lords as examples with respect to their respective heroes, it is Vīrarudra alone who is being described.
Regarding the winning over of these heroines, there are assistants named Pīṭhamarda, Viṭa, Ceṭa, and Vidūṣaka;
their nature is now defined.
A *pīṭhamarda* is slightly inferior [to the *viṭa*]; a *viṭa* is said to be skilled in a single art;
a *ceṭa* is skilled in reconciliation; and a *vidūṣaka* is primarily characterized by humor. (ViPrud 1.46)
The examples of these are clear.

Now, the eight types of heroines of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) are as follows: the one whose husband is under her control (*svādhīnapatikā*), and likewise the one who prepares for her tryst (*vāsakasajjikā*).
The woman longing in separation, the deceived one, and the one whose lover has been unfaithful.
The woman separated by quarrel, the one whose husband is away on a journey, and likewise the woman going to meet her lover— these are described in order according to their characteristics.
She who is constantly cherished by her beloved and whose husband is under her own control is considered a *svādhīnapatikā* (one whose husband is dependent on her). For example:
Constantly caressing his beloved Earth— who endures all things— with various special favors,
King Pratāparudra gazes upon her at every moment.
She who repeatedly adorns the pleasure-chamber as well as herself at the time of her beloved's arrival is known as vāsakasajjikā.
[1.5.2 vāsakāsajñikā] For example:
having adorned the principal chamber with her own splendor, she departed with joy.
At the time of the consecration with glory, Vīrarudra was awaited.
When her beloved tarries too long, she becomes distracted, longing in separation.
[1.5.3 Virahotkaṇṭhitā] As for example:
"There is no other suspicion regarding King Rudra, who possesses such a fragrance of virtues; nor is he difficult to obtain through the company of friends—why then does she linger?"
Go to bring back your beloved; O Madana, here I join my palms in supplication, for your dear friend [the sun] is scattering his rays in all directions.
When she has been deceived by her lover after having communicated a secret rendezvous, she is proclaimed by those skilled in the arts as "the one afflicted by love and betrayed. (ViPrud 1.54)
[1.5.4 Deceived] For example:
"Go ahead, my friend!"
"What talk can there be of the arrival of my beloved? The night has reached its peak at the place of our tryst. You shall depart; you have come in vain and are now made muddy by my tears.

Or rather, since Rudra, the lord of men, the beloved of royal fortune, the lover of Sarasvatī, and the cherished one of the earth, has set his foot [upon us], we have likely been deceived. (ViPrud 1.55)
When her lover has spent the night elsewhere and returns in the morning,
she who is angry due to signs of his union with other women is considered a *khaṇḍitā*.
[1.5.5 Fragmented] For example:
"The night, limited as it is to three watches, was dear to you; yet, due to your attachment to the road, you have arrived at my house only this morning."
"Tell me, what should be done? For all women must be looked upon by kings; what fault is there in me, who am merely following my desire?"
Having driven away her beloved out of anger, she is later filled with remorse;
this state is designated by the wise as "separated by a quarrel" (*kalahāntaritā*).
[1.5.6 The woman separated by a quarrel (kalahāntaritā)] For example:
"In such and such a way my beloved was entreating you, yet you, with a heart turbid with anger..."
Having been abandoned, you did not realize the pain of separation from your husband; now endure it.
O heart, because you repeatedly entreated him so affectionately yet were disregarded by him— clouded as you were by anger—
you did not realize he was a king; now, endure the agony of separation.
When her beloved has gone to another land, the woman whose husband is away becomes distressed;
for example: [1.5.7 Proṣitabhartṛkā]—just as:
While the kings of Kākatīpura lingered for the sake of serving the illustrious Lord Vīrarudra— whose fame and majesty were celebrated throughout the three worlds—

their wives passed their days with eyes fixed upon the palace gates, and their nights with the hope of dawn, their bodies bristling with dense horripilation as they were bound by the contemplation of him, while the arrows of Love were scattered about.
A woman who is intent on going to meet her lover while afflicted by love is called an *abhisārikā*.
[1.5.8 Abhisārikā] For example:
"Enough with your agitations, O woman of little knowledge!"
"May the lord of the earth be dear to us; I neither see nor hear of any woman going to meet her lover mounted upon an elephant."
The assistants in winning over these heroines.
The female messenger, the slave girl, the female friend, the female artisan, the daughter of the nurse,
the neighbor, the female ascetic, the female craftsman, and one's own [wife] are proclaimed to be the assistants.
The essential nature and examples of these [types] are clear.
The specific varieties well-known in the *Kāmaśāstra*, such as the *padmanī*, *nicitrinī*, and so forth, should be understood.
Briefly, the heroine (*nāyikā*) is of three kinds: the youthful (*mugdhā*), the intermediate (*madhyā*), and the mature (*prauḍhā*).
A young girl (*mugdha*) is one whose youth has just dawned and in whom passion is overcome by modesty;
a maiden of middle age (*madhyama*) stands midway between modesty and passion as her youth has emerged;
and a mature woman (*prauḍhā*) is one whose bashfulness is subdued by love and whose youth is fully developed.
The examples are given in order.
An example of the *mugdha* (the innocent) type is as follows:

"O innocent one! Why do you reveal to me everything that should be hidden even from the mind? Am I some mere acquaintance of yours, my dear friend, that you should hide [your feelings] from me and suffer?"
When her friend spoke words of singular affection, saying, "May your attachment to King Rudradeva be hoped for; what might come of it?", the slender-limbed girl gave her reply out of modesty.
An example of the middle [stage] is as follows:

"Friends, behold! Having reached youth, which is the introductory prologue (*pūrvaraṅga*) to the playful movements of amorous sport, the splendor of the manifold dance of the god of love is reflected within the veil of her modesty. In this King of the Kākatīyas, the very course of the drama of erotic passion—vivid with the continuous flow of emotional states—triumphs in this girl of tremulous brows. (ViPrud 1.66)
An example of the mature [heroine] (*prauḍhā*) is as follows:

As the deer-eyed woman gazes playfully at King Rudra—naturally handsome, sweet with the various displays of graceful gestures rising up to meet her at that moment—the artistry of the flower-arrowed god (Kāma) triumphs in her youth; for, through the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the involuntary physical states (*sāttvika-bhāva*) arise simultaneously. (ViPrud 1.67)
Other varieties [of these] may be illustrated as they occur.
In a great poem where rasa predominates, the play of the qualities (guṇas) and ornaments (alaṃkāras) through the manifest word and meaning also becomes a source of delight to the heart.
Furthermore, the blossoming of those two, made beautiful by the sweetness of flowing nectar, triumphs as it follows the life-story of one of most meritorious fame.
This is a summary verse:
when there is a similarity between the qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), which are the causes of embellishment (*upaskāra*), they have fulfilled their purpose.
That very thing which serves as the substratum for the ornaments is, according to worldly convention, the object of ornamentation (*alaṅkārya*).
Therefore, since poetry alone is the substratum for the *guṇas* and *alaṅkāras*, it is poetry itself that is the object of adornment (*alaṅkārya*).
The statement that rasa and so forth are the objects of adornment means that they are primary, just as the self is the object of adornment by necklaces, anklets, and the like.
Because rasa and so forth constitute the very life of poetry, they possess the nature of the soul of poetry (*kāvyātmatā*).
In some cases, the rasa is predominant;
in some cases, the alaṅkāra is predominant;
and in some cases, the vastu is predominant.
(The passage beginning with "upaskārahetūnām" and ending with "atiślāghākāraṇam" is not found in many manuscripts, nor has it been commented upon by Kumārasvāmin Somapīthin.
An example of the predominance of rasa is as follows:

When youth had merely caused the breasts of the slender maiden to bud— her graceful charms having slightly sprouted and the loveliness of her body having put forth its shoots— the god of love both flowered and bore fruit.
These are the words of Pratāparudra, who looked with longing upon a certain young woman;
here, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) is manifested.
An example of the predominance of ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is as follows:
"While the fame of Pratāparudra wanders to the ends of the quarters, the slopes of the Lokāloka mountain are constantly marked by flowing moonstones. (ViPrud 1.70)

Here, the figure of speech *bhrāntimān* (the illusion of error) is suggested by the fact that the moonstones of the pavements and the slopes of the Lokāloka mountain constantly melt due to the perception of them as moonlight within the fame of Lord Rudra.
Even in its state of being suggested (*vyaṅgya*), the figure of speech certainly possesses primacy.
The predominance of the subject matter (*vastuprādhānyam*) is as follows:
"When Vīrarudra, who is honored by the three worlds, descended into the Kākati dynasty, the Lord of Serpents left the Ocean of Milk and returned to his own abode. (ViPrud 1.71)
Here, by the statement that "the lord of serpents has left the ocean of milk and reached his own home," it is suggested (vyañjita) that Hari is no longer present in the Milky Ocean.
By this, the fact (vastu) is suggested that Puruṣottama has descended into the Kākatiya lineage in the form of Pratāparudra.
Thus, there are three types of predominance of the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyaprādhānya).
The play of poetic qualities (guṇas) and ornaments (alaṅkāras) depends upon poetry;
and that poetry brings delight to the hearts of connoisseurs through the manifestation of sound, the manifestation of meaning, and the manifestation of both together.
[1.6.1 The Flashing Forth of Sound (śabdaspuraṇam):
What is called the "flashing forth of sound" is the ostentation of a mature composition.
That ostentation of composition which will be explained in the section on *ārabhaṭī* is this "flashing forth of sound."
For example:

"The pastimes of King Rudra—skilled in protecting the earth, causing agitation to the world of his enemies, with a sequence of movements difficult to behold, and with swords brandished high for the purpose of punishing the faction of base kṣatriyas—are like thunderbolts that shatter the mountain-like pride of wicked men roaring in their arrogance, as he exerts himself with unrestrained vigor. (ViPrud 1.72)
[1.6.2 Arthasphuraṇa] The manifestation of meaning (arthasphuraṇa) is held to be the unimpeded realization of the intended sense.
For example:

"Beholding the reflection of the enemy kings' folded palms upon his sword-blade expanded in battle, the wise imagine it to be the lotus that serves as the dwelling-place for the Goddess of Victory; I believe it is the lotus-seat obtained by Fate, who has come to fetch the life-breaths of the enemies, once they have been seized at the sacrifices by the smoke of the hero's prowess. (Viśvaprakāśa 1.74)
Beholding the reflection of the enemy kings’ folded palms upon his sword as it flourished in battle, the wise consider it the lotus-abode of the Goddess of Victory;
I believe that when the Creator arrived at this lotus-throne to seize the lives of his enemies for the sake of creating them anew in future battles, he was the Lord Pratāparudra, the hero.
[1.6.3 Both Manifesting] An example of both manifesting is as follows:
With the swelling roars of rising clouds, with the grandeur of herds of elephants like rain-clouds, and with those capable of besieging the mountain ranges, [the army] immediately manifested...

The preparations for the victorious expedition of King Calamartigaṇḍa brought about a gloomy day with the outpouring of tears from the wives of his enemies— tears that, like the broad slopes of clouds, foretold the onset of the monsoon.
The beauty of poetry arises from the manifestation of such word and meaning;
furthermore, through the description of the deeds of those of virtuous fame, both the word and the meaning bring joy to the hearts of connoisseurs.
Therefore, the hero alone holds primacy in poetry.
[1.6.4 The Preeminence of the Hero] Descriptions of the hero’s family lineage, conduct, fame, valor, learning, character,
and so forth are presented in such a way that he alone is highly esteemed by many. ViPrud_1.76 //
Alternatively, it is held that in some cases, after describing the many virtues of the adversary, there is a description of the leader’s excellence resulting from his victory over them. (ViPrud 1.77)
The examples in their respective order are as follows:

"He whose supreme ancestor is the Primordial Puruṣa, in whose lineage [there were] the Kākati kings, whose conduct was characterized by deeds that bring welfare to the world, and whose praise has surpassed the celestial tree, the heavenly cow, and the wish-fulfilling gem—he, this King Śrī Vīrarudra, the bearer of the burden of the universe, is victorious. (ViPrud 1.78)

That King Sevaṇa—who was like the sun to the darkness of the pride of rival kings dwelling in his realm, and who acted as the gatekeeper to the harem of the three worlds through the prowess of the bars of his arms—became terrified upon hearing the great sound of King Rudra’s war drums; agitated, he fled from the battle.
Such a description is not appropriate for a hero who is to be created [by the poet];
for him, it is more fitting to describe his lineage and other attributes in various ways for the sake of establishing his renown in the world.
However, when the hero is already established by himself, both types of description are possible.
Since his lineage, reputation, and so forth are well-known in the world, it is appropriate for poets to describe his victory over powerful adversaries.
Thus, there is a twofold division of the hero based on the distinction between those who are established by themselves and those who are to be produced [by the poet].
And therein—
[1.6.5 Classification of the Qualities of the Hero] Just as the fierce emotion (*raudra*) characterized by external agitation is described in the *dhīroddhata* hero,
so too is the erotic emotion (*śṛṅgāra*) produced by many manifestations of feeling described in the *dhīralalita* hero. (ViPrud 1.80)
Such a description is not desired in the case of the *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled) hero;
however, even in that case, the fulfillment of rasa through the action [of the plot] follows the appropriate sequence.
Likewise, the description of other sentiments such as the comic (hāsya) and so forth would possess weak effort and weak consequents when the leading character is a high-spirited hero (dhīrodātta).
Because it transcends all other leaders, the fact that the *dhīrodātta* (the noble-heroic) is its subject matter is the cause for the great praise accorded to these literary compositions.
Thus ends the section on the Hero in the *Pratāparudrayaśobhūṣaṇa*, a treatise on poetics composed by Śrī Vidyānātha.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Hero," in the commentary on the *Pratāparudrīya* named *Ratnāpaṇa*, composed by Kumārasvāmin Somapīthin, the younger brother of the jewel among scholars Peddayārya— whose learning is beneficial to all people— and the son of the venerable Mahopādhyāya Kolacalamallinātha Sūri, who has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of grammar, logic, and epistemology.
[II.1. Now, the section on poetry.
// Now, the definition of the nature of poetry.

[II.1 The Nature of Poetry] Those who know poetry understand poetry to consist of word and meaning endowed with poetic qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṃkāra*), free from defects (*doṣa*), and composed in prose, verse, or both. *ViPrud* 2.1.
[II.2 General Definition of Poetry] “Poetry consists of word and meaning that are free from defects, endowed with qualities, and possessed of ornaments”—this is the general definition of poetry.
Word and meaning are declared to be its body; the power of the suggested (vyaṅgya) is its life.
In that context, figures such as simile (upamā) and the like would function as ornaments, just like necklaces and other such decorations.
In that [poetry], qualities such as *śleṣa* (coalescence) reside like [the virtues of] heroism and the like;
therein, the *rītis* (styles) exist like innate dispositions, bringing about self-elevation.
Just as metrical feet (vṛtti) attain a beauty that brings about their intended purpose,
so too is the repose following the suitability of words considered to be like a bed (śayyā).
The various distinctions of the tasting of aesthetic flavor (rasa) exist like different types of cooking;
this collection [of factors] is renowned in the world as the perfection of poetry.
[II.3 The threefold nature of words as denoters, indicators, and suggestors:

The collection of words is threefold by virtue of being denoters (*vācaka*), indicators (*lakṣaka*), and suggestors (*vyañjaka*). Likewise, the collection of meanings is also threefold by virtue of being the expressed (*vācya*), the indicated (*lakṣya*), and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
The implied meaning (tātparyārtha) is also nothing other than the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha); it is not a separate entity. [II.4 The threefold nature of function]
There are three functions of words known as denotation (*abhidhā*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
[Regarding the fourfold nature of indication: figurative function (*gauṇavṛtti*) is also merely a variety of indication.
This is because [the secondary meaning] is rooted in the impossibility of the primary relationship.

Just as in the expression "The boy is fire," what is intended to be conveyed is the cognition of the boy as qualified by similarity to fire, so too in "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā," what is intended to be conveyed is the cognition of the bank as qualified by its connection with the Gaṅgā.
If the connection with the Gaṅgā were merely an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), then the purity and other qualities residing in the hamlet would not be established.
For this very reason, indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is twofold: based on similarity and based on a relationship.
That which is based on a relationship is further twofold: that which abandons its primary meaning (*jahadvācyā*) and that which does not abandon its primary meaning (*ajahadvācyā*).
That [metaphorical indication] is twofold: based on similarity, it is either superimposition (*sāropā*) or identification (*sādhyavasānā*).
Thus, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is fourfold. [The other three types, such as the Kāśikī and so forth, are different.]
The four *vṛttis*—namely, *kaiśikī*, *ārabhaṭī*, *sāttvatī*, and *bhāratī*—indicate the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) by depending upon literary composition.
As it is stated in the *Daśarūpaka*:
"Kaiśikī, ārabhaṭī, sāttvatī, and likewise bhāratī."
The four modes of operation (vṛtti) should be known as indicators of the location of the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Thus [it is said].

It is well known that even *racanā* (composition) serves to manifest *rasa*. Furthermore, it has been stated that composition consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*) incompatible with *rasa* constitutes a defect.
Specific styles (rīti), such as Vaidarbha and others, are not included within the modes of expression (vṛtti).
Among these, *abhidhā* (denotation) is the function of a word whose scope is a conventional meaning.
It is of two kinds: that preceded by conventional usage (rūḍhi) and that preceded by etymological derivation (yoga).
An example of that preceded by conventional usage is:
"By means of distinguished austerities and the auspicious conduct of the queen of the world, renowned among all people..."
By means of abundant fortunes, Varavīrarudra sustains the sovereignty of this world.
In this context, all words are conventional; those preceded by etymological derivation (*yoga*) are as follows:
"When King Rudra, the lord of men, delights all his subjects..."
"Bhūḥ" is so called because its meaning is manifest; "Vasumatī" because it possesses wealth; "Ratnagarbhā" because it contains jewels within; and "Sthirā" because it is firm.

In this context, terms such as *vasumatī* ("possessing wealth") and *ratnagarbhā* ("womb of jewels") are etymological (*yaugika*). Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is the operation of a word whereby, due to the impossibility of the literal meaning, a [secondary] sense related to it is superimposed.

Among these, *jahallakṣaṇā* (indication with abandonment of the primary sense) is as follows: "Having heard the sound of the drum of the victorious lord of the Kākatīyas, the feudatories' cities cry out loudly on all sides. (ViPrud 2.8)

In this case, the statement "the cities are crying out loudly" lacks logical connection (*ananvaya*) with the literal meaning, because it is impossible for insentient things to cry out; therefore, the people residing therein are indicated [by the term "cities"].
An example of *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication) is as follows:
Their crowns constantly adorn the footstool of their lord, Kākatīnātha, with the shimmering masses of light from glittering jewels.
Here, for the sake of establishing the poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*), the kings who constitute the substratum are indicated by means of their crowns.
An example of *sāropalakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication with superimposition) is as follows:
"The darkness resulting from the friction against the dark-blue rocks at the base of Mount Manthāna..."
That which shines upon the moon is called a *sāraṅga* (a deer);
yet I believe that here, the moon expands while bearing upon its breast the boar marked with the seal of King Vīrarudra’s glory, having been utterly defeated by it.
Here, the nature of a boar is superimposed upon the deer, which is the form of the moon’s spot.
Superimposition (*āropa*) is the apprehension of identity between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*), both of which are explicitly mentioned.
Apprehension of identity through the swallowing up of the object (*viṣayanigaraṇa*) is determination (*adhyavasāya*).
[II.12 Definition of Sādhyavasāna-lakṣaṇā] An example of *sādhyavasāna-lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication based on identification) is as follows:
"This moon arises from the ocean that is the Kākatiya dynasty."
By him, upon his rising, the splendor of the blue water-lily was brought forth.
Here, Pratāparudra is identified as the moon;
thus, in the phrase "of the ocean of the Kākatīya dynasty," there is a superimposition (adhyāropa).

[II.13 Suggestion (vyañjanā)] Now, as for suggestion (*vyañjanā*): when word-meanings are already connected, the function of a word directed toward another meaning for the sake of embellishing the sentence-meaning is the function of suggestion (*vyañjanāvṛtti*).
It is threefold, based on the power of the word, the meaning, or both. [II.14 Suggestion based on the power of the word (śabdaśaktimūlavyañjanā):
Among these, that which is based on the power of the word is as follows:
The armies of the Lord of the Kākatīyas, surging with agitation on all sides,
turn the ocean of the enemy forces into one rich with rising headless trunks.

In this context, although the meanings of the words *vāhinī*, *sarvatomukha*, and *kabandha* are restricted by the context and other factors to signify "an army," "pervading everywhere," and "a headless trunk" respectively, the cognition of "river water" arises from the power of the word itself; this is the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
Denotation (*abhidhā*), which terminates in the contextual meaning, is not capable of producing the cognition of a non-contextual meaning.
Even for a meaning that is not part of the primary context, because it is intended by the speaker for the sake of embellishing the sentence-meaning,
and since that [meaning] is not perceived through any other means, a distinct function of the word called *vyañjanā* (suggestion) is postulated.
In this case, the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not possible.
Because there is no impossibility regarding what is to be expressed,
there is no split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) here despite the communication of meaning through two operations;
for worldly sentences are dependent upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
An example of suggestion (vyañjanā) rooted in the power of the meaning (arthaśaktimūla) is as follows:
"Having heard of the marriage festival of the Kākatīya lord, the kings, with their faces cast down, scratched the footstool with their big toes. (ViPrud 2.13)

Here, by the power of the meaning (*artha-śakti*), it is suggested that the kings are despondent. Furthermore, there is no suspicion of inference (*anumāna*) regarding suggestion based on the power of the meaning,
because there is no necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) and the suggester (*vyañjaka*).
Since effects such as a bowed face have multiple causes,
the cognition of a specific cause arises from the word itself, aided by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
Furthermore, the cognition of various implied meanings (*vyaṅgyārtha*) from a single manifestor occurs in accordance with the speaker's intention.
This perception of multiple suggested meanings is contrary to the process of inference; nor is it the function of denotation (*abhidhā*),
for its scope is limited to that which is conventionally established— such is the extent of this analysis.
An example based on both powers (śabda-śakti and artha-śakti) is as follows:
"Having conquered the cities of his enemies, with all auspicious marks shining upon his form, this crest-jewel of kings shines forth—Rudradeva, the lord of the world. (ViPrud 2.14)

Here, the phrase "vijitāripuraḥ" (having conquered the cities of his enemies) is based on the power of meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*), while "vilasatsarvamaṅgalo rājamauliḥ" (the crest-jewel of kings, radiant with all auspiciousness) is based on the power of sound (*śabdaśaktimūla*); thus, there is a basis in both powers.
Here, there is a suggestion (*dhvani*) of the poetic figure of simile (*upamālaṃkāra*) between Pratāparudra and Śaṅkara.
Now, the nature of Kaiśikī and the others is defined:
Kaiśikī is considered to be a composition of meaning that is exceedingly delicate;
Ārabhaṭī is known as a style of composition whose meaning is exceedingly violent. (ViPrud 2.15)
The *bhāratī* style is held to be one whose composition of meaning is slightly soft;
the *sāttvatī* style is held to be one whose composition of meaning is slightly mature.
In that regard,
the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the pathetic (*karuṇa*) are considered to possess extreme delicacy;
the furious (*raudra*) and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) are proclaimed to possess extreme intensity.
The comic, the tranquil, and the marvelous are proclaimed to be somewhat delicate;
the heroic and the fearful are declared to be slightly mature.

Where the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiments are described with an extremely tender composition, there is the *kaiśikī* style; where the *raudra* (furious) and *bībhatsa* (disgusting) sentiments are presented with an extremely forceful composition, there is the *ārabhaṭī* style; and where the *hāsya* (comic), *śānta* (peaceful), and *adbhuta* (wonderful) sentiments—which are neither too delicate nor too coarse—are woven together with a composition that is neither too delicate nor too coarse, there is the *bhāratī* style.

Where the heroic (*vīra*) and the terrible (*bhayānaka*) sentiments are not overly developed, and are carried out through a composition that is not overly elaborate, there the *sāttvatī* style is employed.
As for the *kaiśikī* style, for example:
[The moon of the Kākatīya lineage has conquered the amorous play of Madana...]

For the women who longed to gaze at the king with unblinking eyes, the splendor of an archway, dark as a garland of water-lilies, was instantly fashioned by their side-long glances reaching toward the heavens.
[II.19 Example of Ārabhaṭī] Ārabhaṭī is as follows:—
The splashes of blood spat out from the heads of enemies severed by the blows of swords—

In the battle, the fierce fire of King Calamartigaṇḍa’s wrath blazed with masses of sparks produced by the clashing of formidable weapons, and with thick, glowing embers resembling lumps of congealed blood, flesh, and bone.
[II.20 Example of Bhāratī:
As for Bhāratī—for example: "The loftiness is something quite different, great indeed..."
I know that this majesty is something quite extraordinary,

his path toward power and fame is altogether unique, and the renown of King Rudra’s arms is truly unprecedented; indeed, everything about him is new, as if there were no one else who fashioned such a being.
By whom, how much, of what kind, or where was this causal complex (sāmagrī) fashioned by the Four-faced One?
[II.21 Example of Sāttvatī:
Sāttvatī is as follows:
Having heard from afar the victorious [trumpets] of Vīrarudra, whose splendor spreads throughout the universe—

The enemy kings, their ears afflicted by the fever of the sound of the war-drums marking the start of the expedition, fled to the mountains; entering the vast forest with their hair snagged on thorns, they implore the trees, mistaking them for rival monarchs: "Save us! Release us! 2.22.
The Madhyamārabhaṭī and likewise the Madhyamakaiśikī are the other two modes;
both of these modes are considered common to all sentiments.
The essential nature of these two is as follows:
Madhyamakaiśikī has a composition that is not overly elaborate, even when the subject matter is trivial. (ViPrud 2.24ab)
In the cases of the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiments, which are exceedingly delicate, a slight degree of maturity [in style] is not considered a fault;
however, an excessively mature composition is not desired, as it results in the defect of using discordant phonemes and forms.
The *madhyamārabhaṭī* style, even when dealing with a mature subject matter, does not follow an excessively soft sequence.
Even in the case of the *raudra* (furious) and *bībhatsa* (disgusting) sentiments, a slightly soft composition is not considered a defect;
however, an excessively soft arrangement is contradictory [to these sentiments].
[II.22 Madhyamakaiśikī]
An example of Madhyamakaiśikī is as follows:
"Even though the great festival is at hand, how can you go away on a journey from here? Fie, fie upon this rashness! Who desires our separation, or what fate [is behind it]?"
O King of the Kākatīyas, having thus awakened from the thought that the departure of her beloved had been averted by a dream, the women among your enemies fall into a swoon.
An example of the *madhyamārabhaṭī* style is as follows:
"In battle, the earth was made by the brave warriors of Andhra to be strewn with flesh and bones, with rivers of flowing blood, and mired in fat. (ViPrud 2.26)
In this same manner, examples should be understood for the other sentiments as well.

The distinction between the Vaidarbhī and other *rītis* lies in their reliance on verbal qualities (*śabda-guṇa*) and their independence from specific meanings, as they concern themselves solely with the smoothness or maturity of the composition itself. "Excessive smoothness" (*atisaumyatva*) refers to a composition consisting of a stringing together of uncombined, soft syllables;
"excessive maturity" (*atiprauḍhatva*) refers to a composition characterized by harsh syllables and a rugged arrangement.
In compositions with soft syllables joined together, there is a slight softness; in compositions with harsh syllables and loose construction, there is a slight maturity.
The Rītis: Now, the nature of the Rītis and their illustrations. A Rīti is considered to be a particular arrangement (*saṃghaṭanā*) of words conjoined with the Guṇas.
It is threefold: Vaidarbhī,
Gauḍī, and Pāñcālī.
The Vaidarbha style is held to be free from harshness of construction, devoid of rigidity in sound, and characterized by compounds that are not excessively long. (ViPrud 2.27)
For example:
"The women of the quarters, having made his virtues their ear-ornaments, perform the anointing of the sandalwood paste of the fame of the Kākatiya lord. (ViPrud 2.28)
Or as it is said:
"While the lord of men, the moon of the Kākatiya lineage, reigns— having gratified the entire world through the play of his virtues in bestowing gifts— "
In the enumeration of the celestial trees and during the discourse on the wish-fulfilling cow,
this assembly of earth-dwellers lost all interest.
The Gauḍīya style is held to be endowed with the qualities of vigor (ojas) and beauty (kānti);
for example:
"He who has shattered the circle of his enemies with the staff-like arms of his most fierce [strength]..."
The lord of Andhra, being powerful, bears the heavy yoke of the earth.
Or for example:

"The vast dust from the vanguard, which was expert at instilling fear in the sun as it seemed to fall away due to the delusion that it was Rāhu— arising from the pride of the enemies' crowns being shattered by the staff-like arms raised aloft like swords— "

The seat of the judicial authority of the Lord of Andhra was such that the moon-like faces of the celestial nymphs were surrounded by clusters of stars consisting of the streams of pearls emerging from the frontal globes of elephants split open by his arrows.
[II.2.3 Pāñcālī] The Pāñcālī style is of a dual nature, consisting of both the Vaidarbhī and the Gauḍī styles.
For example:
When the mass of dust from the earth, raised by the victorious expedition of King Kākativīrarudra— the conqueror— filled the sky intensely, it caused a great delusion regarding the directions.
The river of mortals has become a vast expanse with wide banks, a long celestial pool;
and the river of Gautama, exceedingly deep and hidden, acts as the Ganges of the netherworld.
And as it is said:
"O King Caṇḍanṛpa, it is only fitting that your sword-serpent constantly finds satisfaction with the lives of your enemies."
But this is truly marvelous:
that by drinking the milk of the fame of rival kings, it increases the white radiance of the nectar of your glory— the Fortune of your renown— which fills the three worlds.
Now, as for "bed":
that supreme mutual friendliness among the steps is called the "bed."
For example:
Of the donor, that jewel who ornaments the Kākati dynasty, whose profound majesty has surpassed the virtues of the wish-fulfilling tree through the praise of his boundless liberality...
Bearing the fragrance of the autumnal moonlight, he possesses fame that is generally as sweet as the pallor resting upon the expansive cheeks of the wives of his vassal lords.
In this context, "bed" (śayyā) refers to the conformity of the words [to one another], because the bond cannot tolerate the transposition of words.
Now, regarding the "ripenings" (*pāka*), there are those such as the ripening of grapes and so forth;
however, the ripening that consists in the profundity of meaning is of two kinds, both of which are heart-pleasing.
The grape-ripening and the coconut-ripening [types of yoga] have clearly distinct internal characteristics.
The intrinsic nature and the illustration are given in their respective order:
"The ripening of the grape is said to be that in which the flavor vibrates both externally and internally."
For example:
"Smiling with love, sweet with the fragrance of gentle smiles, charmingly dazed by a touch of bashfulness, and overflowing with the surging waves of the essence of affection..."
The fair-eyed woman casts her sidelong glances all around King Rudra— glances that create thousands of mind-born Cupids and have already formed many heaps.
That is the "cooking of the coconut" (nārikelapāka), in which the emergence of flavor remains hidden within.
For example:

Having attained youth, which is the introductory prologue to the playful grace of amorous dalliance, she possesses the splendor of the manifold dance of the arts of love, reflected within the inner curtain of her modesty.

"Friends, behold! In this king of the Kākatīyas, there triumphs a certain extraordinary sequence of erotic drama, radiant with the persistence of her inner emotion, in this girl with tremulous brows."
In this case, there is no immediate comprehension of the meaning;
the same should be understood regarding the perception of a *vastu* (fact) or an *alaṃkāra* (ornament).
Other types of cooking, such as with honey, milk, and so forth, should be inferred according to what is possible.
The varieties of poetry:
Now, regarding the varieties of poetry,
poetry is of three kinds based on the predominance or non-predominance of the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), and by its being indistinct.
When the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is predominant, the poetry is designated as the highest type, *dhvani*. When it is not predominant, it is celebrated as the middle type, *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*.
When the suggested meaning is indistinct, the poetry is celebrated as the lowest type, *citra*.
An example of *dhvani* (suggested meaning): "O Lord, why now do you make the mountains of our lineage low? Why do you make the oceans deep?"
"Why do you treat these petty lords of the directions as such?"—
having thus silenced all the chatter of his attendants,
the King Śrī Vīrarudra, the sole abode of virtue, was created by the Lotus-born Brahmā as one who seeks righteousness.

Here, the towering height of Pratāparudra surpassing the principal mountain ranges (kulaśaila), his profundity exceeding the ocean, and his sovereignty surpassing that of the world-protectors (lokapāla) are suggested.

Likewise, it is further implied that the majestic power of the Kākatīya creation is entirely unique, transcending the creative efforts of the principal mountains, the oceans, and the world-protectors.
An example of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (where the suggested meaning is subordinated) is as follows:

While King Vīrarudra— the protector of the universe, who occupies the throne and has filled the interior of all quarters with the pervasive power of his ever-expanding majesty— is seated upon the royal seat;...
Various gestures were displayed by the excellent kings who had arrived at the assembly hall, by which the gaze of this lord of the Kākatiyas was made moist with compassion.

Here, before the great king Pratāparudradeva, who has attained the great festival of his coronation, the various gestures of the kings seeking refuge— such as their repeated prostrations and words of such wretchedness— are shown; since these are not superior to the expressed meaning (vācya), there is the state of "subordinated suggestion" (guṇībhūtavyaṅgyatā).

The *citra* (the striking) is of three kinds: striking in sound (*śabdacitra*), striking in meaning (*arthacitra*), and striking in both (*ubhayacitra*). Among these, an example of striking in sound is as follows:

Skilled in protecting the earth, having warded off the disturbances of the world, their progress difficult to behold, with swords raised high for the task of disciplining the faction of base kṣatriyas—
[these were the two] fierce arms of King Rudra as he exerted himself with unrestrained vigor.
His pastimes are like thunderbolts that shatter the mountain of the pride of roaring wicked men.
An example of variety in meaning (*arthacitra*) is as follows:
"Seeing the reflection of the enemy kings' folded palms upon his sword-blade expanded for battle, the wise consider it to be the lotus of the face of Victory."
I believe that the Creator, having stripped Vīrapāla of his arms at the sacrifices,
has taken them to serve as the sacrificial post for the sacrifice of his enemies' lives.
Seeing the reflection of the enemy kings' folded palms in his sword as it flourished in battle, the wise consider it the lotus-abode of the Goddess of Victory;
I believe that in future battles, the Lord Pratāparudra, the hero, will again take up [the world] within it.
[He went] to the lotus-throne of the Creator who has departed for the sake of creating the lives of his enemies.

[II.5.6 Distinctive Sounds] // Now, the distinctive sounds.
Now, the specific varieties of *dhvani* are being defined.

Here, based on whether *dhvani* is rooted in indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or expression (*abhidhā*), there are first two divisions known as "that whose expressed meaning is not intended" (*avivakṣitavācya*) and "that whose expressed meaning is intended but has another purpose" (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*). Of these, the former—being twofold as "that whose expressed meaning is transferred to another sense" (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*) and "that whose expressed meaning is completely set aside" (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*)—is further divided into two types each according to whether it resides in a sentence or in a word; thus, it constitutes four varieties.

The *vivakṣitānyaparavācya* (where the expressed meaning is intended but not primary) has two divisions based on whether the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) involves a perceptible sequence (*saṃlakṣyakrama*) or an imperceptible sequence (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*).

Within the *saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya* rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*), there is a fourfold division based on its nature as either a fact (*vastu*) or an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), and further according to whether it resides in a sentence (*vākya*) or a word (*pada*).

Regarding the *saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya* rooted in the power of meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*), there is a threefold division based on whether the meaning is inherently possible (*svataḥsaṃbhavitva*), established through the bold assertion of the poet (*kaviprauḍhoktisiddhatva*), or established through the assertion of a character created by the poet (*kavinibaddhoktisiddhatva*).
When the threefold [suggestion] is divided into two types based on whether it takes the form of a matter (*vastu*) or an ornament (*alaṃkāra*), there are six types.
When these six types are further divided into two based on whether they function as the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) or the suggester (*vyañjaka*), there are twelve types.

When these twelve types are again divided into three—according to whether they reside in a literary composition (*prabandha*), a sentence (*vākya*), or a word (*pada*)—there are thirty-six varieties of *dhvani* based on resonance (*anuraṇana*) whose root is the power of meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*).
Or, that which is based on both powers (word and meaning) is of only one kind, as it resides in the sentence.
Thus, there are forty-one varieties of *dhvani* with suggestible meaning where the sequence [of suggestion] is perceptible (*saṃlakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*).

*Dhvani* with suggestible meaning where the sequence is imperceptible (*asaṃlakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*), such as *rasa* and so forth, is of six kinds, residing respectively in the literary composition (*prabandha*), the sentence (*vākya*), the word (*pada*), a portion of a word (*padaikadeśa*), the phonetic arrangement (*racanā*), and the individual phonemes (*varṇa*).
Thus, there are forty-seven varieties of *dhvani* with the expressed meaning intended but subordinate (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*).
Together with the four varieties of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*), there are initially fifty-one pure (*śuddha*) varieties of *dhvani*.
When each one of these is combined with each of the others, there are fifty-one varieties for the first variety.

The second has fifty divisions; the third has forty-nine divisions. Following this sequence, by the successive elimination of one division at a time, there are one thousand three hundred and twenty-six (1,326) [divisions].
The mixed varieties:

the variety belonging to the *avivakṣitavācya* (where the expressed meaning is not intended) in its connection with the *vivakṣitānyaparavācya* (where the expressed meaning is intended but has another purpose) is included within that very [latter] category; the variety belonging to the *vivakṣitānyaparavācya* in its connection with the *avivakṣitavācya* is not distinct from it.

By this same sequence, even the variety of *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact) in its connection with *alaṃkāradhvani* (suggestion of a figure) is not distinct from the *alaṃkāradhvani* in its connection with *vastudhvani*; thus, in the connection of each preceding [type] with each succeeding one—
The reduction by one for each individual variation should be understood.
Furthermore, when that same mixture is joined again in four ways— by a combination (*saṃkara*) of three forms and by a commixture (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of one form—
there are five thousand three hundred and four (5,304) variations.
The pure [types] are four hundred and five; the mixed are six hundred and thirty-two;
those resulting from combination and commixture are designated as four thousand three hundred and fifty.
In that regard,

In this regard, a mere indication is given by way of example.
An instance of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*) because it has been transferred to another meaning (*arthāntarasaṃkramita*) is as follows:
"You are our superiors; why do you desire such loftiness?"
Thus, all the rival kings bowed down before Pratāparudra.

In this context, the phrase "our own" (*āsmākāḥ*)—meaning "you who belong to us who are in such a state of constant wretchedness"—is an example of *saṃkramitavivakṣitavācya* (where the literal meaning is transferred to another sense).
An example of *atyantatiraskṛtavācya* (where the literal meaning is completely set aside) is as follows:
"Those which have smeared the sky with clarity and filled all the quarters with whiteness..."
The fair and illustrious [palaces] of the Lord of the Kākatīyas dwell there, filled with glory.
Here, in the phrase "the sky smeared with clarity," there is an instance of *atyantatiraskṛtavācyatva* (complete supersession of the literal meaning).
Following this very same sequence, examples may also be cited as occurring within a sentence.
Now, an example of suggestion of a fact (*vastu-dhvani*) by means of a fact (*vastu*), based on the power of the sense (*artha-śakti-mūla*), is as follows:
The wives of the enemies of the Kākatīyas long for years without seasons, months without fortnights, lunar days without nights.
In this context, because the seasons and so forth are excitants of desire, it is understood that their absence is longed for by the wives of the enemies;
thereby, the fact of their separation from their beloveds is suggested.
Through this, there is a superiority over the literal meaning (vācya) that all the enemies of Pratāparudra have been slain.
Likewise, the wives of enemies, distressed by separation from their beloveds, first desire the absence of seasons out of hope for life for a few years;
subsequently, unable even to pass those, they strive to sustain their lives for a few months and desire the destruction of the moonlit fortnights;
and finally, failing even to dispel the months, they long for the non-creation of nights during certain lunar days out of hope for life—thus, many things are suggested by a single fact.
An example of suggestion through the object (*vastu-dhvani*) as an ornament (*alaṅkāra-dhvani*) is as follows:

"Having seen the fame of King Kākati Vīrarudra pervading the world, Śambhu desires to dwell here; the Lord of Lakṣmī longs to lie down; the host of celestial ascetics runs to bathe; the oceans strive to swell; and even the sky, with playful grace, slowly endeavors to touch [the earth]. (ViPrud 2.47)
Here, the poetic figure *bhrāntimān* (the illusion of error) is manifested, such as Hara’s delusion that [the mountain] is Kailāsa, and Hari’s delusion that it is the Ocean of Milk, and so forth.
An instance of suggestion of a fact (*vastudhvani*) through ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is as follows:
"In battle, the sword of Pratāparudra, its splendor instantly reddened by the rising blood, assumes the manifestations of the sidelong glances of Kālī, who is flushed with rage. (ViPrud 2.48)
Here, by means of the figure of speech *nidarśanā* (illustration) in the phrase "he leaned here," the fact that the destruction of all enemies was accomplished in an instant is suggested.
An example of *alaṅkāra-dhvani* (suggestion of a poetic figure) through a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is as follows:
"When the white lotus of the fame of the Lord of the Kākatīyas has blossomed, the sky, dark as a *tamāla* tree, bears the play of bees. (ViPrud 2.49)

Here, by means of the figure of speech *nidarśanā* (poetic illustration)—in which the sky bears the play of bees upon the lotus of fame—the figure of *adhika* (the excessive) is suggested, characterized by a lack of proportionality between the locus (*āśraya*) and that which rests upon it (*āśrayin*).
Through the depiction of the similarity between the sky and the bees, the vastness of the locus, the lotus of fame, and the smallness of the sky are perceived.
In these examples, the basis is the power of the meaning established by itself (*svataḥ-siddhārtha-śakti-mūlatva*).
Now, an example of suggestion based on a fact (*vastudhvani*) rooted in the power of the meaning established by the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a poet:

"Having repeatedly heard [the news] from throngs of bards moving along the path of the ears under the guise of the holes made by the arrows of Kārttikeya while he was practicing in the training ground..."
The mountain Kauñca stands with its limbs motionless from great wonder at the fame of the Lord of the Kākatīyas, which is eternally sung and honored by the world.
Here, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is that the fame of Pratāparudra causes wonder even to the immobile beings.
An example of suggestion through the object (*vastu-dhvani*) as an ornament (*alaṃkāra-dhvani*) is as follows:
"Seeing the heroic Rudra-warriors surrounded by the Goddess of Victory in battle, the thorny trees in the forest pull the hair of their enemies' wives. (ViPrud 2.51)

Here, upon seeing the heroic soldiers of Rudra embraced by the Goddess of Victory (*jayalakṣmī*), the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is suggested that the thorny trees, as if filled with passion, seem to grasp the hair of the wives of the enemies.
An example of the suggestion of a fact (*vastudhvani*) by means of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is as follows:
"Shame departs along with her friends from the bride as she becomes relaxed..."
As if out of fear of being seized by her husband, she remained with her beloved, who was charming even while accompanied by his bird.
Shame departs along with her friends from the bride, whose pride has slackened, as if out of fear of being seized, when her beloved, the captivator of the heart, draws near.
Here, by means of poetic fancy (utprekṣā), the actual fact in the form of an embrace is suggested.
An example of *alaṅkāra-dhvani* (suggestion through poetic figure) by means of a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is as follows:
"The forest, as if refusing to grant protection to the enemies of the Lord of the Kākatīyas who are begging for safety, seems to reject it by the trembling of the tips of its branches. (ViPrud 2.53)

Here, by means of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that "it does not indeed accept," there is suggested another poetic fancy that even the forest fears to provide protection for the enemies of Pratāparudra.
