"O Lord of Men, whether it be right or wrong, grant protection to the Moon;
for you have commanded the firebrands of your side-long glances to reduce him to ashes."

Here, a noble lady (āryā), distressed by separation and unable to endure the moonlight, turns the moon into ink with a spark of a sidelong glance ignited by anger; by this fact—that "he [the moon] must be protected"—the further matter is suggested: "She will no longer live beyond this point, therefore you must come right now."
An example of suggestion through a poetic figure (*alaṅkāradhvani*) by means of a literal object (*vastu*) is as follows:
"Who are you, wandering about with all your limbs so radiant? Surely it is the fame of Vīrarudra. What is this divine body of yours that shines forth in my presence?"

"My dear friend, his majesty [Pratāparudra] has completely concealed [the sun] with shimmering night-lotuses and day-lotuses; thus your true nature has been revealed by you who possess the forms of the moon and the sun. Welcome to you both! Indeed, I have become a mountain devoid of darkness.
Here, because the majesty of Pratāparudra’s fame and his actual majesty are perceived as being similar to the moon and the sun, a simile (*upamā*) is suggested.
An example of suggestion through ornament (*alaṅkāradhvani*) by means of an ornament is as follows:
"O friend, the intense pride of the young woman, though it had mounted so high, now recedes as if fearing the onset of the king’s arrival.
(ViPrud 2.56)
(Observe, friends! Though her intense pride was so firmly rooted, it now retreats as if out of fear born from the agitation of meeting the king.)

Here, by means of poetic fancy (utprekṣā), the figure of speech known as "causation without a cause" (vibhāvanā) is suggested, wherein the mind of the proud woman is shown to be serene even without her making a request to her beloved.
An instance of suggestion based on a fact (*vastudhvani*) through ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is as follows:
"O Lord, having failed to obtain an opportunity for service while you are surrounded by your beloved, the Night, as if serving your fame, has become pale throughout her entire body. (ViPrud 2.57)
Here, by means of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) "as if serving," the reality consisting of her being entirely worthy of acceptance and so forth is suggested.
In this manner, examples occurring in continuous compositions and so forth should be understood according to their respective possibilities;
they are not stated here for fear of prolixity.
Now, there is suggestion (dhvani) based on the power of words (śabdaśaktimūla). It is of two kinds, according to whether it pertains to a matter of fact (vastu) or a poetic figure (alaṃkāra).
Thus it has been said:
“Where either an ornament or a mere fact appears as the primary element through the power of words, that [suggested meaning] is to be known as arising from the power of words; it is of two kinds.”
Thus [ends the section on *alaṅkāradhvani*].
Among these, an example of *alaṅkāradhvani* (suggestion of poetic ornament) is as follows:
"This is the truth: you two are indeed equal in appearance.
Why then is no talk of malice seen between you? This is truly a marvel. (ViPrud 2.58)
"This king is indeed truthful, and you are truly dark-complexioned; the union of these two is fitting.
Yet, why is the talk of evening not seen? This is indeed a marvel!"
In this context, through the power of the situation, the words *śyāmā* and *rāja*, which denote a beloved woman and a king respectively, suggest the simile of the night and the moon.
An example of suggestion based on a fact (*vastudhvani*) is as follows:
"O lords of men, scorched by dwelling in the wilderness, listen to what is beneficial! Now, perform service at the feet of the King. (ViPrud 2.59)
Here, through the power of the words "service to the king’s feet," the understanding of the subject at hand, Pratāparudra, arises from the context.
By this, the underlying matter (*vastu*) is suggested: "Service should be rendered to Pratāparudra; what is the use of dwelling in the forest while suffering from distress?"
An example of suggestion based on both powers (*ubhayaśaktimūladhvani*) is as follows:
"This victor, whose wondrous weapons are unfolding from his pillar-like arms—let all the kings abandon the display of their own partisan factions. (ViPrud 2.60)
In this context, let the kings abandon their display of partisan zeal; that "this one is victorious" is based on the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūlatā*),
while "he whose wondrous weapon causes the paralysis of [their] pillar-like arms" is based on the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktimūlatā*).
The suggestion of rasa and so forth is one in which the sequence [of its manifestation] is imperceptible (*asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*).
Thus it has been stated in the *Śṛṅgāratilaka*:
"Rasa, emotion (*bhāva*), their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), the subsidence of emotion (*bhāvaśānti*), and so forth, are without sequence (*akrama*)."
Distinct from rasa and the other ornaments, it exists as that which is to be ornamented.
Thus [it is said].
An illustration of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) and the emotional state (bhāva) will appear in the section on rasa, within the detailed exposition defining their essential nature.
The eightfold *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (poetry of subordinated suggestion) is now defined.
*Guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* is intermediate poetry and is of eight types.
Thus it has been stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*:
“Not hidden (agūḍha), being a subordinate element of another [figure], being a subordinate factor for the establishment of the expressed meaning (vācyasiddhyaṅga), being indistinct (asphuṭa),
having equal prominence with the doubtful (saṃdigdhatulyaprādhānya), suggested by intonation (kākvākṣipta), and being unpleasant (asundara).”
Thus:

[II.5.22 *Agūḍha* (Unconcealed)] Because it is precisely the concealed that produces aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), like the jar-like breasts of a passionate woman, poetry with unconcealed suggested meaning (*agūḍhavyaṅgya*) is middling poetry.
For example:
"If the height of the mountain is described, the lowly ones become indignant; if the depth of the oceans is praised, they are agitated when their depths are measured.
Therefore, O Lord Śrī Vīrarudra, I am afraid to describe you—unless, indeed, I am Agastya born, standing by your side, O jewel-mountain of the gems of virtue. (ViPrud 2.61)
Here, by the statement "I am born as Agastya and remain [here]," the suggested meaning— that he does not fear the oceans or mountains— is unhidden (agūḍha).

[II.5.23 Subordinate element of another: That which is a subordinate element of another— wherein, for instance, one rasa or the like is a subordinate element of another rasa or the like— that too is indeed *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (poetry of subordinated suggestion).
For example:

"O Lord of the Earth, Kākatiya! [His state was] one where shame had vanished, pride cast aside, where hoarseness of voice arose, perspiration appeared, intense trembling of the limbs occurred, fainting set in, tears flowed, and a total dissolution of self was produced."
Agitated by passion, kings flee to solitary mountain caves, embraced by fear.
In this case, the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) functions as a subordinate element to the sentiment of fear (bhayarasāṅgatva).
[II.5.24] An example of that which is a subordinate element for the establishment of the expressed meaning (vācyasiddhyaṅga) is as follows:
The formidable, fresh cloud-like sword of the Lord of Kākatīya extinguishes the fierce fire of his enemies' prowess with its stream [of blood].
Here, a stream of water is suggested;
and since that suggestion serves to establish the expressed metaphor (rūpaka) in the phrase "the sword-blade is a fresh cloud," this is an instance of subordinated suggestion (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya).
[II.5.25 *Asphuṭam* (Unclear)] An example of the unclear (*asphuṭa*) is as follows:
"The majesty of Vīrarudra’s sword is some indescribable, unrestrained thing."
He who, having drunk the river of his enemies' blood, brought forth the Ganges of his own fame.
Here, through the demonstration of the superiority of Kṛpaṇa over Jahnu, the figure of speech *vyatireka* (contrast) is perceived as being most clearly manifest.
[II.5.26 Ambiguous Predominance] An example of ambiguous predominance is as follows:
"The glance of King Kākatīya, rippling with affection..."
It rested upon her two high breasts like a garland of white water-lilies.
Here, there is a doubt as to whether the sentence comes to rest in the desire for an embrace, or rather in the mere sight of the circle of her breasts.
[II.5.27 Equal Prominence (tulyaprādhānyam): An example of equal prominence is as follows:
"O kings, serve the lotus-feet of Pratāparudra!"
Otherwise, his mind, which is so serene, becomes turbid.

In this case, if service at the feet of Pratāparudra is abandoned, then residence in cities becomes difficult to obtain; thus, there is an equal prominence of both the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha) and the expressed meaning (vācya).
[II.5.28 *Anusaṃdhāna*] An example of the unattractive (*asundara*) is as follows:
"Having heard the news of the sight of the king from the women of the palace..."
The face of the bride, brought low by her elders, was darkened.
(Hearing of the joy of seeing the king from the women of Ekaśilā, the face of the bride, though restrained by her elders, turned dark with longing.)
In this case, for the bride who perceives joy at the occasion of seeing the king, the explicit meaning—that her face is dark—is indeed beautiful;
however, the suggested meaning—that "I did not go to see the king because I was restrained by my elders"—is not beautiful.
[II.5.28 *Kāvākṣiptam*]:
Where another meaning is suggested by means of intonation (*kāku*), that too is indeed *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (where the suggested sense is subordinate).
For example:
"Dear friend, tell me: between the earth, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī, whom does the king—who is distinguished by his virtues—hold in the highest esteem? (ViPrud 2.68)
"Dear friend, tell me: is the earth, fortune, or eloquence superior to me?
For this lord of men, who discerns excellence, holds her in high esteem."
Here, by the employment of a plaintive intonation (*kāku*) in the phrase "the earth is not greater than me," the fact that it is not greater is suggested.
Poetry, however, is diverse and manifold due to the variety of its figures of sound and sense;
its detailed elaboration will also become clear in the section on poetic figures (alaṅkāra).
An exposition on the compositions of great epics (*mahākāvya*), minor epics (*upakāvya*), and so forth.
Now, literary compositions such as the *mahākāvya* are defined:
the description of cities, oceans, mountains, seasons, and the rising of the moon and sun;
as well as excursions to gardens, sporting in waters, drinking honeyed wine, and festivals of love. (ViPrud 2.69)
Separation, marriage, and the description of the prince’s birth;
the mission of the messenger, the departure, the sacrifice, and the hero’s triumph. (ViPrud 2.70)
That work in which these [qualities] are described is called a Mahākāvya;
it is held that among these eighteen [features], it may even be desired if some are lacking.
That is of three kinds:
consisting of prose, consisting of verse, and consisting of both.
A prose composition (*gadya*) is a collection of words without metrical feet;
verse (*padya*) consists of four feet.
An example of prose poetry (*gadyakāvya*) is the *Kādambarī* and similar works.
Padyakāvya consists of works such as the *Raghuvaṃśa*; that which is proclaimed as *upakāvya* is also [included], even if it lacks the structure of formal cantos (*asargabandha*).
The *asargabandha* includes works such as the *Sūryaśataka*. Poetry (*kāvyam*) consisting of both prose and verse is designated as *campū*.
The distinguishing features [of these] are the *vaktra*, the *aparavaktra*, and the presence of *ucchvāsa* sections. (ViPrud 2.73)

That in which specific metrical forms named Vaktra and Aparavaktra are described by those learned in poetry is considered an *ākhyāyikā* (prose narrative); that which is divided by *ucchvāsa*s is an *ākhyāyikā*, such as the *Harṣacarita* and others.

II.7 Examination of Minor Continuities.
Now, the minor compositions (*kṣudra-prabandha*) are defined. [Example:
Whatever the *tāla* may be, it consists of both prose and verse. (ViPrud 2.74)
Victorious is that which begins with *jayati*, variegated by the insertion of *mālinī* and other meters; its illustration is indeed joined with the eight case-endings (*vibhakti*). (ViPrud 2.75)
In this work, first a beautiful verse composed in the *mālinī* meter and other such meters is set forth as the opening;
thereafter, eight sentences beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*) are composed for each division, complete with prose and rhythmic cadence.
Next are the apparent case-endings;
the example for that is [II.7.2] *cakravālakam*.
That which abounds in vocative case endings, begins with verses,
and consists of words that are released and then drawn back again, is the *cakravālaka*.
It is composed of verses joined at the beginning and end, consisting of both Sanskrit and Prakrit,
and is endowed with the [five] aggregates (skandhas) through either eight or four statements.

[II.7.3 Bhogāvalī] This *Bhogāvalī* is considered to be that which possesses a distinct syntactic style for each verse-line, is appropriate for gods and kings, and begins with the word "deva" (god) in every instance. (ViPrud 2.78)

[II.7.4 Birudāvalī] That which is abounding in descriptions of the titles (biruda) corresponding to the subjects being described, radiant, and joined with a grand display of phrasing, is considered to be a *birudāvalī*. (ViPrud 2.79)
[II.7.5 *Tārāvalī*] A *tārāvalī* is considered to be composed of verses equal in number to the stars (*tārā*).
In this manner, minor compositions established by the bold assertions (*prauḍhokti*) of poets are to be inferred as appropriate.

Now begins the section on drama (*nāṭaka*).
Now, the compositions in which drama is predominant are described.
[III.1.1 The Nature of Drama] Therein, the nature of drama (nāṭya) is defined:
by means of the four types of representation, beginning with the internal (sāttvika) and the physical (aṅgika).
Drama is the imitation of states such as the *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled), and it has the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) as its basis.
Dance (*nṛtya*) is that which is based on emotional states (*bhāva*), whereas *nṛtta* is accompanied by rhythm (*tāla*) and tempo (*laya*).
This is the procedure as described in the *Daśarūpaka*.
Since dance and *nṛtta* are constituent parts of drama (*nāṭaka*) and other forms, their essential nature has been defined here.
Thus it is stated in the *Daśarūpaka*:
"That [dance] is again twofold, distinguished as sweet (*madhura*) and exuberant (*uddhata*);
furthermore, in the form of *lāsya* and *tāṇḍava*, it serves to assist the *nāṭaka* and other dramatic forms."
Thus, by means of that dramatic art (nāṭya), there are ten types of drama (rūpaka). [III.1.2 Daśavidharūpakanirdeśāḥ]

The ten types of dramatic composition (rūpaka) are: the play (nāṭaka), the mixed play (prakaraṇa), the monologue (bhāṇa), the farce (prahasana), the grand performance (ḍima), the short play (vyāyoga), the combined performance (samavakāra), the scenic interlude (vīthī), the episode (aṅka), and the deer-play (hāmṛga). 3.0.6 //
The objection that there is no distinction [between the various forms] because they all rely upon drama is not tenable;
for it is the plot, the characters, and the sentiments that distinguish these dramatic forms.
The object is of three kinds: well-known, to be produced, and mixed.
Thus it is stated in the *Daśarūpaka*:

"It is considered to be of three kinds, according to the distinction between the well-known (*prakhyāta*), the invented (*utpādya*), and the mixed (*miśra*). [III.1.3: The plot (*itivṛtta*) and other elements of the ten types of dramatic compositions.]
The historical composition is well-known, the invented is imagined by the poet,
and the mixed is dependent on a combination; thus, there is a mutual distinction among dramatic forms (rūpaka) due to such differences in subject matter and differences in the hero (nāyaka).

For instance: in a drama (*nāṭaka*), the plot (*itivṛtta*) must be well-known; the hero (*nāyaka*) must be noble and dignified (*dhīrodātta*); and there must be the predominance of either the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) or the heroic (*vīra*) sentiment (*rasa*).
Other sentiments enter as subordinate elements;
the plot is to be invented for the occasion,
and the hero is the wise-and-calm (dhīraśānta) type.
The erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) alone is predominant. In the *bhāṇa*, the plot is invented, and the hero is a rogue or a libertine (*dhūrta-viṭa*).
In the *prahasana*, the essence consists merely in the indication of the sentiments of love (*śṛṅgāra*) and heroism (*vīra*); its plot (*itivṛtta*) is to be imagined,
and its protagonists are heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*) and the like.
The sentiment of humor (hāsya-rasa) is predominant.
In the *ḍima*, the plot is well-known; the heroes are gods, gandharvas, piśācas, and others who are resolute and haughty (*dhīroddhata*), and they number sixteen.
The Furious sentiment (raudrarasa) is predominant, with the Heroic and the Erotic sentiments entering into it;
in the Vyāyoga, the plot is based on a well-known historical event.
The hero is the bold and haughty (dhīroddhata) type;
the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa) is predominant.
In the Samavakāra, there are twelve heroes, including gods, asuras, and others.
The heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is the primary element;
the plot (*itivṛtta*) may be either invented or well-known. In the *vīthī*, the plot is invented.
The hero is bold and haughty;
the essence consists merely in the indication of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*);
and the plot (*itivṛtta*) is well-known within the act (*aṅka*).
The hero is an ordinary person (prākṛta),
the predominant sentiment is the pathetic (karuṇa),
and the plot in the *īhāmṛga* is mixed (*miśra*).
The hero is *dhīroddhata* (bold and haughty); this constitutes the semblance (*ābhāsatva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*).
[III.1.4 da.rū. sāmagrī]
Now, their combination (sāmagrī) is examined.
In that regard, there are five junctures (sandhi).
And so it is stated in the *Daśarūpaka*:
“*Mukha*, *pratimukha*, *garbha*, *sāvamarśa*, and *upasaṃhṛti*.
[This is the analysis of the five junctures (*saṃdhi*).
A *saṃdhi* is the connection between intermediate purposes of narratives that are unified by a single primary purpose.
Among these, the connection between the commencement and the seed is the *mukha* juncture;
the connection between the effort and the drop is the *pratimukha* juncture;
and the connection between the hope of attainment and the banner is the *garbha* juncture.

The connection between the attainment of certainty and its intensification is the *vimarśa* juncture (*saṃdhi*). The connection between the arrival of the fruit and the final action is the *nirvahaṇa* juncture (*saṃdhi*).
Thus it is stated in the *Daśarūpaka*:
“[The elements of dramatic structure] are characterized by the seed (bīja), the drop (bindu), the banner (patākā), the episode (prakarī), and the business (kārya);
and they consist of the commencement (ārambha), the effort (yatna), the attainment (prāpti), the hope (āśā), the certainty of attainment (niyatāpti), and the arrival of the fruit (phalāgama).”
The five fundamental elements of the plot, endowed with five stages,
give rise respectively to the five junctures beginning with the *mukha*.
Thus [it is said].
Now, the definition of *ārambha* (the undertaking) and the others is being examined: *Ārambha* is merely the eagerness for the attainment of a greater fruit.
Effort, moreover, is the activity directed toward the attainment of a result, characterized by great urgency.

The hope for attainment arises from both the presence of means and the absence of obstacles; the certainty of accomplishing the task arises from the absence of obstacles; and this is the state of assured attainment.
The attainment of the complete fruit is declared to be the "arrival of the fruit.
Now, the pentad beginning with the seed is defined: the causal factor for an effect that has been briefly indicated is the "seed," which expands in manifold ways.
When there is an interruption of intermediate matters, the *bindu* (drop) serves as the cause of non-interruption;
the *patākā* (banner) would be a constituent part of the narrative to be established, while the *prakarī* (subplot) is a pervasive narrative element.
The *prakarikā* is non-pervasive; it brings about the accomplishment of the task regarding the result.
[III.2 The Junction of the Introduction] Now, the introduction is defined:
The introduction is the emergence of the seed, from which various meanings and aesthetic flavors arise. (ViPrud 3.0.8cd)
It has twelve limbs because of the connection with the commencement of the seed-syllables.
The constituent parts of the *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture) should be employed in accordance with the commencement of the seed (*bīja*):
the introduction (*upakṣepa*), the preparation (*parikara*), the conclusion (*parinyāsa*), and the seduction (*vilobhana*).
Reasoning (yukti), attainment (prāpti), resolution (samādhāna), application (vidhāna), and cultivation (paribhāvanā) are, respectively,
the [five] means of penetration and differentiation according to their literal meanings.
Their essential natures are defined in due order:
the deposition of the seed (bījanyāsa) is the introduction (upakṣepa);
the expansion of the seed is the elaboration (parikara).
The establishment of the seed-syllable is the "arrangement" (parinyāsa);
the description of the qualities of the seed-syllable is the "enticement" (vilobhana);
and the investigation into the purpose of the composition that accords with the seed-syllable is the "reasoning" (yukti).
The arrival of the seed-happiness is attainment (*prāpti*);
the proximity of the seed is concentration (*samādhāna*);
and the cause of the seed's pleasure and pain is the arrangement (*vidhāna*).
The penetration of the seed-object is *paribhāvanā*;
the manifestation of the hidden seed is *udbheda*;
and the encouragement in accordance with the seeds is *bheda*.
The commencement of the present action in accordance with the seed (bīja) is the "Effort" (karaṇa).
These are the twelve components of the "Introduction" (mukhasandhi).

Among these, the necessity lies in the "Proposal" (upakṣepa), the "Preparation" (parikara), the "Resolution" (parinyāsa), the "Artifice" (yukti), the "Discovery" (udbheda), and the "Reconciliation" (samādhāna).
[III.3 *Pratimukhasandhi*] Now, regarding the *pratimukhasandhi*:
the manifestation of the seed, which is both discernible and indiscernible, is considered the *pratimukha*.
Due to the following of the effort of the *bindu*, its limbs are thirteen.
The members of the *pratimukha-sandhi* (the introductory juncture) should be employed in accordance with the effort regarding the *bindu*:
*vilāsa*, *parisarpa*, *vidhūta*, *śama*, *narman*, *narmadyuti*, *pragamana*, *nirodha*, and *paryupāsana*. (ViPrud 3.0.12)
The vajra, the flower, the presentation, and also the withdrawal of colors.
Their essential natures are defined as follows:
*vilāsa* (amorous play) is the longing for objects of enjoyment;
*parisarpa* (wandering) is the pursuit of things that have been seen and then lost.
Distraction by undesirable objects is *vidhūta*;
the pacification of discontent is *śama*;
and joking speech is *narma*.
The joy arising from the disclosure of affection is the "glow of jesting" (*narmadyuti*).
The manifestation of the seeds of affection through a series of progressively deeper words is "courtesy" (*pragamana*).
The prevention of one's arrival under a pretext while actually seeking to bring about benefit is "obstruction" (*nirodha*).
Winning over beloved people is attendance;
harsh words directed at the chief person are a thunderbolt;
and distinguished speech that reveals affection is a flower.
The presentation of the composition of sentences that cause passion;
the examination of the four classes of sounds (*caturvarṇa*), which is the collection of phonemes (*varṇasaṃhāra*).
Among these, the primary elements are the *parisarpa*, *pragamana*, *vajra*, *upanyāsa*, and *puṣpa*.
[III.4 The Junction of the Womb] Now, the junction of the womb (garbhasaṃdhi):
The womb, however, is the repeated searching for a seed that has been seen and then lost. (ViPrud 3.0.13cd)
The arrangement of the limbs is in accordance with the banner of hope for its attainment.
The components of the *garbha* juncture should be employed in accordance with the hope of attaining the *patākā*.
These are: the fabrication of the unreal (*abhūtāharaṇa*), the path (*mārga*), form (*rūpa*), illustration (*udāharaṇa*), and sequence (*krama*).
Inclusion (saṃgraha), inference (anumāna), toṭaka, and likewise adhibadha;
agitation (udvega), confusion (saṃbhrama), and objection (ākṣepa)—these are the twelve components in their proper sequence.
Their essential nature is now defined:
the practice of hypocrisy for the sake of one's current interests is *abhūtāharaṇa*;
the proclamation of the true meaning [of the teachings] is the *mārga*.
The statement that establishes an inquiry is *rūpa*. The expression of excellence regarding the subject at hand is *udāhṛti*. The attainment of the intended meaning is *krama*.
*Saṃgraha* is speech employing conciliation that is useful for the matter at hand.
(An alternative reading is: "speech employing a resolution that is useful for the matter at hand.")
Inference (*anumāna*) is the deduction [of a fact] from a sign (*liṅga*).
*Toṭaka* is speech characterized by anger and agitation. *Adhibala* is the deception of a beloved person.
Fear of harmful persons is agitation; apprehension and terror are consternation;
and the pursuit of means to achieve a desired object is exertion.
Among these, the preeminence belongs to *abhūtāharaṇa*, *mārga*, *toṭaka*, *adhibala*, and *ākṣepa*.
[III.5 *Vimarśasaṃdhi*] Now follows the *vimarśasaṃdhi* (the juncture of deliberation):

The *vimarśa* (reflective juncture) is held to be the consideration of the meaning of the seed (*bīja*), which was established at the *garbha-sandhi* (embryonic juncture), by means of any cause whatsoever. *ViPrud* 3.0.16.
Because of the statement regarding the excellence of attaining certainty, there are thirteen ancillaries here.
The components of the juncture of deliberation (*vimarśasaṃdhi*) should be employed in accordance with the intensity of the attainment of the inevitable (*niyatāpti*).
Among them are: the refutation (*apavāda*), the clash (*saṃpheṭa*), the flight (*vidrava*), and the power (*dravaśakti*).
Lustre, attachment, movement, resolve, obstruction, incitement, agitation, and grasping—these are the thirteen [functions]. (ViPrud 3.0.18)
The nature of these is defined as follows:
*apavāda* is the public exposure of faults;
*saṃpheṭa* is speech characterized by anger.
Killing, binding, and so forth constitute *vidrava*;
severe humiliation constitutes *drava*;
and the pacification of conflict constitutes *śakti*.
Threatening and causing agitation constitute brilliance;
proclaiming the greatness of the Guru constitutes the context;
and comparison constitutes movement.
*Vyavasāya* (resolution) is the praising of one's own power.
*Nirodhana* (suppression) is the mutual distraction of those who are agitated by anger.
*Prarocana* (incitement) is the speaking of future benefits as if they were already accomplished.
The manifestation of one's own qualities is *vicalana*;
the gathering of tasks is *ādāna*.
Among these, *apavāda*, *śakti*, *vyavasāya*, *prarocanā*, and *ādāna* are predominant.
Now, the *nirvahaṇa-sandhi* (concluding juncture):

"That is indeed the *nirvahaṇa* where the various elements introduced from the beginning, containing the seed-plot (*bīja*), though scattered according to their respective places, are brought together toward a single purpose. (ViPrud 3.0.19)
There are fourteen ancillaries for this [path], according to their suitability for the task of attaining the fruit.
In accordance with the attainment of the fruit and the fulfillment of the purpose, the fourteen elements of the *nirvahaṇa* (concluding) juncture (*saṃdhi*) are to be set forth:
*saṃdhi* (reconciliation), *virodha* (conflict), *grathana* (knotting), *nirṇaya* (resolution), and *paribhāṣaṇa* (dialogue).
Faith, joy, the pledge, the ritual action, speech, embracing, the prior state, the withdrawal, and the eulogy—these are the fourteen [topics]. (ViPrud 3.0.21)
The essential nature of these is defined as follows:
*saṃdhi* (reconciliation) is the pacification of the seed;
*virodha* (conflict) is the seeking of a purpose.
The introduction of the plot is *grathana*;
the proclamation of an action consistent with the seed (*bīja*) is *nirṇaya*;
and mutual conversation is *paribhāṣā*.
Attending upon [the teacher] is *prasāda*;
attaining the desired object is *ānanda*;
the pacification of suffering is *samaya*.
The stabilization of what has been attained is "action" (kṛti);
the rejoicing in the task accomplished is "addressing" (ābhāṣaṇa).
The attainment of a marvelous object is *upagūhana*;
the observation of a desired effect is *pūrvabhāva*;
and the withdrawal for the sake of the purpose of the effect is *saṃhāra*.
*Praśasti* is the proclamation of auspiciousness.
Thus, the five junctures (*sandhi*) endowed with sixty-four constituent parts have been explained.
Regarding these junctures, six purposes are possible: the communication of the intended meaning, ... [III.6.1 *Sandhīnāṃ prayojanāni*] ... [and so forth].
The concealment of what is to be hidden,
the revelation of what is to be revealed, and the perfection of the passion of dramatic representation.
[The elements are] wonder and the expansion of the plot.
Therein, the plot is of two kinds: that which is to be indicated and that which is not to be indicated.
That which is not to be indicated (*asūcya*) is also of two kinds: the visible and the audible.
Regarding that, the method of indicating what is to be indicated (*sūcya*) is fivefold.
As it is stated in the *Daśarūpaka*:
"By means of the *viṣkambha*, *cūlikā*, *aṅkāsyam*, *praveśa*, and *aṅkāvatāraṇa*.
The nature of these is now defined:
they indicate portions of the plot that have already occurred or are yet to occur.
In brief, however, the *viṣkambha* is enacted by a character of middle rank.
It is of two kinds: pure and mixed.
That which consists mostly of pure Sanskrit is pure;
that which is a mixture of Sanskrit and Prakrit is mixed.
Now, regarding the *cūlikā*:
"The *cūlikā* is the indication of a matter [occurring] by means of those situated behind the inner curtain. (ViPrud 3.0.23ab)
Where the plot is indicated by actors remaining in the dressing room (nepathya), that is the *cūlikā*.
Now, as for the *aṅkāsyam*:

IV.1. Now, the essential nature of *rasa*, which constitutes the life-force of all literary compositions, is defined.

*Rasa* is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) manifested by the totality of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), involuntary emotions (*sāttvika*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*).
Thus it is stated in the *Daśarūpaka*:

“The stable emotion (sthāyībhāva), being brought to a state of relish through the excitants (vibhāvas), the ensuants (anubhāvas), the involuntary manifestations (sāttvikas), and the transitory emotions (vyabhicārins), is known as Rasa.”
Thus:

the stability of an emotion (*bhāva*) consists in its remaining present throughout the duration of the experience, by virtue of not being overwhelmed by emotions of its own kind or of a different kind.
And so it is said in the *Daśarūpaka*:
"A stable emotion (sthāyībhāva) is defined as that which exists for the duration of the aesthetic flavor (rasa), its form unobstructed by emotions of the same or different classes."
Now, the specific flavors (rasas): Love, mirth, pathos, fury, heroism, terror,
disgust, wonder, and tranquility— these are the flavors declared by the ancients.

The stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) of these [rasas] are as follows: love, laughter, sorrow, anger, energy, fear, as well as disgust, wonder, and tranquility; these are the nine stable emotions in their respective order. (ViPrud 4.1)
Now, regarding the excitants (vibhāva): therein, the excitant is said to be the cause for the production of rasa;
it is proclaimed to be twofold, consisting of the objective (ālambana) and the contributory (uddīpana).
The determinants that serve as the inherent causes of the rasa are the objective determinants (*ālambana-vibhāva*);
all other causal factors are the excitant determinants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*).
These are of four kinds.
And so it is said in the *Śṛṅgāratilaka*: “The excellence of the object, its activity, its adornment,
and the neutral [stimulus]— thus the process of excitation is to be known as fourfold.”
The quality of the object (*ālambanaguṇa*) is said to consist of beauty, youth, and so forth;
its activity (*tacceṣṭā*) is considered to be the gestures (*hāva*) and expressions (*bhāva*) arising from youth.
Ankle-bells, armlets, necklaces, and so forth are considered "ornaments" (alaṅkāra);
the Malaya breeze, the moon, and so on are proclaimed to be "indirect factors" (taṭastha).
Now, as for the *anubhāva*:
the *anubhāva* is that which has become an effect; it is born of the body, such as a sidelong glance and so forth.
Now, as for the *sāttvika* states:
*sattva* is the state of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) being permeated by the contemplation of happiness and other qualities residing in another.
Those which arise from that are *sāttvika*.
Stupefaction, fainting, horripilation, perspiration, change of color, trembling, tears, and faltering voice—these eight are proclaimed as the *sāttvika* [emotions]. (ViPrud 4.4)

It is of two kinds:
union (*saṃbhoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*). "Union belongs to those who are joined, while separation belongs to those who are parted."

Thus, in the *Śṛṅgāratilaka*, although sexual union (*saṃbhoga*) consists of an infinity of activities—such as mutual gazing, conversation, embracing, and kissing—it has been enumerated as being of a single type. For example: [The verse follows: "O beautiful one, you who possess the wealth of youth, having drunk the nectar of the lips of that [beloved] whose face is like the moon, you now lie down on the bed of fresh lotus petals; yet, even so, your eyes are not satisfied. (Śṛṅgāratilaka 1.2) In this way, it is shown that the pleasure of union is not exhausted by the mere act of drinking the nectar of the beloved's lips, but rather it is further increased by the enjoyment of other objects such as the bed of lotus petals. This is because the pleasure of union is infinite due to its nature consisting of many activities, such as mutual gazing, conversation, embracing, and kissing. Now that King Rudra, the beloved of your heart, is close at hand in private, your commands of pride have ceased and even your play of modesty has become sparse. What else remains for you to hide? You are smooth with an outward joy that spills over beyond itself.
"O dear friend, some inexplicable possession by the god of love overcomes me through this king."
Furthermore, *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) is fourfold, being caused by longing (*abhilāṣa*), jealousy (*īrṣyā*), separation (*viraha*), and living abroad (*pravāsa*).
Longing refers to the passion that precedes union (*saṃbhoga*).
As for example:
Mutual conversation, assemblies for the play of love, and a bed shared together— these are the unattainable paths of desire,
wherein love is interwoven with a burgeoning and intense passion.
Or one obtains the vision of King Rudra.

Envy (*īrṣyā*) is a disturbance of the mind arising from the hero’s perception that his beloved is attached to another. Separation caused by this is as follows: "Lakṣmī resides in the lotus of his eye; she is jealous when you look upon him."
And Sāsvatī, residing at your mouth, will not tolerate conversation with you;
the Earth, who creates obstacles to your playful advances, stands upon your arm, O Lord of the Kākatīya realm.
O fortunate one, there are indeed no deceits here—why do you languish out of pride?
Separation (*viraha*) is defined as the prolongation of the time until reunion for two lovers who have already attained union, due to some cause.
As it is said:
"When the limbs have grown weary, even a change in the arrangement of ornaments is beautiful for but a moment."
"O friends, let that be; let the manner of preparation be brought forth—what else is needed from King Rudra? 4.127.
Separation due to residence in another land is "sojourn" (*pravāsa*).
An example of separation by that [means] is as follows:
"May King Rudra be served by all the lords of men..."
"Our beloveds are indeed not easily obtained during great festivals"—
thus, due to the torment of the pain of separation, the limbs of the beautiful women of Kaliṅga grow thin, and the days pass like eons.
An example of a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa) is as follows:
[She sees] a female dove upon the parapet of the upper chamber within the palace,
her tip of the beak kissed by her mate.
Beholding her whose throat was reddened by the manifest cries of passion during lovemaking, the Lord of the Kākatiyas broke into a smile.

An example of the emergence of a state (*bhāvodaya*): "O charming girl, what dwells in your heart? Only the god of love, and nothing else; I swear it, my friend! What further task is there for him here, other than his respectful regard for the abode of his birth?"
"Who else is there? Only his reflection is skillful.
"Do you know that King Rudra is more beloved to you than Kāma?"—when thus addressed, the bride lowered her face.
Here is the arising of shame (*lajjā*).
An example of the subsidence of emotion (*bhāvaśama*) is as follows:
"You are Lakṣmī; Puruṣottama is your husband; King Śrīvīrarudra is [your] lord."
"In this creation of the Lotus-Seated One, a union of two such as yourselves has been long prepared;
therefore, this momentary dejection of yours, though artificial, is ill-suited.
Having thus addressed her friend who was bowing down, the proud woman’s lotus-face blossomed. (ViPrud 4.131)
In this case, there is the subsiding of anger.
An example of the conjunction of emotions (bhāvasandhi) is as follows:
By the thunderous sounds of kettledrums, produced by the victorious expeditions of Pratāparudra to the ends of the earth...
And likewise, by the affectionate chatter of the soldiers, their bodies became covered with the armor of horripilation.

Here, there is a junction (*sandhi*) between the joy produced by the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*) and the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). An example of the commixture of mental states (*bhāva-śabalatā*) is as follows: "May the women of noble family censure me today; by whom can a beloved husband be obtained with ease?"
"Has it not been approved by my elders through destiny? Which friend shall be sent?
What will become known to the world before long? When shall I ascend his lap at my own will?
When shall steadiness arise in my heart? The beloved must indeed be approached. (ViP Rudra 4.133)
Herein lies the commingling (*śabalatā*) of longing (*autsukya*) and other emotions.
Now, an example of the commingling of aesthetic flavors (*rasasaṃkara*): [the commingling of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the pathetic (*karuṇa*)].

In this regard, the blending of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the pathetic (*karuṇa*) sentiments is as follows: "Even though the great festival is near, why do you go abroad from here, abandoning me? Fie, fie upon our rashness! Who would desire such a separation, or what fate [could cause it]?"
O Kākatiya king, having thus awakened from the thought that her beloved’s departure had been averted by a dream,
the wife of your enemy faints.
Now, an example of the commingling (*saṃkara*) of the Furious (*raudra*) and the Disgusting (*bībhatsa*) sentiments:
Having drunk the stream of *maireya* wine flowing from the temples of elephants, accompanied by the relish of meat...
Intoxicated by the skulls of slain kings, with visible fangs and bearing a garland of fierce entrails, the sword of Vīrarudra— terrible in its fearsome form and inspiring dread in the people—
performed a sacrificial offering upon the earth of battle for the Kaliṅgas.
In this manner, other instances may also be cited according to their possibility.
Here, rasa has its locus solely in the protagonist;
it is merely brought forth directly by the audience through the skillful performance of the actor and the power of hearing such poetry.
In that case, it is not contradictory for even a rasa belonging to another to produce unsurpassed bliss in another through proper cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Alternatively, when the words *mālatī* and so forth evoke the notion of womanhood in general (and the words *rāvaṇa* and so forth evoke the notion of an enemy in general), there is no contradiction in that [rasa] residing in the members of the audience (*sāmājika*) by means of those specific women or [specific enemies] who are the objects of imitation (*anukārya*) and have ascended to the level of memory.
Since the actor’s purpose consists merely in imitation, he lacks the fitness to be the locus of rasa;
even if one were to admit that he possesses the quality of being an emotional participant (*bhāvuka*), he remains nothing but a spectator (*sāmājika*).
Furthermore, the manifestation of the transitory emotions (*anubhāva*) and so forth occurs solely through proficiency in training and practice.
Even when tastes (*rasa*) and other elements are mutually opposed, their coexistence in a single place is not contradictory when based upon the bold poetic assertion (*kaviprauḍhokti*) of the poet.
The sequence of such oppositions is stated in the *Śṛṅgāratilaka*:
"The erotic and the loathsome tastes, as well as the heroic and the terrifying..."
"Likewise, the Furious and the Marvelous, as well as the Comic and the Compassionate, are mutually antagonistic. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the arising of one rasa from another is also accepted;
as it is stated in the *Śṛṅgāratilaka*:
“From the erotic arises the comic; from fierce action, the pathetic;
likewise, from the heroic arises the marvelous; and from the loathsome, the terrifying.”
The suitability of the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) to their respective aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*) has been thus established in the *Śṛṅgāratilaka*. For instance:
"Doubt, envy, fear, languor, disease, anxiety, memory, fortitude, eagerness, wonder, agitation, shame, madness, intoxication," and so forth.
Despair, dullness, sleep, dissimulation, restlessness, and death—
these transitory states (vyabhicāribhāvas) are to be employed in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
Fatigue, fickleness, sleep, dreaming, exhaustion, as well as apprehension, envy, and dissimulation— these are the emotional states (bhāvas) that occur in the comic sentiment (hāsya).
In the Bhayanaka rasa, there are terror, death, wretchedness, and exhaustion;
also epilepsy, despondency, fear, agitation, death, and intoxication.
And insanity—these states are to be known as arising from the loathsome (bībhatsa).
Furthermore, agitation, stupor, delusion, joy, wonder, and memory [arise from the marvelous].
Thus should the mental states be composed in the marvelous rasa by those who know rasa:
dejection, anxiety, as well as languor, despondency, stupor, and memory.
Sickness and compassion are to be expressed in the *karuṇa* [rasa] by those skilled in the emotions (*bhāvas*);
likewise, joy, envy, pride, energy, and intoxication.
Fickleness and ferocity are proclaimed as the states in the Furious [rasa]; likewise, impatience, discernment, deliberation, intelligence, and fortitude.
“Anger, envy, delusion, agitation, exhilaration, pride, intoxication, and ferocity—these are the mental states (*bhāvas*) that arise in the heroic sentiment (*vīra*).
And: “Every rasa, when fully developed, eclipses other rasas.”

Thus, although according to the method stated by the Indian [theorists] there is but one single rasa, nevertheless, the blending of rasas (rasasaṅkara) is accepted on the basis of the established usage of great poets.
In that regard, when the rasa and so forth are subordinate, they constitute the alaṃkāras such as rasavat and the rest.
When rasa is depicted as a subordinate element, it is the *rasavad* ornament;
when *bhāva* is so depicted, it is the *preyaḥ* ornament;
and when *rasābhāsa* (semblance of rasa) or *bhāvābhāsa* (semblance of bhāva) is so depicted, it is the *ūrjasvin* ornament.
The ornament of composure (*samāhita*) consists in the restraint of emotional states (*bhāvaśānti*);
likewise, there are also the emergence of emotions (*bhāvodaya*) and so forth.
This has been explained in detail in the *Alaṅkārasarvasva*.

“Based on the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the emotion (*bhāva*), their semblance (*tadābhāsa*), and their pacification (*tatpraśamana*), there are the figures *rasavat*, *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, and *samāhita*; as well as the emergence of emotion (*bhāvodaya*), the conjunction of emotions (*bhāvasandhi*), and the commingling of emotions (*bhāvaśabalatā*)—these are distinct figures of speech. Examples of these will appear in the section on ornamentation (*alaṃkāra*).

Adorned with the splendor of virtues and poetic ornaments, a treasury of aesthetic emotion, manifesting in radiant appearance, and whose mind has gradually dissolved all distinction between the knower and the known— may such a state of consciousness, whether it be pleasure or pain, firmly establish itself within the hearts of the two youths.
You are the self of infinite bliss; you are the fullness of the abundance of rasa.

The aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) shines forth as the meaning of the sentence, while these word-meanings— the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth— indeed find their proper repose within it; therefore, the emotional states (*bhāvas*) alone, arising in succession and mutually enhancing one another’s power, [constitute the essence].
And yet they bear a state of fluidity, like threads that possess the nature of cloth.
In the stable, ever-increasing state of the primary emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) such as love (*rati*), various transitory emotions (*bhāvas*) arise and dissolve repeatedly like waves in the ocean;
aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is the excellence of one's own internal relish, cultivated through the enjoyment of these [transitory] states such as detachment (*nirveda*).
In the world, he is said to be merely an object of imitation; however, in drama, he is the spectator.
Thus ends the section on *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) in the *Pratāparudrayaśobhūṣaṇa*, a treatise on poetics composed by Śrī Vidyānātha. V.1.
Now begins the section on *doṣa* (poetic defects).

Now, following the definition of *rasa*, which constitutes the very life of poetry, the defects (*doṣa*) are defined for the sake of a correct discernment of the excellences (*guṇa*), which are the causes of its embellishment.
Among these, the general definition of a defect is as follows:
A defect is a cause of the diminution of poetry, pertaining to both word and meaning.
Since poetry consists of both word and meaning, its defects—which cause its impairment—are likewise twofold: residing in the word and residing in the meaning.
Those residing in the word are further divided into two types: those residing in the individual word and those residing in the sentence. [The defect residing in a single word:]
In that regard, the faults pertaining to words are stated:

the unidiomatic (*aprayukta*), the non-nourishing of meaning (*apuṣṭārtha*), the incompetent (*asamartha*), the meaningless (*nirarthaka*), the requiring further interpretation (*neyārtha*), the corrupted in formation (*cyutasaṃskāra*), the ambiguous (*saṃdigdha*), and the purposeless (*aprayojaka*). (ViPrud 5.1)

Defiled, obscure in meaning, vulgar, having a different intended meaning, unintelligible, having an undiscerned predicate, contradictory, as well as indecorous and harsh— these are remembered as the seventeen defects. (ViPrud 5.2)
The nature of these [faults] is now defined.
That which has not been employed by poets is called "unemployed" (aprayukta). That whose meaning is not useful for the context is called "insufficiently nourished" (apuṣṭārtha). (ViPrud 5.3)
That which is established merely by convention and is ineffective is called *yogamātraprasiddha*;
that which serves merely to fill out a verse-line is called *nirarthaka* (meaningless). ViPrud_5.4 //
That which has a meaning established by one's own convention is proclaimed as being of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*);
that which is contrary to the science of grammar is said to be corrupt in its linguistic formation (*cyutasaṃskāra*).
That opinion which produces a cognition of a doubtful meaning is itself doubtful; that which is non-conclusive is that which prescribes without distinction.
That [expression] is called "obscure" (gūḍhārtha) when it is employed with an unestablished meaning, because the comprehension of its sense would be extremely remote and afflicted. ViPrud_5.7 //
That which is well-known only in the usage of common folk is called *grāmya* (vulgar); a name that has fallen from its conventional usage is cited as *anyārtha* (used in another sense). *ViPrud_5.8*
That which is said to be "unintelligible" (apratītika) is that which is established by the technical terminology of the treatises alone;
it is that in which the element to be enjoined has not been clearly discerned, and where the element to be enjoined has become subordinate. (ViPrud 5.9)

That which produces a contrary understanding of the meaning is considered "contradictory" (viruddha); that which causes an inauspicious, loathsome, or shameful thought is "indecorous" (aślīla). (ViPrud 5.10)
That which is composed of harsh syllables is indeed called "harsh" (paruṣa).
Here, faults in the speech of enemy women living in the forest are illustrated.
An example of *aprayukta* (unconventional usage) is as follows:
"All those deities of ours, Duścyavana and the others, have turned their faces away."
Alas, by whom have we been conceived as forest-dwelling householders!

In this instance, the use of the masculine form *daivatāḥ* is a defect; furthermore, the term *duścayavana* is not employed by poets when referring to Indra. An example of lack of nourishment of meaning (*apuṣṭārtha*) is as follows:
"How can we endure such a state for these beings whose arms are rendered useless—four in number? Fie, fie upon this cruel life! (ViPrud 5.12)
In this context, while "of those whose two arms are useless" was intended to be expressed, the phrase "of those whose arms are half of half of eight" is inappropriate.
This very example illustrates the fault of an undiscerned predicate (*avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa*);
for when the uselessness of the two arms is the property to be predicated (*vidheya*), that [uselessness] is perceived as being merely subordinate (*upasarjana*).
An example of the "impossible" (asamartha):
"Having abandoned this earth surrounded by the four oceans, where indeed should we go? Even in the forest, our stay would be unhappy. (ViPrud 5.13)
In this context, the word *ambudhara* (cloud) is semantically inadequate because it refers to the ocean (*jaladhi*).
Examples of the meaningless (*anarthaka*), the ambiguous (*neyārtha*), the ungrammatical (*cyutasaṃskāra*), and the doubtful (*saṃdigdha*) are as follows:
"Having indeed abandoned those houses, they, with their physical postures reversed..."
When will our dwelling be upon the ridges of the great mountains?
In this context, "vai" is redundant.

Because the perception of a forest from the word "nava" used in an inverted order depends solely on one's own convention, it is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*). The use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for the root *bhū* in the form "bhaviṣyate" contradicts the science of grammar; thus, it is a lapse in refinement (*cyutasaṃskāra*).
The phrase "dwelling on the ridges of the earth-possessors" is ambiguous because of the doubt as to whether it refers to kings dwelling in cities or mountains dwelling on their slopes.
An example of a non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*) reason that is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*):
"Alas! We exist before the striking of the thunderbolt, amidst those whose natures are mobile, who oppose the foremost tip of the banner of the enemy of the teeth of the wind. (ViPrud 5.15)
Here, "nabhasvadaśanāḥ" refers to serpents; their enemy is Garuḍa;
and he whose banner is that very [Garuḍa] is Viṣṇu.

The phrase *tasyāgraja indraḥ* (his elder brother was Indra) is *kliṣṭa* (obscure) because the intended meaning—that [Indra] was among the mountains hostile to him—is perceived only after a great distance [of thought].

The phrase *calātmasu* (restless-natured), used as an epithet for the mountains before the striking of the thunderbolt in the context that "dwelling on the mountains brings suffering," is *aprayojaka* (irrelevant) because it serves no purpose.
Examples of *gūḍhārtha* (obscure meaning), *grāmyārtha* (vulgar meaning), and *anyārtha* (meaning something else) are as follows:
With eyes like red lotuses, dark cheeks and waists,
and hearts full of wit, the princesses were consumed by the fire of grief.
In this context, because the word *śoṇita*, which is well-known to mean blood, is used to refer to the color red (*pāṭalavarṇa*), it is "obscure" (*gūḍhārtha*).
The words *galla* and *kaṭi*, when used to refer to the cheek and the hip respectively, are "vulgar" (*grāmya*) usages.
The qualifier *vidagdhahṛdayāḥ* (those with clever hearts) is "meaningless" (*anyārtha*) because the term *dagdhahṛdaya* (burnt heart) is not expressive [of that intended meaning].
An example of the unintelligible (*apratītika*):
"Where have the instructions of Manu gone, as proclaimed by the family preceptors? (ViPrud 5.17)
In this context, the word *manu* is known only within the science of mantras (*mantra-śāstra*) as referring to a mantra; therefore, its use here is unintelligible.
An example of that which produces a contradictory understanding is as follows:
"How could service to the feet of the Beloved of Ambikā ever be in vain? [This is contradictory because the feet of Śiva, the beloved of Ambikā, are not the object of worship.]
Of kings who have met with destruction due to unrighteous friends.
In this case, from the word *ambikāramaṇa*, there arises the perception of one who engages in sexual union with his mother;

from the word *akāryamitra*, the perception of friends in regard to improper acts; and from the word *vināśa*, used with a focus on the suffering of separation, there arises the perception of destruction. Thus, it is "producing a contradictory cognition."
The threefold *aślīla* (indecorous) consists of that which causes the perception of inauspiciousness, shame, or disgust, as follows:
"When will our dwelling in the desired place come to pass? [For] these [desires], which subsist solely on the rejection of others, have base means of accomplishment. (ViPrud 5.19)

In this context, because the word *padāvāsa* (abode of feet) implies the abode of the world of hungry ghosts (*preta*), it is inauspicious. By the phrase "a base means," because it implies something trivial and delusive, it causes shame.
In the expression "those who live on the excrement of others," because of the word *utsarga*, it implies downward wind, and thus causes disgust.
Regarding the harsh (paruṣa), for example:
"How can there be a desire for fulfillment for us, who live in the wilderness?
Here, the phrase "desire for fulfillment" (*kārtārthyārthitva*) is an instance of being composed of harsh-sounding phonemes. V.3
Now, the defects of speech.

Devoid of proper words, with the sequence of syllables lost, with faulty euphonic junctions (*saṃdhi*), containing tautologies, disjointed, with sentences intermingled, incomplete, or with one sentence interrupting another; (ViPrud_5.20)
Two [types of] dissimilarity in gender and number, two types of deficient and excessive simile, broken meter, loss of caesura, lack of body, and lack of style. (ViPrud 5.21)

That which has a dropped visarga, lacks a compound where one is required, is devoid of an expressed meaning, has a subject resumed after it has been concluded, and likewise lacks syntactic connection; // ViPrud_5.22 //
Falling excellence, redundant words, and violation of the established order— these twenty-four defects are said to reside in the sentence.
Their essential nature and examples are as follows:
A sentence corrupted by grammatical rules is proclaimed to be "deficient in words" (*śabdahīna*).
For example, as found among the utterances of enemies: [text omitted].
Alas, we did not heed the beneficial advice offered by our trusted friends, by which we would have avoided serving the Kākatiya lord and thus not been destroyed. (ViPrud 5.24)

In this case, because the fault is revealed by the employment of the two words "atra" and "na saṃśṛṇumahe," it is the sentence itself that is defective; thus, there is no suspicion of a word-level defect.
This is because when the root *śru* is preceded by the prefix *sam*, it is necessarily ātmanepada, and there is a rule that the object must not be omitted [in such a construction].
Now, for the "disordered in sequence" (*kramabhraṣṭa*).
A violation of sequence occurs where there is no sequential order, whether it pertains to the meaning (ārtha) or the words (śābda).
For example:
"O Lord of the Kākatīs, we have been deceived by fate for failing to present you with either horses or elephants as a gift upon your accession. (ViPrud 5.26)
In this context, although one should have said "elephants" or "horses," they are mentioned in reverse order because elephants are superior to horses;
alternatively, by saying "elephants," there is a violation of the logical sequence of meaning.
An example of the disruption of the sequence of words (śabdakramabhaṅga) is as follows: "What possible count can there be of us compared to the King of Kākatīya?
Even the sun and the moon are submerged in his fame and majesty. (ViPrud 5.27)
In this case, although it would have been appropriate for the sequence of words to state that "the moon and the sun are submerged in fame and majesty," it was not stated thus.

Since the connection of the two pairs as a whole—namely, that "the sun and the moon are submerged in fame and majesty"—is established through a corresponding connection of meanings, there is no contradiction in the sequence of meaning;
rather, there is only a breach of the sequence of word-usage.
Now, *visandhi*: that whose *saṃdhi* (euphonic combination) is either absent or irregular is *visandhi*. For example—
"Such were his heroic deeds; where has his vast sovereignty gone?
Here, "atra śauryāṇi īdṛśāni" is an example of *avisandhi* (absence of euphonic combination), while "pṛthvaiśvaryam" is an example of *saṃdhivairūpya* (irregularity of euphonic combination).
Furthermore, it is characterized by tautology;
when there is a redundancy of word or meaning, that sentence is said to possess tautology. (ViPrud 5.28)
For example:
"In the Vindhya mountains, which are filled with ancient forests, those who live by the forest way... (ViPrud 5.29).
In this case, "in this forest-thicket" (*kānanasaṃkīrṇe*) followed by "those whose livelihood is the forest" (*kānanavṛttayaḥ*) constitutes a tautology (*punaruktamat*).
Now, regarding the confused (*vyākīrṇa*):
confusion occurs when there is a mixing of case-endings (*vibhaktīnām*) and when there is a mutual syntactic connection (*mitho 'nvaye*) among them.
For example:

"O rulers of the earth who desire happiness, conduct yourselves as subjects of the Lord of the Kākatīyas, bearing his command upon your chests and the seal-ring from his lap upon your heads. (ViPrud 5.30)
Here, the connection is that she bears the breast-seal on her chest and the command upon her head;
or else, it is "intermingled with sentences" (*vākyasaṃkīrṇa*).
That which is intermingled with words from other sentences is called "intermingled with sentences. (ViPrud 5.31)
Just as it was said:
"By our great pride, we did not remain silent in the forest;
today that life of the Vindhya has been made as straw. (ViPrud 5.32)

In this instance, there is a mutual entanglement (*saṃkīrṇatā*) of the words in these two sentences: "That we did not put even a blade of grass in our mouths out of great pride has today resulted in our lives being sustained while staying in the Vindhya forest.
Furthermore, regarding the incomplete (*apūrṇa*): "That would be incomplete where the connection of the action (*kriyānvaya*) is not complete."
"Just as our dwelling is among the mountains and we are sustained by wild creatures,
may the Creator rejoice upon seeing us, who possess such kinsmen."
In this case, while one intends to say, "seeing those who dwell on the mountains, subsist on forest fare, and are friends to deer," the intended connection is not complete.
Alternatively, it is "vākya-garbhitam" (an embedded sentence); that is called vākya-garbhitam in which another sentence occurs within its midst. *ViPrud_5.34*
Just as—
having realized that the fire of the wrath of the Lord of Andhrapura was exceedingly difficult to endure,
yet destiny cannot be transgressed, we have fallen upon him. (ViPrud 5.35)

In this context, "vākya-garbhitatva" (the inclusion of another sentence within a sentence) occurs when, in the midst of the statement, "Even though we knew that the fire of anger was unbearable, we fell into it," another sentence—"Fate cannot be transgressed"—is inserted.
Next, regarding "different gender and number" (*bhinnaliṅga-vacana*): where there may be a simile that possesses different numbers and different genders.
The wise say that [the word for the soul] has a different grammatical number and a different gender than that [word for the body].
An example of two [similes] together is as follows:
"The mind of the Yādava king was deep like the ocean, yet it was turbidified by the army of the Andhra monarch, as if by a mountain. (ViPrud 5.37)
In this regard, "deep like the ocean" (*samudrā iva gambhīram*) is an instance of a difference in number;
"the army like a mountain" (*giriṇeva dhvajinī*) is an instance of a difference in gender.
Now, for the cases of the simile being excessive or deficient:
Where the standard of comparison is either excessive or deficient due to its qualifiers,
there the former is called "excessive comparison" (adhikopamā) and the latter is "deficient comparison" (nyūnopamā).
The examples for the two [types] are given in their respective order:
"The beloved women of the Lord of Mālava, with their faces exceedingly emaciated in the forest during the summer, were like rivers whose lotuses, water-lilies, and stalks have withered. (ViPrud 5.39)
In this case, regarding the rivers that serve as the points of comparison for beloved women with exceedingly emaciated faces, one should have mentioned only the state of having withered lotuses;
the phrase "withered blue lotuses and muddy lotus stalks" is redundant.
An example of an inferior comparison (*nyūnopamā*) is as follows:
Just as we are beautiful in our cities with necklaces and body-unguents,
so too do these mountains shine, strewn with cascading waterfalls.

In this case, waterfalls are mentioned in place of necklaces, and nothing at all is mentioned in place of body-unguents; thus, there is a deficiency in the simile. Now, regarding that which has failed in meter and caesura:
Where the speech has its meter violated, that is called "broken meter" (bhagnacchanda);
where there is a lapse in the caesura at the proper place, that is called "lapsed caesura" (yatibhraṣṭa). // ViPrud_5.41 //
For example:
"What good fortune can there be for a person like me, who has made a home and protects his family in the Vindhya forest? (ViPrud 5.42)
Here, in the third syllable of "vindhyāraṇya," there is a breach of the pause (yati);
and because the final syllable of the quarter lacks heaviness, there is a breach of the meter.
Now, for the "bodiless" (aśarīra) [metre]:
That which is devoid of a verb is proclaimed to be bodiless; for example:
"Alas! The Creator is pitiless, playing upon the jeweled floor."
These sons of the Pāṇḍya king were staying in a forest overgrown with thorns.
In this case, no verbal action (kriyāpada) has been prescribed; this very point constitutes the fault known as "lack of syntactic connection" (ananvaya). Now, [the next] is the "unrefined" (ārītika).
That in which the *rīti* (diction) is not in accordance with the *rasa* (sentiment) is called *arīti*.
For example:

"Alas! All my circles of kinsmen, whose arms were difficult to restrain due to their short stature and pride, and who were unrestrained by the bolt of their throats, have been made guests of the God of Death. (ViPrud 5.45)
In this context of *karuṇa* (the pathetic sentiment), elaborate ornamentation of phonemes is inappropriate. Now, regarding the elision of the *visarga*:
the substitution of *o* and the elision of the *visarga* occur repeatedly; such is "that which has its *visargas* repeatedly elided."
That [verse] in which the *visarga* undergoes elision (*lopa*), or becomes *bahudhauta*, is called *visargalupta*.
For example: *vyartho manoratho yāto jāto vāso dhruvo marau* (The desire has gone in vain; dwelling in the desert is certain).
Faded, dejected, ruined, and worn out—such as we are in the depths of the forest.
Now, the compound in an improper place: that is a compound in an improper place where it is not appropriate. (ViPrud 5.47)
"How can the Brahmin, who is so harsh-natured, show such aversion toward us?"— thus they spoke, their faces contorted by brows that quivered with even greater intensity. (ViPrud 5.48)

In this case, there is no compound in the speech of the kings who are angry with the piercer (the sage), yet there is a compound in the poet’s own words; thus, this is a "compound out of place" (*apadasthasamāsa*).
Alternatively, it is a "devoid of the expressed meaning" (*vācyavarjita*).
That which ought to be said but is not stated is called *vācyavarjita* (the omission of what is to be expressed).
For example:
"The life of us who have fallen into a miserable state is considered [to be nothing]. (ViPrud 5.49)
In this context, the word "even" (*api*) should have been stated [in the phrase] "even for those who have fallen into a miserable state," yet it was not said.
Furthermore, there is the fault of *patatprakarṣa* (falling excellence);
that is, the excellence [of the description] declines, which constitutes the fault of *samāptapunarāttaka* (resuming what has already been concluded).
When a sentence is completed and then begun again, it is called *samāptapunarāttaka*;
they say that is *patatprakarṣa* where the excellence [of the expression] falters. (ViPrud 5.50)
An example of two [types] is as follows:
"Running after deer, wandering among elephants, with hyenas rising up, we stay in the Vindhya forests where rows of bears are agitated. (ViPrud 5.51)
In this case, having concluded with "we stay here in the Vindhya forests," the author resumes with "among rows of agitated bears"; thus, it is *samāptapunarāttaka* (resuming what has been concluded).
Furthermore, while one ought to have said "among wandering elephants, rising hyenas, and running deer," he did not say so; thus, there is *patatprakarṣatā* (falling excellence).
Finally, there is *saṃbandhavarjita* (lack of connection).
That [sentence] would be devoid of connection where the intended syntactic relation is destroyed;
for example:
"The rocks are auspicious seats, and the trees are umbrellas."
Alas, we have once again been consecrated as kings over a realm in a state of misery!
In this verse, the connection between "the thrones" and "stones" in the phrase *bhadrāsanāni dṛṣadaḥ* and so forth has not been explicitly stated.
Now, regarding the redundant word (*adhikapada*): where there is the utterance of a redundant word, that is considered a redundant word (*adhikapada*). (ViPrud_5.53)
For example:
"Separated from their lovers in the depths of the forest, these women of Ghuṛjara are as pale as the gradual whiteness of the orb of the moon. (ViPrud 5.54)

In this context, since the description is already complete with the phrase "having the form of the orb of the moon," the addition of "the whiteness of the form of the orb" constitutes a violation of the sequence of figures (*rūpakabhanga*).
Now, regarding the violation of the established order (*prakramabhanga*):
"The violation of the sequence is said to occur here when there is an abandonment of the established rule. (ViPrud 5.55)
For example:
"Caves are our houses, the Śabaras are our kinsmen, the Vindhya region is our city, the rivers are our long ponds, and alas, the forests are our pleasure gardens for us. (ViPrud 5.56)

In this instance, having begun with the plural number in "atra" (here), one speaks of "the city of Vindhyamūla" in the singular; thus, there is a lapse in the initial mode of expression (*prakramabhraṣṭa*).
Now, the defects of meaning (*arthadoṣa*).
That which is meaningless, redundant, repetitive, ambiguous, out of order, disjointed, excessive, harsh, and likewise unpleasant; (ViP Rudra 5.57)
There may be the inferior-superior simile, the dissimilar simile, the unestablished simile, the reasonless simile, and the ornamentless simile. (ViPrud 5.58)
The indecorous, the contradictory, and likewise that which deviates from conventional association—thus eighteen defects based on the meaning have been declared. (ViPrud 5.59)
Their essential nature and examples [are as follows]:
that which is devoid of the meaning of the aggregate is proclaimed to be "meaningless" (*apārtha*).
For example:
Whence come the rivers whose waters are drying up? What news is there from the land of Chola?
How many are the Kulaparvatas that serve as the burden for the thousand hoods of Śeṣa?
In this case, no sentence-meaning whatsoever is perceived; thus, it is redundant. That which is devoid of purpose is proclaimed to be redundant. (ViPrud 5.61)
For example:
"Your lineage is stainless, your prowess surges forth, and your fame is celebrated;
why then is the footstool of the Andhra lord not served by the Pāṇḍyas? (ViPrud 5.62).

In this context, praises such as "the stainless family" and so forth are not useful for the instruction that service must be performed. Now, regarding "single meaning" (*ekārtha*): that which expresses an identical meaning to what has been stated is declared to be "single meaning."
For example:
"Seeing the boys in a swoon, my mind shattered into a hundred pieces;
seeing the infants unconscious, my heart was broken a hundredfold. (ViPrud 5.63)
In this case, there is identity of meaning between the first and second halves [of the verse].
Now, as for *sasaṃśaya* (the doubtful):
that in which there is doubt regarding the meaning of the sentence is intended to be *sasaṃśaya*. (ViPrud 5.64)
For example:
"May the elephant's temples, now that they have become like breasts, be victorious;
may the creepers, having reached witheredness, mock the beauty of the bodies of women. (ViPrud 5.65)
In this instance, there is a doubt regarding the agency and the objectivity of both the frontal globes of the elephant and the breasts, as well as of the creepers and their splendors.
Now, for *apakrama* (inconsistency of sequence): where there is a violation of the proper temporal succession between preceding and following elements, that is *apakrama*.
For example:
"Alas! The women within the forest sleep with their mouths wide open;
by the grass falling from them, they teach us how to proceed. (ViPrud 5.66)
In this case, since the priority in time of the primary gift is stated after the time of sleep, there is a violation of the proper sequence (*apakrama*).
Now, as for "disconnected" (*bhinnam*): that which is devoid of a connection is declared to be "disconnected. (ViPrud 5.67)
For example:
"Surely the Creator did not write our destiny upon the foreheads of the Lāṭas, since our families are perishing in this desert. (ViPrud 5.68)
In this case, there is no connection between the despondency caused by dwelling in a desert region and the absence of inscriptions on the surface of the forehead.
Furthermore, regarding "excessive" (*atimātra*):
that which transcends all the world is proclaimed as "excessive."
For example:
"Lest the entire world become a single ocean, the women of Lāṭa, with their tears constricted, created countless rivers in the forest. (ViPrud 5.69)
In this context, the statement that "the world became a single ocean of tears" is illogical.
Now, regarding the harsh (paruṣa): that which is accompanied by an excessively cruel meaning is proclaimed to be the harsh. (ViPrud 5.70)
For example:
"Let these children be made immediately into fuel for the forest fire. (ViPrud 5.71)
In this context, there is an excessively harsh expression directed toward children who are begging for meat.
Now, regarding "virasa" (discordant flavor): that which possesses a flavor irrelevant to the subject at hand is proclaimed to be *virasa*.
For example:

"Enough with grieving," said the afflicted Kirātas to the beautiful-browed women of Cōla, as they gazed upon us with moon-faced countenances raining nectar through their sidelong glances. (ViPrud 5.72)
In this context, the request for sexual union with forest-dwellers by women distressed by separation from their husbands is tasteless.
Now, as for the "inferior simile" (hīnopamā):
that in which the object of comparison is inferior is considered an inferior simile. (ViPrud 5.73)
Just as deer are slain by dogs, so have you struck down your enemies;
where has that manliness of yours gone, you who dwell solely in the forest? (ViPrud 5.74)
In this case, "like dogs" [said of] you is an inferior simile (*hīnopama*). Now, as for the superior simile (*adhikopama*):
where the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is superior, that would be the superior simile.
For example:
"These cranes on the far bank of the lake stand with motionless forms;
today they have been made to suffer distress by us, as if they were great seers. (ViPrud 5.75)
In this regard, "the cranes were like great sages" is an excessive simile (*adhikopama*).
Now, for the dissimilar simile (*asadṛśopama*):
that which possesses a non-corresponding point of comparison would be a dissimilar simile. (ViPrud 5.76)
For example:
"This Vindhya mountain, with its waterfalls gushing from dense groves, is like Lord Śiva, with the mass of flames from the fire flashing from his crescent-moon eye. (ViPrud 5.77)
In this case, there is no mutual similarity between the Vindhya mountain, with its waterfalls gushing from its groves, and Lord Śiva, whose forehead-eye is a flickering fire;
thus, it is an "unfamiliar simile" (*aprasiddhopama*).
An "unfamiliar simile" is considered such when the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is not well-known.
For example:
"The faces of the deer-eyed women, their eyes moistened by tears, were like unfading water-lilies whose petals are discolored by frost. (ViPrud 5.78)
In this context, lilies are not well-known in the world of poets as a standard of comparison for faces.
Now, [the figure] *hetuśūnya* (devoid of reason):
they declare that stating a matter without a reason is *hetuśūnya*. (ViPrud 5.79)
"Just as—'A vain pursuit has occurred on this path marked by pearls; I shall go elsewhere to search, for this is not the track of the fair-browed one. (ViPrud 5.80)
In this case, the reason why "this path does not belong to the fair-browed one" has not been stated. Now, regarding *niralaṃkāra*:
that which is devoid of ornament (*alaṃkāra*) is called *niralaṃkāra*.
For example:

"The forest was thrown into total agitation on all sides by great bulls with long penises and hanging testicles, who, having smelled the source of fragrance, stood with their faces upturned. (ViPurāṇa 5.81)
In this case, there is no poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*).
Because of the absence of praiseworthy qualifiers (*ślādhyaviśeṣaṇa*), it is not *svābhāvokti* (description of nature).
Now, as for the objection that it is indecorous (*aślīla*):
The speaking of indecent matters is proclaimed as *aślīla* (indecorum).
An example of this has already been given previously.
Now, for the contradictory (*viruddha*):
the contradictory is said to be of many kinds, such as that which contradicts place, time, and so forth.
Just as:
"Though the salt ocean is near in the northern direction, even in the desert land, the Gaṅgā will quench our thirst. (ViP 5.83)
Here, "the salt ocean in the northern direction" is a contradiction regarding direction;
"the Gaṅgā in the Maru desert" is a contradiction regarding place;
and [the phrase] "born from the bellies of the fierce horns of wild buffaloes in the forest... [is a contradiction regarding cause].
Even when the price of pearls is high, women are adorned with pearl ornaments.
In this case, the claim that pearls originate from the horns of buffaloes contradicts worldly consensus (*lokavirodha*). Other such contradictions may likewise be cited.
Next is *sahacarabhraṣṭa* (falling away from association).
It is considered a deviation from the established rule when applied to things that are unequal in their connection.
For example:
"By tranquility, sacred learning; by modesty, a woman; by the god of love, the festival of union;
by learning, wisdom; and by living in the forest, their enemies live. (ViP Rudra 5.86)
In this instance, because learning and intellect are inferior to the festival of the beauty of women, there is a "separation from the companion" (sahacarabhraṣṭa).
Other defects should be inferred in the same manner as far as possible.
Furthermore, the direct verbal expression of rasa, bhāva, and so forth, is indeed defective.
Thus ends the section on defects (doṣaprakaraṇa) in the *Pratāparudrayaśobhūṣaṇa*, a treatise on rhetoric composed by Śrī Vidyānātha. VI.
Now begins the section on excellences (guṇaprakaraṇa).
Now the poetic qualities (*guṇas*) are defined:

cohesion (*śleṣa*), clarity (*prasāda*), evenness (*samatā*), sweetness (*mādhurya*), delicacy (*sukumāratā*), explicitness of meaning (*arthavyakti*), loftiness (*udāratva*), as well as beauty (*kānti*) and sublimity (*udāttatā*). (ViPrud 6.1)
Vitality, euphony, loveliness, vigor, and then expansion;
concentration, subtlety, profundity, brevity, and likewise the state of being real. ViPrud_6.2 //
Proportionality, maturity, style, expression, and likewise movement—
these twenty-four are the qualities that illuminate poetry.

Among these, some possess the status of *guṇas* (excellences) because they serve to eliminate defects; others possess the status of *guṇas* because they are themselves causes of superiority. Among them, those which are themselves causes of an excellence of beauty are the most superior.
The status of the causes for the avoidance of defects as being "qualities" (*guṇa*) is not universally accepted.
For those who maintain that qualities are such by virtue of being the absence of defects, it is precisely softness (*saukumārya*) and the like that are recognized as qualities.
Softness is accepted as the means for eliminating the defect known as harshness of sound (*śrutikaṭu*).
Lucidity (*kānti*) is accepted for the purpose of eliminating vulgar defects;
clarity of meaning (*arthavyakti*) is considered for the purpose of eliminating underdeveloped meanings;
