and propriety (*saṃmitatva*) is considered for the purpose of eliminating deficient or redundant words.
Elevatedness (*udāttatā*) is accepted for the purpose of excluding inappropriate meanings;
vigor (*aurjitya*) is considered for the purpose of excluding faulty euphonic junctions (*visaṃdhi*); and style (*rīti*) is desired for the purpose of excluding falling excellence (*patatprakarṣa*).
Clarity is intended for the avoidance of what is defiled;
eloquence is accepted for the purpose of avoiding the vulgar;
and phonetic excellence is desired for the sake of avoiding lapses in grammatical refinement.
Equanimity (*samatā*) is considered [a quality] for the sake of avoiding a break in the progression;
the "pleasing" (*preyas*) is considered [a quality] for the purpose of removing the fault of harshness.
Thus, in this way, according to the circumstances, certain qualities function as the avoidance of specific defects.
The essential nature and illustration of these qualities are as follows:
*śleṣa* (coalescence) is defined as the mutual joining of words.
*Śliṣṭatva* (the state of being coalesced) is the appearance of many words as if they were a single word.
For example:

"The illustrious Kākati Vīrarudra, whose feet are colored by the luster of the rubies sparkling on the crowns of all sovereign kings, and whose rise of valor is renowned throughout the entire world..."

We are unable to praise this one, whose celestial abode is pervaded by the canopy of moonlight from his inexhaustible qualities, which is ever-awake in its universal protection and possesses immeasurable majesty.
In this regard, at the time of recitation, because the words appear as a single unit, there is *śleṣa* (punning condensation).
Now, regarding *prasāda*:
that which consists of words whose meanings are well-known is called *prasāda*. (ViPrud 6.5)
For example:
"This King Pratāparudra shines as the Lord of Fortune himself, by whom his two eyes have been made as beautiful as blooming white lotuses. (ViPrud 6.6)
Here, *prasāda* (clarity) exists because the words convey the meaning instantaneously.
Now, regarding *samatā* (evenness): speaking with uniformity is what is called *samatā*.
For example:
"In this world, the virtues of the lord Vīrarudra— fragrant like the blossoms of a generous tree— bring fulfillment to the ears of the virtuous."
They were masters in the art of eclipsing the sweetness of nectar,
and they touched the very core of the waves sporting in the celestial river.
In this regard, there is "evenness" (*samatva*) because of the uniformity of expression across all four quarters of the verse.
Now, as for "sweetness" (*mādhurya*):
that which consists in the distinctness of words within a sentence is proclaimed as sweetness. (ViPrud 6.8)
For example:

"The fame of the Kākatīya king is like silken garments upon the rounded hips of the quarters; it possesses the grace of pearl necklaces upon his breasts, and is radiant with garlands of jasmine flowers upon his heads. (ViPrud 6.9)
In this sentence, there is sweetness (*mādhurya*) because even at the time of recitation, the words are perceived as distinct.
Now, regarding delicacy (*sukumāratva*):
delicacy is said to consist primarily of soft-sounding syllables.
"Sukumāratva" (delicacy) refers to the quality of having soft phonemes accompanied by anusvāras; for example:
"amandānandaniṣyandasundarīvadanendubhiḥ" (by the moon-like faces of beautiful women, which overflow with intense bliss).
In the city of the Lord of Kākati, moonlight shines even by day.
Now, as for clarity of meaning (*arthavyakti*): that which they call clarity of meaning is the state of having a complete sentence. (ViPrud 6.11)
For example:
"By that very fortune which now governs the middle world, King Vīrarudra— whose emergence of boundless heroism has been preserved by it— is born and sports [in glory]."
Or rather, even the three worlds possess blessedness because a portion of Hari has descended in person into the Kākatīya lineage and flourishes there at its own will.
In this context, *arthavyakti* (clarity of meaning) arises because the sentence is complete (*paripūrṇatva*) due to its lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatā*) in conveying the intended sense.
Now, as for *kānti* (loveliness):
the extreme brilliance of the composition is what is desired as *kānti* in poetry.
For example:
When the mass of dust raised from the earth by the victorious expedition of King Kākati Vīrarudra, the conqueror,
filled the sky so intensely that it bore the delusion of being the earth itself.
The river of mortals has become a vast, long expanse stretching across the sky;
and the river of Gautama, profoundly hidden and most secret, acts like the Gaṅgā of the netherworld.
Now, regarding loftiness:
the Noble Ones maintain that loftiness consists in the composition of grand syllables. (ViPrud 6.14)
For example:

"Having devoured vast quantities of flesh with a competitive 'I first, I first' spirit, those fierce tusked beasts— whose tips were made terrible by the *kaṭat* sound produced as they repeatedly tore at the bones with relish and affection— "
Carrying night-stalkers who were well-versed in rivers formed by the streams of fat dripping from elephants,
those [weapons] unleashed by the Andhra army cause terror upon the battlegrounds of the kings.
Now, elevation (*udāttatā*):
that which is the connection with praiseworthy epithets is indeed elevation.
For example—
The army of the pervasive Lord Rudra was crowded with swelling elephants, agitated by neighing horses, with chariots maneuvering about, and warriors shouting war-cries.
Now, *ojas* (vigor): *ojas* is the abundance of compounds. (ViPrud 6.17)
For example:
"The courtyards were made resonant by the melodic humming of swarms of bees wandering about, lured by the fragrance of the waves of ichor from a multitude of unrestrained elephants."
The rows of houses belonging to the learned rejoice on earth, for they are fond of undertaking the manifestation of boundless and preeminent prosperity under King Vīrarudra.
Now, regarding *suśabdatā* (grammatical correctness): the derivation of *sup* (nominal) and *tiṅ* (verbal) suffixes is proclaimed as *sauśabdya* (correctness of expression). For example:
Supporting the shores of the circle of his hopes with splendors that scrape the clouds,
protecting his subjects through his noble offspring, and performing rites that bring security to the three worlds—
he was destined to become preeminent on earth through incomparable virtues for the sake of subduing the wicked.
Today, Hari, the incarnation of Rudra, moves about extensively among the flocks of crows.
Now, *preyaḥ*: *preyaḥ* is that which is prescribed in flattering speech as a more pleasant narrative. (ViPrud 6.20)
For example:
"Courtesy is in you; skill is in you."
Compassion is in you, loftiness is in you, boldness is in you,
and manliness is in you.
Perfection of artistry resides in you; glory resides in you; magnanimity resides in you;
fortitude resides in you.
And the leadership of the world rests in you, O illustrious Kākatinātha;
protect the earth for a hundred cycles of Brahmā.
Now, *aurjitya* (forcefulness) is the state of having firm bonds; for example—
Expert in protecting the earth, having quelled the agitation of the world, their movements difficult to behold, with swords raised high for the task of punishing the faction of base kṣatriyas—
[these were] the two fierce arms of King Rudra as he exerted himself with unrestrained vigor.
His pastimes are like thunderbolts that shatter the mountains of the pride of roaring wicked men.
Now, as for concentration (*samādhi*):
concentration is the superimposition of other qualities upon something else. (ViPrud 6.23)
For example:
"Inquiring after the well-being of the Ocean of Milk, following with devotion the Mountain of Śaṅkara,
honoring the River of the Gods repeatedly with sweet words, and smiling at the moon before her..."
The great fame of the heroic Rudra prevails throughout these three worlds, as it compassionately imitates a row of swans on the celestial river Vaidhātrī while uttering a welcome.
Now, as for "expansion" (*vistara*): it is the detailed exposition through reasoned elaboration (*samarthanaprapañca*) of a point already stated.
For example:
In the three worlds, the sole leader capable of repeatedly praising, beholding, hearing, and greatly rejoicing in the virtues of the Lord of Kākatīya is the serpent-king;
for his thousand mouths, his two thousand eyes— [are sufficient for this task].
Those very same Vedic revelations are the thousand hoods for the most wondrous swaying.
Now, regarding conciseness (*saṃmitatva*): conciseness is exemplified as the quality of having only as many words as are necessary for the purpose. *ViPrud_6.26*
For example:
"The women of the quarters, having made his virtues their ear-ornaments, perform the anointing of sandalwood paste with the fame of the Kākatīya lord. (ViPrud 6.27)
Now, as for profundity (*gāmbhīrya*):
profundity consists in the possession of resonance (*dhvanimattā*).
For example—
The poison is seen in the sword, the Gaṅgā in the fame, the sky-clad one (Śiva) in the enemy,
and the moon in the face of Rudra, the Kākatīya king.
Here, Śaṅkara has poison upon his neck, Gaṅgā upon his head,
and the directions as his garment at his waist.
It is suggested that "the moon is upon his head.
Now, as for *saṃkṣepa* (conciseness): the expression of a condensed meaning is proclaimed to be *saṃkṣepa*. (ViPrud 6.29)
For example:
"There exists the lineage of the Kākatīyas; in it there were many kings.
This King Vīrarudra is the manifestation of their accumulated fortune. (ViPrud 6.30)
Here, "conciseness" (*saṃkṣepa*) refers to the statement in brief of a meaning that would otherwise require an extensive explanation.
Now, "subtlety" (*saukṣmya*):
the subtlety of words is said to consist in their nature as internal discursive thought (*antaḥ-saṃjalpa*).
For example:
"The verbal roots √sthā, √kṛ, and √bhū always occur in the sense of 'standing' when joined with *adhi* and *adhas*;
they function in the active voice (*kartari*) under the Kākatīya lord, and otherwise in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*). (ViPrud 6.31)
In this state, because it consists of internal discursive thought (*saṃjalpa*), there is subtlety (*saukṣmya*) in the sense that it presides over, acts upon, and subordinates [objects].
Then comes maturity (*prauḍhi*);
those who know poetry understand maturity to be the full development of expression.
For example:

"The repetition of the lotus-born [Brahmā], the recurrence of the moon-crested [Śiva], the reflection of the enemy of the Daityas [Viṣṇu], and the intensification of the mountain of the gods [Meru] by the moon."
Poets conjecture that the Lord Śrī Vīrarudra is the re-emergence of Karṇa and others, and the manifestation of the very essence of the celestial tree and the divine cow.
Now, as for *ukti*:
the wise know that *ukti* is that which constitutes the speech of the clever.
For example:
"O happy one, the power of the lotus has been seen in the movements of your mind, O King;
even while speaking of you, it displays the splendor of the blue water-lily. (ViPrud 6.34)
"O fortunate one of wondrous deeds, you have been seen by the king to be attached to the lotus;
yet even you, like the sun, adorn that beauty of the night-lotus.
Now, the *rīti* (style).
The manner in which a commencement is brought to completion is designated as *rīti*.
For example:
"The king cultivates the six virtues, disregards the six enemies, adopts the six philosophical systems, and observes the six powers. (ViPrud 6.36)
Now, regarding *bhāvika*:
that which is the function of words (*vākya-vṛtti*) belonging to the speaker (*bhavataḥ*) is cited as *bhāvika*.
For example:
"O Lord, O Father, O Ornament of the lineage, O Vīrarudra, O Master of the world!
By means of this son, I have been placed by you upon the foremost rank of those who possess sons. (ViPrud 6.38)
In this context, due to the influence of the emotion (*bhāva*) consisting of love (*prema*), there occurs the verbal expression "O Master, O Father.
Now, as for *gati*:
*gati* is the state of being very beautiful, [arising] from the ascent and descent of the musical notes (*svara*). (ViPrud 6.39)
For example:
"While the three worlds are constantly illuminated by the boundless splendors of the Lord of Kākatīya— splendors that are incomparable and as capable of rivaling the sun's rays as they are..."
The entire darkness, possessing the radiance of a blazing fire of grief, constantly overflows even within the minds of his enemy kings, despite their familiarity with it.
In this case, because the first half-verse consists mostly of long syllables, there is an ascent (*āroha*) of the tone; in the second half-verse, there is a descent (*avaroha*).
Some also maintain that these qualities reside in the meaning as well.
According to the opinion of the ancient masters, the qualities (guṇas) have as their sole basis the structure (saṃghaṭanā) [of the composition].
As it is stated in the *Alaṃkārasarvasva*: "The distinction between qualities and ornaments is established by their being attributes of the structure and attributes of the word and meaning.
It is precisely through this method that the difference in the essential nature of qualities and ornaments has been defined.
Otherwise, the distinction between their essential natures would be difficult to define.
The very nature of the *guṇas* and *alaṃkāras* consists in their being that which produces the beauty of poetry.
As it has been stated by Rudraṭa:
"That which is the cause of the beauty of poetry is proclaimed as an *alaṃkāra* (ornament);
a *guṇa* (quality) should also be known as such [a cause], while its opposite would be a *doṣa* (defect).
Therefore, it is logical that the qualities (*guṇas*) have composition (*saṃghaṭanā*) as their sole substratum.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Section on Qualities (*guṇaprakaraṇa*), in the *Pratāparudrayaśobhūṣaṇa*, a treatise on poetics composed by Śrī Vidyānātha.
Now begins the Section on Verbal Figures of Speech (*śabdālaṃkāraprakaraṇa*).

The Definition of the Nature of Figures of Speech (Alaṅkāra). Now, following the definition of the poetic qualities (guṇas), the figures of speech are defined. That by which something is adorned is a figure of speech; thus, an alaṅkāra is a cause of beauty.

And so it has been said in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: "Those [figures] such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and simile (*upamā*), which, by resorting to the [poetic] limbs [of sound and sense], embellish that [poem] which is already excellent, are called ornaments (*alaṃkāra*), like necklaces and the like."
Thus,
just as the whole (the body) is adorned by bracelets, anklets, and so forth— which reside in its parts such as the hands and feet— and which are well known as various ornaments,
so too is poetry— which constitutes the whole— enhanced by alliteration, simile, and so forth— which reside in its parts consisting of word and meaning, and which are well known as various ornaments.
The relationship between the adorned and the adornment, by way of the relation between the substratum and that which rests upon it, is accepted in poetry just as it is in the world.
Although both qualities (*guṇas*) and ornaments (*alaṃkāras*) are causes of beauty, they are designated as distinct based on the difference in their substrata:
the qualities have *saṃghaṭanā* (structural arrangement) as their substratum.
Ornaments (alaṃkāra) depend upon both word and meaning.
Among them, first, the class of ornaments is threefold according to whether they reside in the word, the meaning, or both.
Furthermore, the ornaments of meaning are fourfold.

Some have suggested meanings that are explicitly perceived as real entities (*vastu*); some have suggested meanings that are explicitly perceived as similes (*aupamya*); some have suggested meanings such as aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and emotional states (*bhāva*) that are explicitly perceived; and some have suggested meanings that are perceived only indistinctly.

In the figures of speech *samāsokti*, *paryāyokti*, *ākṣepa*, *vyājastuti*, *upameyopamā*, *ananvaya*, *atiśayokti*, *parikara*, and *aprastutapraśaṃsā*, as well as in *viśeṣokti* where the cause is unstated, the suggested matter (*vastu*) serves as an embellishment for the poetry.

In *rūpaka*, *pariṇāma*, *saṃdeha*, *bhrāntimad*, *ullekha*, *apahnuti*, *utprekṣā*, *smaraṇa*, *tulyayogitā*, *dīpaka*, *prativastūpamā*, *dṛṣṭānta*, *sahokti*, *vyatireka*, *nidarśanā*, and *śleṣa*, it is the simile (*aupamya*) that is manifested.
In *rasavat*, *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, *samāhita*, *bhāvodaya*, *bhāvasaṃdhi*, and *bhāvaśabalatā*, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), emotion (*bhāva*), and so forth, are suggested.

Among the figures of speech— simile (*upamā*), *vinokti*, corroboration (*arthāntaranyāsa*), contradiction (*virodha*), *vibhāvanā*, *uktanimittaviśeṣokti*, *viṣama*, *citra*, *adhika*, *anyonya*, *kāraṇamālā*, *ekāvalī*, *vyāghāta*, *mālādīpaka*, *kāvyaliṅga*, inference (*anumāna*), *sāra*, enumeration (*yathāsaṃkhya*), presumption (*arthāpatti*), succession (*paryāya*), exchange (*parivṛtti*), exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), option (*vikalpa*), conjunction (*samuccaya*), resolution (*samādhi*), the adversary (*pratyanīka*), the counter-image (*pratīpa*), distinction (*viśeṣa*), concealment (*nimīlana*), generality (*sāmānya*), incongruity (*asaṅgati*), "that-quality" (*tadguṇa*), "not-that-quality" (*atadguṇa*), indirect expression (*vyājokti*), ambiguity (*vakrokti*), naturalness (*svabhāvokti*), the visionary (*bhāvika*), the sublime (*udātta*)— there is nothing clearly perceived that delights the hearts of the connoisseurs.
Herein is the classification of the levels of poetic ornaments (alaṃkāra).
Similarity (*sādharmya*) is threefold: that in which difference is predominant, that in which non-difference is predominant, and that in which both difference and non-difference are predominant.
Because the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) are inherently distinct, this [first type] is verbal and not real.
*Rūpaka*, *pariṇāma*, *saṃdeha*, *bhrāntimad*, *ullekha*, and *apahnuti* are based on similarity in which non-difference is predominant.
Dīpaka, Tulyayogitā, Nidarśanā, Dṛṣṭānta, Prativastūpamā, Sahokti, Pratīpa, and Vyatireka are based on similarity where difference is predominant.
Upamāna, Anvaya, Upameyopamā, and Smaraṇa are rooted in similarity that is common to both difference and non-difference.
Utprekṣā and Atiśayokti are rooted in identification (adhyavasāya).
Vibhāvanā, Viśeṣokti, Viṣama, Citra, Asaṅgati, Anyonya, Vyāghāta, Atadguṇa, Bhāvika, and Viśeṣa have contradiction as their foundation.
Yathāsaṃkhya, Parisaṃkhyā, Arthāpatti, Vikalpa, and Samuccaya have the logic of sentences as their foundation.
Parivṛtti, Pratyanīka, Tadguṇa, Samādhi, Samasvabhāvokti, Udātta, and Vinokti have worldly convention as their foundation.

The figures *kāvyaliṅga*, *anumāna*, and *arthāntaranyāsa* are rooted in the logic of reasoning (*tarka-nyāya*). The series *kāraṇamālā*, *ekāvalī*, *mālādīpaka*, and *sāra* are rooted in the variety of wordplay (*śṛṅgāvaicitrya*).
*Vyājokti*, *vakrokti*, *mīlana*, and *apahnuti* are rooted in concealment (*apahnava*).
The figures *samāsokti* (brief expression) and *parikara* (periphrasis) are rooted in the variety of adjectives. Now, the mutual distinctions between the figures of speech are being examined.
Even though they both consist of superimposition (*āropa*), *pariṇāma* and *rūpaka* are distinguished by whether the object being superimposed is useful or useless for the context at hand.
*Ullekha* and *rūpaka* are distinguished by whether the locus of superimposition can or cannot assume the form of the object being superimposed.
*Saṃdeha*, *bhrāntimad*, and *apahnuti* are mutually distinguished from one another by the presence of doubt, error, or concealment regarding the locus of superimposition.

Although they share the same basis in similarity (*sādharmya*), *upamā* (simile), *anvaya-upamā* (simile by recurrence), and *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile) are distinguished from *tulyayogitā* (parallelism), *dīpaka* (illumination), *nidarśanā* (illustration), and *vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta* (contrastive example) because in those latter figures similarity is merely implied, whereas here it is explicitly expressed. Furthermore, the distinction between *upameyopamā* and *prativastūpamā* (simile by correspondence) arises from the fact that in the former similarity is expressed, while in the latter it is implied. Finally, the distinction between *prativastūpamā* and *dṛṣṭānta* (example) is based on the relationship of "thing-to-counterpart" (*vastu-prativastu*) versus "image-to-reflection" (*bimba-pratibimba*).

The distinction between *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) and *dīpaka* (illumination) arises from whether the subjects mentioned are relevant (*prastuta*) or irrelevant (*aprastuta*), and whether they are taken individually (*vyasta*) or collectively (*samasta*).
The distinction between simile (*upamā*) and poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is based on whether the object of comparison is well-known or not.
The distinction between simile and paronomasia (*śleṣa*) is based on whether there is a similarity of meaning or a similarity of words.
The distinction between simile and self-simile (*anvaya*) is based on whether there is a difference or non-difference between the object compared and the subject of comparison.

The distinction between *upameyopamā* and *anvaya* lies in whether the relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*) occurs successively or simultaneously.
The distinction between *aprastutapraśaṃsā* and *samāsokti* lies in whether the non-contextual subject is expressed directly (*vācyatva*) or implied (*gamyatva*).
When both the expressed and the suggested are contextual, it is *paryāyokti*; when the expressed is non-contextual, it is *aprastutapraśaṃsā*.

The poetic figure *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) is distinct from inference (*anumāna*) because it lacks the requirements of pervasion (*vyāpti*), presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), and so forth.
When a distinction is not perceived due to the connection with common qualities, it is *sāmānya* (commonality).
When inferior qualities are concealed by the connection with superior qualities, it is *mīlana* (concealment).
Because there is no intention to exclude anything else, this differs from *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification), which is a subsequent figure of speech.

*Samādhi* occurs when another cause intervenes to accomplish an effect by chance (*kākatālīyataḥ*). The second type of *samuccaya* (conjunction) occurs when many causes strive together to accomplish an effect through a spirit of competition (*ahamahamikā*).
The distinction between *apahnava* (concealment) and *vyājastuti* (disguised praise) lies in the fact that concealment may be either expressed (*vācya*) or implied (*gamyatva*).
The distinction among the others is indeed clear.
Although there exists some degree of similarity in certain respects among *vyājokti*, *chala*, and *sāmānya*;
Nevertheless, because it is not intended to be expressed, it is not counted among those based on similarity;
rather, verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṃkāra*) are now defined.
Now, following the classification of the nature of ornaments, since between word and meaning the word is more intimately related to the cognition of the meaning, verbal ornaments are first defined.
Chekānuprāsa (alliteration) occurs where there is a repetition of two pairs of consonants without any intervening [vowels];
that is what is intended by the learned as Chekānuprāsa.
Where there is a repetition of two pairs of consonants that are not separated [by other sounds], there is *chekānuprāsa* (alliteration).
For example: *mahīmahīna-vibhave dhatte kṣemaṃkare kare* (In the hand of the one who possesses great power and brings security, the earth rests.)
The king was victorious over his kinsmen and rivals, and the source of the emergence of royal virtues.
Vṛttyanuprāsa (alliteration):
When there is a repetition of one, two, or more consonants as they occur, that is desired by the name Vṛttyanuprāsa. (ViPrud 7.3)
For example:
"O you petty kings!
For a moment, behold from here the army of the illustrious King Kākatīya, with its formidable warriors who have raised their swords."

If you will fight, the state of imperishability may be attained; otherwise, the side of the wilderness is in vain—for how can there be protection for oneself from the multitude of jackals prowling within the belly of the mountain?
The Yamaka [figure]: Yamaka, however, consists in the repetition of pairs of vowels and consonants.
In *chekānuprāsa* and *vṛttyanuprāsa*, the repetition of vowels is incidental;
however, in *yamaka*, there is a repetition of pairs of consonants together with their vowels.
Due to its occurrence at the beginning, middle, or end [of a word or line], it possesses many varieties.
Here, a mere indication is given by way of example:
"The majesty of the Lord of Kākatīyas, whose splendor is of great and supreme majesty, bestows fortune upon the lotuses, which possess great and supreme majesty and splendor. (ViPrud 7.6)
When a certain meaning appears at the outset as if it were redundant,
that is considered by the wise to be the ornament known as *punaruktavadābhāsa* (the semblance of tautology).
That figure of speech in which the meaning appears to be redundant, yet becomes otherwise at the time of syntactic connection, is the ornament known as *punaruktavadābhāsa*.
Although this [repetition] is a figure of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*), its definition is provided in the section on figures of sound (*śabdālaṅkāra*) because it relies upon the repetition of words.
For example:
"The victorious Indra among kings, the Lord of Fortune, the Supreme Person."
The Lord of the Kākatīyas shines like the radiant sun, with its flashing splendor.

Now, the figure of speech known as *lāṭānuprāsa*, which consists of the repetition of both word and meaning, is described: it is that wherein there is a repetition of both sound and sense, accompanied by a difference in intended meaning (*tātparya*).
That is considered by those who know the essence of poetry to be *lāṭānuprāsa*.
Lāṭānuprāsa occurs where there is merely a difference in the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the words and their referents, but no difference in their essential form (*svarūpa*).
For example:
"Those virtues, those virtues are counted which have taken refuge in King Rudra."
Policy is policy; it is his prosperity, and that prosperity is said to be Lakṣmī herself.
The *citrālaṅkāra* (figure of speech) consists of the *padmabandha* (lotus-arrangement) and so forth.
When syllables serve as the cause for the form of a lotus and the like, it is called *citra*.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the *cakrabandha* (wheel-arrangement) and others are also intended.
In that regard, the arrangement of the eight-petaled lotus (*aṣṭadala-padma-bandha*) is as follows: May she, whose seat is fixed in the golden abode, who has reached the incomparable state here,
who is seated upon a vehicle to which she is not attached, and whose nature is the excellent knowledge of the practice of Kamalā— may she grant happiness.

She who is modest, well-bred, devoted to her kinsmen, fond of song, intent on sacrifice, knowledgeable in pleasures, skilled in virtuous deeds, and as expansive as the ripening crops of a village; // ViPrud_7.11 //
The wheel-arrangement (*cakrabandha*) is as follows:

Of the Lord of the worlds, whose majesty is beheld by Lakṣmī, who possesses auspicious glory, and who bestows upon the quarters a brilliance born from his own commenced valor that is heavy with splendor;
The earth, ever fit for reliance, shines eternally upon the arm of the victorious lord of the Rudras— a firm arm that delights in protecting its subjects— due to its being supported by him.
In this wheel-diagram (*cakrabandha*), it is understood as "the fame of Vīrarudra, composed by Vaijanātha.
An example of the serpent-diagram (*nāgabandha*) is as follows:
"O Rudeva, who possesses vigor, who manifests greatness, and whose majesty has not been surpassed by others!"
O most excellent of the learned, when the vast deeds of the Lord of the Universe are being enacted within the expanse of the world,

the hosts of enemies— whose ill-repute is stained black, pierced by the gods, and rendered homeless by various creatures— take refuge in the forest like travelers seeking water in a parched wilderness.
Thus ends the section on verbal figures of speech (*śabdālaṃkāra*) in the *Pratāparudrayaśobhūṣaṇa*, a treatise on poetics composed by Śrī Vidyānātha.
VIII. Now, the figures of sense (*arthālaṃkāra*).

Among these, simile (*upamā*) is defined first, as it serves as the seed for many other ornaments: "When the similarity of the subject of description with another [object]—established by itself, distinct, and recognized as such through its attributes—is expressed at once, it is called Simile. (ViPrud 8.1)

Where there is a similarity between the subject under description (*prakṛta*) and something non-contextual (*aprakṛta*), which is established in itself, distinct from itself, and approved by those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*), and where this similarity is expressed at one time as a formal attribute (*dharmataḥ*), there is *upamā* (simile).
By the phrase "established in itself," *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is excluded;
for in *utprekṣā*, even that which is not well-known can possibly function as the object of comparison (*upamāna*).
For example:
"The fame of King Kākati Vīrudra, who sits upon the throne,
possessing a splendor equal to ten million moons, eclipses the glory of the kings of the East."
Arising from the intense joy born of obtaining the southern king as a protector— a laugh of triumph for the three worlds— it flashes forth across the horizons.
In this context, the word *prabhā* (light) denotes a genus (*jāti*).

Since the "laughter-light" (*aṭṭahāsaprabhā*) of the three worlds is established through the bold poetic assertion (*kaviprauḍhokti*) of the poet, there is no room for the suspicion that it might be a mere simile (*upamā*).
By the phrase "distinct by its very nature," the possibility of it being a non-parallel (*ananvaya*) is excluded.
In the case of *ananvaya* (non-comparison), because a single entity alone can function as both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison; for instance:
"Let there be in this world mountains of gold, mines of jewels, and moons of nectar;
nevertheless, this Vīrarudra is himself like Vīrarudra. (ViPrud 8.3)
By the term "by consensus" (*saṃmatena*), examples such as the "deficient simile" (*nyūnopamā*) and others are excluded. For example:
"The Lord of Kākatīya is deep like the ocean, lofty like the Mountain of Gold (Meru), and the leader of the earth like a great elephant of the quarters. (ViPrud 8.4)
In this case, since the ocean, gold, mountains, and the elephants of the directions are suitable as points of comparison, this is indeed a simile (*upamā*).
By the phrase "by way of their nature" (*dharmataḥ*), its distinction from the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is indicated;
for in *śleṣa*, only a similarity of words is admitted, not a similarity of qualities or actions. To illustrate:
The beautiful women of the city performed the lustration ceremony for the noble hero Rudra with networks of lamps,
just as the moon-faced nights honor the Lord of Mountains with shimmering clusters of stars.
In this case, the statement "the women of the city perform the *nīrājana* ceremony for Pratāparudra, as the stars do for Mount Meru" is not a simile (*upamā*),
because there is no similarity in the intended meaning of the qualifier "lord of the mountain" (*gotrapati*).
For in the context of the king, the word *gotra* conveys the sense of "lineage."
In the case of Mount Meru, there is the perception of a festival day (*parvan*).
Likewise, in the case of women, the compound *candrānanāḥ* means "those whose faces are like the moon.
In the case of nights, however, it means "those whose faces are the moon itself"; thus, because there is a mere similarity of words, no actual simile (*upamā*) is achieved.
Rather, it is indeed *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
By the phrase "the similarity of the subject with another," the figure of speech *pratīpa* (the inverse) is excluded. For instance:
"This world is ignorant of distinctions; what can we do? To whom can this be told?"
That the king of Kākatīya was compared to Mount Sumeru by him.
Here, because there is a similarity between the non-contextual Meru and the contextual king, this is the figure of speech *pratīpa* (the inverse comparison) and not *upamā* (simile).
By the phrase "similarity at one time," the figure *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile) is excluded;
for in *upameyopamā*, the establishment of similarity between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison occurs more than once.
In King Rudra, Dharma possessed the full glory of Artha as Artha was established in Dharma,
and both were present in Kāma as Kāma was in them.

Here, by means of two instances of the word *iva*—in "dharma is as if artha" and "artha is as if dharma"—the similarity between dharma, artha, and kāma is established; thus, this is an example of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile). By the term "expressed" (*vācya*), the distinctness of this from those figures where the comparison is implied—namely, *rūpaka*, *saṃdeha*, *bhrāntimad*, *ullekha*, *apahnuti*, *tulyayogitā*, *dīpaka*, *prativastūpamā*, *dṛṣṭānta*, *sahokti*, *vyatireka*, and *nidarśanā*—is indicated. For instance: [The verse: "Is this the moon? No, for it has no spot. Is this a lotus? No, for it does not have stalks. Is this a swan? No, for it has no feet. Is this a mirror? No, for it is not dark. In this case, the doubt (*saṃdeha*) regarding whether the face is the moon, a lotus, a swan, or a mirror is resolved by the final statement that it is none of these; therefore, it is not *saṃdehālaṃkāra*. Furthermore, because the face is not actually the moon and so forth, and because there is no superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the nature of the moon onto the face, it is not *rūpaka*. Since the face is not the object of the cognition of being the moon, it is not *bhrāntimad*. Because the moon and so forth are not mentioned as the objects of the cognition of being the face, it is not *ullekha*. Since the face is not denied in favor of the moon and so forth, it is not *apahnuti*. Because the face is not presented as having a common property with the moon and so forth, it is not *tulyayogitā*. Since the face is not the illuminator of the moon and so forth, it is not *dīpaka*. Because the face is not the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the moon and so forth, it is not *prativastūpamā*. Since the face is not the object of comparison (*upameya*) for the moon and so forth, it is not *dṛṣṭānta*. Because the face is not mentioned together with the moon and so forth, it is not *sahokti*. And since the face is not shown to be superior to the moon and so forth, it is not *vyatireka*. Nor is it *nidarśanā*, because the face is not shown to be connected with the moon and so forth through the relationship of cause and effect. Therefore, it is indeed *upameyopamā*. [The verse: "The earth is like a woman, the sky is like a man; the night is like a woman, and the day is like a man. In this case, the similarity between the earth and a woman, and between the sky and a man, is expressed by the first *iva*; likewise, the similarity between the night and a woman, and between the day and a man, is expressed by the second *iva*. Thus, this is *upameyopamā*. However, because the similarity between the earth and the sky, and between the woman and the man, is not intended to be expressed, it is not *tulyayogitā*. Since the similarity between the earth and a woman, and between the sky and a man, is not expressed by a single word, it is not *dīpaka*. Because the similarity between the night and a woman, and between the day and a man, is not expressed by a single word, it is not *prativastūpamā*. Since the similarity between the earth and the sky, and between the woman and the man, is not expressed by a single word, it is not *dṛṣṭānta*. Because the similarity between the earth and a woman, and between the sky and a man, is not expressed by a single word, it is not *sahokti*. And since the similarity between the night and a woman, and between the day and a man, is not expressed by a single word, it is not *vyatireka*. Therefore, it is indeed *upameyopamā*. [The verse:]
The Rahu of the sword-blade of King Pratāparudra,
unrestrained by his unbroken valor, devours the circle of rival kings.

Here, because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the "moon" (*maṇḍalāgra*) and the "Rāhu" (*vidhuṃtuda*) would otherwise be inexplicable, similarity is indicated; thus, this is not a simile (*upamā*), but rather the figure of speech known as metaphor (*rūpaka*).
Is this the ninth Lord of the Quarters, the abode of unyielding prosperity?

"Is this the tenth Prajāpati with his unprecedented method of creation? Or is this Hari, the one skilled in rescuing the earth, appearing as the eleventh?"—thus was the Lord of the Kākatīyas pondered upon by the people in the world for a long time. (ViPrud 8.9)

In this passage, because the identity between the Lord of Kākatīya and [the gods] such as Indra is perceived, similarity is implied through the necessity of accounting for the otherwise inexplicable basis of the doubt;
thus, there is the figure of speech *saṃdeha* (doubt).
When the fame and majesty of the Kākatīya sovereign pervade the two worlds...
Even during the day, the cakora birds attain delight by perceiving it as moonlight.

Here, because the notion that the glory and wealth are moonlight is impossible without a resemblance to actual moonlight, there is the figure of speech *bhrāntimān* (illusion) due to the implication of similarity (*sādṛśyākṣepāt*).
"The abode of the residence of Lakṣmī"—thus all kings [perceive him];
"a mine for the highest level of valor"—thus the hosts of enemy heroes [perceive him].
And those whose fame has been won for their mastery of the stages of learning constantly praise the city of the illustrious Kākati king.

In this city, the superimposition of various objects is not possible without similarity; thus, because of the conceptualization of similarity, there is the figure of speech *ullekha* (poetic delineation).
"The column of smoke from King Vīrarudra, who is performing a sacrificial offering for victory over kings, shines forth; it is not the dust raised by his army. (ViPrud 8.12)

Here, having observed the dust of the army rising up, there is a superimposition [of "line of smoke"] based on the concealment [of the reality]; since this is rooted in similarity (*sādṛśya*), it is a Concealment (*apahnuti*) arising from the implication of similarity.
Likewise, even in cases such as Equal Pairing (*tulyayogitā*), because similarity is what is implied, there is no suspicion of it being a Simile (*upamā*).
Therefore, this Simile is distinct from all those figures whose roots lie in similarity.
That [simile] is first of two kinds: complete (pūrṇā) and elliptical (luptā).
It is complete when there is the employment of all four—the object of comparison, the subject of comparison, the common attribute, and the word expressing similarity.
It is elliptical when one, two, or three of these are omitted.
The *pūrṇopamā* (complete simile) is of two kinds: verbal (*śrautī*) and objective (*ārthī*).

It is verbal when words such as *yathā*, *iva*, and so forth—which directly express similarity—are employed; it is objective when [similarity] is expressed through the mediation of the substratum (*dharmī*).
When words such as *sadṛśa*, *saṃkāśa*, *nīkāśa*, and *pratīkāśa* are employed, the simile is based on meaning (*ārthī*).

Each of these two types [the verbal and the meaningful] is further divided into three varieties according to whether they occur in a sentence (*vākya*), a compound (*samāsa*), or a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
Thus, the complete simile (*pūrṇopamā*) is of six kinds.
The elided simile (*luptopamā*) has nineteen varieties.
When the suffix *vati*— prescribed in the sense of similarity by the rule "when [an action] is equal to that, the suffix *vati* is used"— is employed, it is an implied (*ārthī*) simile.
In the case of the expression "tatra tasyeva" (as if it were that), when the suffix *vati*—prescribed in the sense of "like"—is employed, it is a direct (*śrautī*) simile.

For this very reason, when *vati* is used in the sense of similarity, since the connection is easily established only when the common property (*dharma*) is explicitly mentioned, there is no instance of a direct simile based on a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) where the property is unexpressed; such a case would be considered "elliptical" (*luptā*).
But in the case of a construction beginning with *kalpa* (as in *kalpam*, *iva*, etc.), it is indeed *ārthī*.
Now, for examples:
the *śrautī* *pūrṇā* residing in a sentence (*vākya*) is as follows—
Just as in the Kṛta age it was in the arm of Yayāti, whose valor was exalted; just as in the Tretā age it was in the celebrated arm of the Lord of the Raghus;
and just as in the Dvāpara age it was in the staff-like arm of Yudhiṣṭhira, resplendent with heroism—so too [is it] here.
Thus, in this Kali age, the earth now rejoices with confidence in the arm of the lord of Andhra.
An example of the *pūrṇā* (complete) *śrautī* (based on explicit words) occurring within a compound is as follows:

"Like the sun rising from the mountain of sunrise, Varavīrarudra, seated upon his auspicious throne, completely dispels the dullness of the lotus-eyes of the people of the Andhra city who gaze upon him. (ViPrud 8.14)
In this context, the phrase "like the sun" (*bhāsvān-iva*) constitutes an obligatory compound with the particle *iva*.
An example of the full (*pūrṇā*) Śrautī [Upamā] involving a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is as follows:
"Like a tortoise, like the serpent Śeṣa, like the mountain of the lineage (Meru), and like the great elephant of the quarters."
The earth shines upon the arm of Pratāparudra, which is pre-eminent among those who bear the burden.
An example of a sentence that conveys a complete meaning (*vākyagā pūrṇārthī*) is as follows:

"By means of various arrangements for protecting the earth and through various splendors of pleasing the subjects, the current Lord of Fortune of the Kākatīyas shines forth, equal to the son of Daśaratha. (ViPrud 8.16)
An example of a compound containing a complete meaning (*pūrṇārthī*) is as follows:
"By virtue of his excellence in such power of protection, the Lord of the Kākatīyas, resembling the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva), rules over the middle world. (ViPrud 8.17)
An example of those occurring with secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) that convey a complete meaning is as follows:
"In loftiness he is like the Golden Mountain (Meru), in profundity like the Ocean of Milk, and in majesty he shines like the Sun; thus does King Vīrarudra appear. (ViPrud 8.18)

In these examples, because the four elements—the object of comparison (*upameya*), the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and the word expressing similarity (*sādṛśyapratipādaka*)—are all expressed, there is "completeness" (*pūrṇatva*).

Now, here are examples of the elliptical simile (*luptopamā*): an example of the elliptical simile where the common attribute is not stated and which is based on a verbal suffix (*śrautī*) is as follows:
Just as female cakravāka birds [cling] to their mate, the sun; just as female cakora birds [cling] to the moon;
and just as bees [cling] to a cluster of blossoms, so did the subjects cling to Vīrarudra of the Kākatiya dynasty.
An example of the elliptical *śrautī* simile based on a compound where the common property (*dharma*) is not explicitly stated is as follows:
"Kings incessantly worship the footstool of King Pratāparudradeva, bowing down to it as if it were a deity. (ViPrud 8.20)
Or, when the unexpressed attribute resides in the sentence, it is an implied ellipsis (*ārthī luptā*), as in:
"The enemy kings hear the sound of King Kākatīya’s war-drum at the time of his victorious expedition, which is equal to the roar of the thunderbolt. (Viśvaguṇādarśa 8.21)
An example of the elliptical *ārthī* compound where the attribute is not explicitly stated (*anuktadharma*) is as follows:
"Having beheld the city named Ekaśilā, which is like Vasvokasārā, the kings on earth bow down, highly esteeming the establishment of the Kākatīya kingdom. (ViPrud 8.22)
An implied *taddhita* suffix, where the suffix is elided and its meaning remains unexpressed (*luptārthī*), is as follows:
"The women of the Andhra city behold the form of King Pratāparudra, whose splendor spreads throughout the world, as being like that of Kandarpa. (ViPrud 8.23)
In these examples, there is no mention of the *dharma* (the quality).
An unstated *dharma* is elided through the *karmakyaṅ* suffix, as in:
"He treats the oceans like the Ocean of Milk; he treats the mountains like Mount Kailāsa."
The majesty of the clarity of the fame of King Pratāparudradeva.
An example of the elision of the suffix *kyac* due to the identity of the substratum (*ādhārakyac*), even though the property (*dharma*) and so forth are not explicitly stated:

"On the peaks of the mountains of his lineage, he acts as a pleasure-mountain; on the islands, he acts as a palace for assembly; in the oceans, he acts as a long pond; and in the quarters, he acts as a secluded home."
The vast rising of King Vīrarudra’s majesty makes the forested slopes of the boundary mountains appear like pleasure gardens, and the noble mountain peaks appear like palaces.
An example of the *karmamūla* suffix being elided when the object is not explicitly stated:

They behold the son of their own self as the moon; they behold the river of the gods as the one with excellent waves; they behold the ocean of milk as the one with excellent water; and they behold the silver mountain as the one with a beloved friend.

The fame of King Vīrarudra, pervading the entire world, sports like a stainless mirror for Līlā to behold herself as the stars and other celestial bodies, and as a pearl necklace for her to gaze upon.
An example where the suffix *ṇamul* is elided after a verb whose root meaning is not explicitly stated:

"This sword of King Rudra moves among kings as the movement of the rod of punishment prescribed by the rules of training; among beloved women, it moves like the movement of the bow of the Flower-Armed God (Kāmadeva); and among the subjects, it moves like the movement of a supporting staff. (ViPrud 8.27)
An example where the suffix *kvip* is elided after a verbal root that has not been explicitly mentioned as such is as follows:
"The expansion of the moonlight of the virtues of King Vīrarudra acts as a stream of nectar for the virtuous and as the *kālakūṭa* poison for the wicked. (ViPrud 8.28)
In these examples, there is no mention of two [of the three factors].

In the case of *ambhodhīn dugdhārṇavīyati*, where the suffix *kyac* is applied to the object, it means "he makes them like the Ocean of Milk"; and in the case of *gotraśikhareṣu krīḍādrīyati*, where *kyac* is applied to the locus, it means "he behaves as if on pleasure-mountains."
In the example *candramātmajadarśaṃ paśyanti*, the suffix *karmaṇamul* is used [to express that they see him] as if he were their own son (*ātmajam iva paśyanti*).

In the example *śikṣāvidhidaṇḍacāraṃ carati*, the suffix *kartṛṇamul* is used [to express that he behaves] as if he were the punishment prescribed by the rules of training (*śikṣāvidhidaṇḍa iva carati*). Since the word "as if" (*iva*) is internal [to the compound], it is elided. An example where the suffix *ivārthe kyaṅ* (expressing similarity) is elided when the agent is not explicitly stated is as follows:
The bright, great waves of King Pratāparudra’s fame act everywhere as moonlight, as nectar, and as sandalwood paste.
In this instance, the nature of fame (*kīrti*) is the object of comparison (*upameya*).
An example where the common property (*dharma*), the particle *iva*, and so forth are not expressed, and the agentive suffix *kyac* is elided, is as follows:
"It acts like the serpent Śeṣa to bear the earth; it acts like the wish-fulfilling tree for the sake of supplicants."
The staff-like arm of Pratāparudra acts as the rod of Death for his enemies.
An example of the elliptical simile (*luptopamā*) occurring within a sentence where the object of comparison is not explicitly stated:
"In the three worlds, there is no other donor equal to King Rudra, whose fame for his multitude of virtues has eclipsed the glory of Indra, the lord of the quarters."
The courtyards of the jewel-like houses of wise men are made fragrant by the scent of elephant ichor wafting forth from all sides.
An example of the elided simile occurring within a compound, where the object of comparison is not explicitly stated, is as follows:
"There is no king on the face of the earth equal to Vīrarudra; indeed there is none, for by his adherence to righteousness, the Kali age has been turned into the Kṛta age. (ViPrud 8.32)

An example of the elliptical simile (*luptopamā*) residing in the sentence (*vākyagā*), where the property (*dharma*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) are not explicitly stated, is as follows:

"In this world, there is nothing anywhere that can be compared to the fame of King Kākati Vīrarudra, whose sovereign splendor is unrestrained, and which is as white as the moonlight of the month of Kārttika."
Now, beholding her neck— the venom of which has been destroyed by the manifestation of his sweetness—
the Daughter of the Mountain offers an unrestrained embrace around the neck of her Lord.
An example of the elliptical simile (*luptopamā*) contained within a compound, where the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is not explicitly stated, is as follows:
"In the three worlds, there has never been, nor will there ever be, anything equal to the majesty and glory of the victorious Lord of Kākatīya."
Just as sunstones shine day and night on the slopes of the mountain that illuminates the world, due to their long-standing familiarity with the rising radiance [of the sun].
In the two preceding examples, the common property of being disposed toward giving and of pleasing the subjects was expressed by the words "munificent" (*vadānya*) and "king" (*rāja*).
In the two subsequent examples, the distinction lies in the fact that even the word "dharma" is not employed.
In these four examples, there is no suspicion of the figure of speech *pratīpa* (the contrary).
This is because there is no negation of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*),
nor is there an intention to suggest the superiority of the object compared (*upameya*).

The figure of speech *pratīpa* (the inverse) occurs only in cases where the status of being the standard of comparison is predicated with the intention of suggesting the superiority of the object compared.
The elided *anukta-vādi* (omitted subject) occurring within a compound is, for example:
"The conduct of King Pratāparudradeva—which is hot like the sun for the wicked and cool like the moon for the virtuous—is an auspiciousness for the entire world. (ViPrud 8.35)
An example of the elided simile (*luptopamā*) occurring within a compound, where the object of comparison and so forth are not explicitly stated, is as follows:
"The Lord of the Kākatīyas shines in battle with the prowess of Bhīmasena; however, all his rival kings are incapable of being subdued. (ViPrud 8.36)
In this case, "Bhīmasenaparākrama" refers to one whose valor is like the valor of Bhīmasena; thus, the comparison is elided by the very word "Dharma" (virtue) and so forth.
Thus have the elided similes been demonstrated. Now follows the twofold division regarding the employment of the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

The indication of the common property (*dharma*) as residing simultaneously in both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), and its separate mention as residing in both;

and this separate mention is of two kinds: by way of the relation between thing and counterpart (*vastu-prativastu-bhāva*) and by way of the relation between image and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*).
The expression of a single meaning by two words is the relation of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding object).
The double employment of two meanings is the relation of *bimba-pratibimba* (original image and reflected image). An example of simultaneous mention is as follows:
With their heads bowed in prostration, kings serve the Lord of the Kākatīyas from all sides— just as disciples attend upon a teacher who is the discipliner of the wicked.
In this context, the commonality between the lords of men and their disciples—that they have their heads bowed—is stated only once;
likewise, the shared quality of the king and the teacher—that they are the discipliners of the wicked—is stated only once.
An illustration of the twofold presentation by way of correspondence (*vastu-prativastu-bhāvena*) is as follows:
This lineage of the Kākatīyas has been adorned by Vīrarudra,
just as the dynasty of Kakutstha was graced by Rāma.
In this instance, because the words *bhūṣita* (adorned) and *pariṣkṛta* (decorated) convey the same meaning, there is the relation of *vastu-prativastu-bhāva* (correspondence of things).
An example of the relation of *bimba-pratibimba-bhāva* (original and reflection) is as follows: "The Lord of the Kākatīyas possesses the splendor of a shimmering white parasol."
It shines like the Mountain of Gold (Meru), with the orb of the moon clinging to its peak.

Here, through the similarity between the white umbrella and the lunar disc, there is a similarity between the Lord of the Kākatīyas and the Golden Mountain (Meru); this constitutes the relationship of the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).
Furthermore, this ornament has two other varieties: that which has all things as its object (*samastavastuviṣayā*) and that which resides in only one part (*ekadeśavartinī*).
The examples for these two follow in order:
The city of the Kākati king shines like the earth with its mountains; it resplends like Amarāvatī;
its citizens are renowned like the gods; and Vīrarudra possesses prosperity like Indra.
This [type of simile] has all things as its object.
An example of that which pertains to only one part is as follows:
"Whether by moving elephants or by mountains, by rows of horses or by waves..."
Nor can the army of the lord of Triliṅga be overcome by various weapons or by predatory beasts and sea-monsters.

In this instance, because the meaning "the strength of the Lord of the Three Realms is like the ocean" is understood through implication (*arthāt*), it possesses the quality of being a partial metaphor (*ekadeśavartin*).
This ornament is also seen in the form of a series (*mālārūpa*); for example:
"It acts as a jasmine, acts as a night-lily, acts as a swan, acts as a pearl necklace, acts as [the moon] that steals [the beauty], and acts as the maker of the night."
And the fame of Vīrarudra possesses the splendor and clarity of Mount Kailāsa.
Here, because multiple points of comparison (upamāna) are seen for a single object of comparison (upameya), it possesses the nature of a "garland" (mālā).
In simile (upamā), the commonality (sādharmya)—which is shared by both difference and non-difference—is the operative factor.
In this manner, other varieties [of simile] should be illustrated as they occur.
The figure of speech *ananvaya* (non-comparison):
When one and the same thing serves as both the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), it is considered *ananvaya*. (ViPrud 8.43)

Where the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison is established for a single entity alone, for the purpose of excluding a second fellow-practitioner (of religious life), that is the figure of speech *ananvaya* (non-comparison). For example:
"Let there be in the world the golden mountain [Meru], the ocean of jewels, and the moon;
nevertheless, this Vīrarudra is himself like Vīrarudra. (ViP Rudra 8.44)
The figure of speech *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison):
when two things are compared to each other by turns, that is considered *upameyopamā*. (ViPrud 8.45)
In that [verse], there is a reference to both the object of comparison and the subject of comparison. For example:
"Virtue possessed full splendor like wealth; wealth remained as if it were virtue;
and both of them were like desire—[all] in King Rudra. (ViPrud 8.46)
The Ornament of Recollection (smaraṇālaṃkāra):
Recollection is said to be the memory of something else arising from the experience of a similar object. (ViPrud 8.47)
The figure of speech *smaraṇa* (recollection) occurs where, through the perception of an object similar [to another], there arises a reflection upon another similar entity. For example:
"This earth, protected by King Pratāparudra, calls to mind former kings such as Hariścandra, Nala, and others. (ViPrud 8.48)
Here, the Earth, having obtained Pratāparudra as her protector— one who is skilled in ruling like Nala, Nahuṣa, and others— remembers her former kings.
Thus, the poetic figures based on similarity (sādharmya), which may be characterized by either difference or non-difference, have been demonstrated.
Now begins the section on the poetic figure of superimposition (*āropagarbha*).
Among those, because it is the most prominent, *rūpaka* (metaphor) is first defined.
This is the poetic figure of *rūpaka*.
When that which is being superimposed acts as a coloring agent for the object of superimposition, whose form is not concealed, that is considered *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification). 8.49.

By the phrase "of the object of superimposition" (*atrāropaviṣayasya*), there is the exclusion of figures such as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), which involve the element of determination (*adhyavasāya*), as well as figures such as *upamā* (simile) and others, which are not rooted in superimposition.
By the phrase "whose form is not concealed" (*atirohitarūpiṇaḥ*), there is the exclusion of figures such as *saṃdeha* (doubt), *bhrāntimad* (error), and *apahnuti* (denial).
In the figure of *saṃdeha*, the object is concealed by virtue of being the subject of doubt.
In the figure of speech *bhrāntimān* (error), there is the concealment of the object by means of error;
in the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment), there is the concealment of the locus of superimposition by means of concealment.
By the term "coloring agent" (*uparañjaka*), the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation) is excluded.
In a *pariṇāma* (transformation), the superimposed object is connected to the subject by virtue of its utility to the context, not by its power to color or embellish it.
Therefore, *rūpaka* (metaphor) is distinct from all figures based on similarity.
Its first division is threefold: *sāvayava* (with parts), [niravayava (without parts), and saviśeṣaṇa (with qualifiers)].
[Metaphor is] partless and derivative.
The part-possessing [metaphor] is of two kinds: that which has all things as its object and that which is partial.

The partless (niravayava) is of two kinds: the simple (kevala) and the garland-like (mālārūpa). The relative (paramparita) is also twofold, according to whether its basis is based on wordplay (śliṣṭa) or not (aśliṣṭa). Each of these two is further divided into four types by way of being either simple or garland-like.
Thus, there are eight types of *rūpaka* ornament.
Now, the examples:
where the description of both the parts and the whole is composed in their entirety, [that is *rūpaka*].
That is *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) having all things as its subject matter,
as for example:
"In the rainy season of King Vīrarudra’s expedition, when the clouds of his trumpets are raining down..."
Roaring repeatedly like a terrifying thundercloud that shatters the mountain of the enemy kings' pride,
and raining down the tears from the eyes of their wives' enemies, her stalks of fame— which bring joy to the world— grow ever more abundantly in every direction.
That is *ekadeśavivarti* (partially manifest) *rūpaka* where, through the description of the parts, the form of the whole is understood;
for example—
Kākati Vīrarudra, a mine of valor who has adorned the interior of the circle of the quarters,
perfumes the three worlds with the blossoming flowers of his virtues through his latent disposition.
Here, by describing the qualities of the king’s limbs as having the nature of flowers, his status as a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpaśākhin) is established;
therefore, this is a case of *ekadeśavivarti* (partial metaphor). Or, for example:
"From the ocean of the enemy host churned by the Mandara mountain of his arm..."
The fame born of Pratāparudra gladdens these worlds.

Here, by the metaphorical representation of the enemy host as the ocean and the arm as Mount Mandara, the resulting fame attains the state of nectar (sudhā) by implication, and the immortality of the people follows; this is therefore an *ekadeśavivarti* (partially developed) metaphor.
Where the poet’s creative effort comes to rest upon the metaphorical representation of the whole alone, that is a *niravayava* (uncompounded) metaphor.
Even in the case of a mere description of its parts, it is the same;
therein, simply as follows:
by the repeated war-cries of brave warriors swelling at the commencement of the expedition.
With the sounds of their war-drums clearly filling the hollows of the cosmic shells on every side,
the oceans were agitated and the mountains shaken; at the mere sound of them,
the rival kings of King Kākati Vīrarudra, seized with fear, gave up their lives.
In this instance, the state of being the shell of the two worlds (heaven and earth) is metaphorically represented.
An example of a garland that lacks constituent parts is as follows:
"The stainless garland adorning the crest of kings [is present] upon the ears of the elephants of the quarters."
The Ganges river serves as a vast chowrie-adornment upon the peaks of the mountains;
the sky is a brilliantly white canopy of silk; and the earth is a wide expanse of pearl-strings—this is the manifest splendor of the fame of Kākatīya Vīrarudra.
Metaphor based on a cause (*rūpakahetu-rūpaka*) and chain metaphor (*paramparita-rūpaka*):
because these two are established as consisting of only two metaphors each, they are not included within the category of metaphors whose objects are entire entities (*samastavastu-viṣaya*).
An example of a chain metaphor that is both based on wordplay (*śliṣṭa*) and simple (*kevala*) is as follows:
The moon-eclipsing Rahu to the orb of Pratāparudradeva—
the king whose valor is unrestrained and unbroken— devours the circle of rival monarchs.
An example of a *śliṣṭamālāparamparita* (successive pun-based chain) is as follows:
He who possesses the thousand-rayed sun that causes the lotuses to bloom; who is wise in the practice of the true path;
who is a thunderbolt for splitting the wings of the mountains; and who is the full-moon night for the ornamentation of the blue water-lilies.

This King Śrī Vīrarudra is a fragrant expanse of ever-blossoming, joyful mind; he is the ocean that serves as the refuge for the world, including the mountains, the earth, and the heavens, which is rich with the prosperity of auspiciousness.
An example of the unconnected simple *paramparita* (metaphor upon metaphor) is as follows:
"The playful great waves of the fame-ocean of the Kākatīya king, surging with pride against the shores of the quarters and rising to touch the clouds, sport about. (ViPrud 8.57)
An example of the non-sequential *mālā-paramparita* (garlanded succession) is as follows:
By the tongue of the serpent-arm, by the great whirlwind of the forest-ranges of enemies, by the smoke of the fierce fire of valor, and by the playful brow of the maiden Jayaramā;

King Rudra sports with his sword-blade, which is like a creeper of compassion— the bolt for the gate of grace toward the world, and the staff for the dwelling of the peahen that is the earth’s exuberant joy.
The *paramparita* (successive) type of *aśliṣṭa* (non-phonetic) simile can also occur through contrast (*vaidharmya*). For example:
"The playful sports of the hero Rudra on the battlefield—consisting of midday [when it is] the darkness of terror, and the three nights [which are] the deceitful heat—triumph. (ViPrud 8.59)
Thus, since each of these eight types of *rūpaka* can reside within either a sentence or a compound, sixteen varieties of *rūpaka* are possible.
The figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation):
When that which is being superimposed exists as the very nature of the object of superimposition, and serves a purpose for the subject at hand, it is illustrated as *pariṇāma*. (ViPrud 8.60)
By the phrase "being superimposed as useful to the subject at hand," all other poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) are excluded.
That [superimposition] is twofold, by virtue of being either in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
An example of *pariṇāma* through coreferentiality is as follows:
The hosts of kings, ever longing for the performance of acts of adoration,
pay homage with bowed crowns to the illustrious King Vīrarudra, the conqueror of the quarters.
A garland made of jewels, possessing the splendor of intense grace.
Transformation by way of grammatical non-co-ordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is as follows:

"Desiring the fruits [of their rule], the lords of the earth who are enemies of other kings worship [the King]—offering a handful of flowers formed by the networks of rays from the rubies in his crown—by making the boundary of the footstool of King Rudra their limit. (ViPrud 8.62)

In *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation), even though the object being superimposed serves the purpose of the subject at hand, it is not included within *pariṇāma* (transformation) because it is not explicitly stated.
The figure of speech *saṃdeha* (doubt):
where, due to a resemblance recognized by the poet, the object (*viṣaya*) and the object of superimposition (*viṣayin*) [are confused].
If these two should become objects of doubt, that is the figure of speech known as *saṃdeha* (doubt).
It is threefold: pure, containing certainty within,
and ending in certainty.
An example of the pure [type] which results in mere doubt:
Is this the ninth Lord of the Greens (Indra), the seat of unflagging prosperity?
Is this the tenth Prajāpati, whose method of creation is unprecedented?
"Why is it that Hari, who is so skilled at uplifting the earth, is only after eleven births seen by people in this world as Vīrarudra? (ViPrud 8.64)
An example of *niścayagarbha* (containing a resolution):
"Is this a black serpent that bears a coil as soft as a lotus stalk? Or is it a frown of Time (Death) that expands right upon his face?"
"Is this the trail of smoke from the fire of the god of death, or is it being fanned by the wind?"— thus is Rudra's sword conjectured by his adversaries.
An example of that which culminates in certainty:
"Are these garlands of blossoms from the wish-fulfilling tree, or are they the oceans of milk, or perhaps the most radiant manifestations of the *cintāmaṇi* jewel?"
Or rather, having reflected for a long time on what the waves of the perfected elixir might be,
the virtuous conclude with smiles that they are the sidelong glances of King Kākati Vīrarudra.

The ornament of Illusion (bhrāntimad-alaṅkāra): Where there is the perception of something being superposed upon a subject whose own nature is concealed due to a resemblance accepted by the poet, that is considered Illusion. (ViPrud 8.67)
For example:
"In the splendor of the fame of the lord of the Kākatīyas, which has pervaded the two worlds..."
Even by day, the cakora birds attain delight, perceiving it as moonlight.
The figure of speech Apahnuti (Concealment):
Apahnuti occurs when, having denied the object [of description], one superimposes another due to similarity. (ViPrud 8.69)

Its threefold nature consists of: superimposition through concealment, concealment of the object of superimposition, and the demonstration of unreality by means of words such as "quibble" (chala) and the like.
An example of the first two [types of *śleṣa*] is as follows:

"This is not the tumultuous roar of an army surging from the four oceans; this is not the thundering of kettledrums, but the sound of the *ḍhakkā* drum at the end of the aeon sounded by the Conqueror of Tripura."

Thus, when the heads of all the remaining kings— bowed down by the weight of the earth during the military expeditions of King Rudra— were struck with wonder, they were then cast down even by the lords of the directions.
An illustration of the demonstration of unreality through words such as *chala* (deceit) and so forth:

"Under the guise (*chala*) of Kākati Vīrarudra, the lord of the earth, Śiva himself has become the self-existent one (*svayaṃbhū*) who has attained the station of the central world-guardian (*madhyamalokapāla*) in order to protect the entire earth."
If it were not so, how could the cities of the enemies have been reduced to ashes by the mere art of his uneven glances, and how could the hosts of mountains have been rendered speechless?

The multi-faceted delineation (*ullekhana*) of a single object through its meanings, associations, inclinations, and wordplays—arising from the diversity of perceivers—is considered *ullekha* by the wise. (ViPrud 8.72)
Examples of [the use of the genitive] with verbs meaning "to please" (ruc) and with the word "yoga":
"All kings consider him the abode of the goddess Lakṣmī;
the hosts of enemy heroes consider him a mine for the highest degree of valor."
And those whose fame has been won for their mastery of the stages of learning and conduct praise incessantly the city of the illustrious Kākatīndra.
By means of paronomasia (śleṣa), for example:
"Fierce toward his enemies, radiant in his virtues,"
The lords of poets declare King Rudra to be Rāma in his countenances, Bhīma in battles, and Puruṣottama in the graces of Lakṣmī.
This is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
Now, two figures of speech based on *adhyavasāya* (identification) are defined.
*Adhyavasāya* is the apprehension of identity between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*) through the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of one or the other.
It is of two kinds: by swallowing the object and by swallowing the subject.
O wise ones, that in which the subject matter, through its connection with the attributes of another, is perceived as being that other, is called *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). (ViPrud 8.75)
Where, through a connection with the qualities or actions of something non-contextual, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) consisting of the imagining of the contextual as being non-contextual,
that is of two kinds: expressed (*vācyā*) and implied (*pratīyamānā*).
When words expressing probability— such as *nūnam*, *dhruvam*, or *prāyaḥ*— are employed, [the suggested meaning] is expressed (*vācyā*);
however, when they are not employed, it is implied (*pratīyamānā*).
That [determination] is twofold by virtue of being the object of determination for the four— genus, action, quality, and substance;
and each of these is fourfold.
When these two are divided into two types each—by way of being positive (bhāva) or negative (abhāva)—there are eight varieties.
When *adhyavasāya* (determination) is divided into two types—by way of having a quality (*guṇa*) as its cause and by way of having an action (*kriyā*) as its cause—each of these has sixteen modes.
Furthermore, the cause is divided into two types by way of being expressed (*vācya*) or implied (*gamyatva*), and this distinction applies only to *utprekṣā* where the cause is expressed.

In the case of suggested (pratīyamāna) poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), when words such as "as if" (*iva*) are not employed and the ground (*nimitta*) for the fancy is not stated, the fancy would be without support.

Likewise, there is a manifold variety [of suggested fancy] depending on whether the universal (*jāti*) and so forth are the objects of the mental determination (*adhyavasāya*) in their own form, as the cause, or as the effect.
Even in the case of expressed (*vācya*) poetic fancy, when the cause or the effect is the object of the fancy, the ground must necessarily be stated.

For instance: just as when the probandum (*sādhya*) is not mentioned, its designation as the "probans" (*sādhana*) does not sustain the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), so too is it when the probans is not mentioned, its designation as the "probandum" likewise fails to do so;
this is because the two are mutually dependent.
In the case of a poetic fancy regarding a cause (*hetūtprekṣā*), the effect is the motive.
If that [effect] were not apprehended, with respect to what could it be construed as an effect? For instance:
"In the shoreless ocean of fame of King Pratāparudra..."
The three worlds were as if overwhelmed by the contact with the foul reputation of that wicked lord.

In this case, since the cause for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), namely "immersion," is not explicitly mentioned, the fancy regarding the cause—that it is "due to attachment"—does not bring forth any aesthetic charm. Or, for example:
"The sun enters the sword of the Andhra king under the guise of a reflection, as if for the sake of causing the lotus upon which the Goddess of Victory resides to bloom. (ViPrud 8.77)

In this case, since the cause of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā)—the entry of the sun—is not mentioned, the fancy regarding the result (*phalotprekṣā*), namely "as if for the sake of the blooming of the lotuses that are the abodes of the Goddess of Victory," is improper.
Therefore, within the category of fancy regarding the essential nature (*svarūpotprekṣā*) alone, there is a twofold division based on whether the cause is mentioned or not.
Consequently, the enumeration of the varieties of expressed fancy (*vācyotprekṣā*) is as follows.

1. Poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the nature of the existence of a genus, caused by an apprehended quality. 2. Poetic fancy regarding the nature of the non-existence of a genus, caused by an apprehended quality.
3. Poetic fancy regarding the nature of the existence of a genus, caused by an apprehended action.
4. Poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the nature of a genus, where the cause of the action is expressed and the absence [of the genus] is the essence.

5. Poetic fancy regarding the nature of a genus, where the cause is unexpressed and presence is the essence. 6. Poetic fancy regarding the nature of a genus, where the cause is unexpressed and absence is the essence.

7. Poetic fancy (utprekṣā) based on the cause of the existence of a genus, with a quality as the apprehended cause. 8. Poetic fancy based on the cause of the non-existence of a genus, with a quality as the apprehended cause.
9. Poetic fancy based on the cause of the existence of a genus, with an action as the apprehended cause.

10. Poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the non-existence of a genus caused by an action based on an apprehended [quality] as its cause. 11. Poetic fancy regarding the existence of a genus as a result caused by a quality based on an apprehended [quality] as its cause.
12. Poetic fancy regarding the non-existence of a result as a genus caused by a quality based on an apprehended [quality] as its cause.
13. There is the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of an effect produced by an action whose cause is apprehended, and the poetic fancy of a genus.
Thus, there are fourteen varieties of the poetic fancy of a genus (*jātyutprekṣā*).
In this very same sequence, the poetic fancies of quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and substance (*dravya*) are also to be enumerated.
Thus, there are fifty-six varieties of expressed *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy),
while there are forty-eight varieties of implied *utprekṣā*.

Here, even within the category of *svarūpotprekṣā* (fancy regarding the nature itself), because of the rule that a cause (*nimitta*) must be provided, and because no specific excellence of beauty arises when the cause is merely understood— whether it takes the form of a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*)— only one single variety is counted.
It is accepted that both qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*) can be the objects of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) as well as the causes for such fancy.
In the classical treatises on poetics (*alaṅkāra*), there is merely a numerical enumeration of ninety-six varieties of *utprekṣā*.
The excellence of beauty, however, consists of exactly fifty-six varieties.
Among these, examples are given according to their possibility.
An example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the nature of a genus arising from the cause of an assumed quality is as follows:
The fame of King Kākati Vīrarudra, seated upon his throne— possessing a splendor equal to ten million moons, eclipsing the glory of the kings of the East,
and arising from the intense joy born of obtaining the protection of the southern monarchs— [has spread].
It flashes at the horizons of the quarters like the laughter of the three worlds.
Here, the word *prabhā* (light) denotes a genus (*jāti*).

Since the "laughter-light" (*aṭṭahāsaprabhā*) of the three worlds is established through the bold poetic assertion (*kaviprauḍhokti*) of the poet, there is no room for the suspicion that it is a simile (*upamā*).
An example of a figure of speech where the nature of a genus is poetically imagined (*utprekṣā*) based on a genus that serves as the cause for an expressed action is as follows:
The rows of thick pollen immediately swelled up from that [lotus] which had been turned into a lake by the consecration waters of King Rudra, the beloved of heroes.
It was like a cluster of blossoms on the sprouts of the hair-follicles of joy upon the earth.
Here, in the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that "it is a cluster of sprouts of horripilation," the cause is the act of making [the body] moist, which takes the form of an action.

An example of a poetic fancy regarding the essential nature of a genus where the cause is not explicitly stated is as follows: "The luster of the moon-like nails of Pratāparudra [falls] upon the feet of kings who prostrate themselves."
Like a lamp for reading the series of letters inscribed by fate upon her forehead.

Here, by the expression "just like a lamp," a genus (*jāti*) is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*). An example of a poetic imagination regarding the very nature of the absence of a genus, caused by a quality that has been adopted, is as follows:
"Washed by the waves of the nectar of Pratāparudra’s virtues, [the people] shine forth with their limbs rendered stainless."
Kings who have been excessively arrogant are washed clean by the waters of the sword and become even more transparently pure.
An example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the nature of the non-existence of a cause whose sign is unappropriated (*anupāttanimitta*) is as follows:
"Arising from the crushing of the elephants and horses prepared for the expedition of victory of King Rudra— the conqueror of the quarters and whose great splendor extends over the entire universe— "
