Having eclipsed his rival forces with his dust, as if making the sky devoid of the sun,
he establishes other suns known as his own majesty in every direction.
In this case, "asūryām" (sunless) indicates the absence of a genus (*jāti*).
An example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on a genus as the cause is as follows: "By the noble arm of Pratāparudra, the sole sustainer of the universe..."
The Earth, as if upon a soft bed, had been made to forget her dwelling upon the mountains of her lineage.
In this case, "as if it were a bed" constitutes a *jāti-hetu-utprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause for a universal).

An example of *jāty-abhāva-hetu-utprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause for the absence of a universal) is as follows: "The Creator, reflecting that the earth lacked the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*)," and so forth.
He created the Lord of Kākatīya, whose majesty lay in his guileless generosity.

Here, the absence of the universal (jāti) serves as the cause for the state of not being a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa). An example of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the fruit of a universal is as follows: "Surely, in order to become the long supporting pillars of the earth..."
The arms of King Vīrarudra hang down as far as his knees.

In this instance, "becoming a pillar" constitutes the result of the genus (*jāti*). An example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the result of the absence of a genus (*jātyabhāvaphalotprekṣā*) is as follows:
"Beholding the animals that were not to be slaughtered, the enemies of the Lord of Kākatīya..."
For the most part, they have resorted to subsisting on grass in order to attain a superhuman state.
In this instance, "for the sake of superhumanity" constitutes the fruit of the absence of caste (jāti).
An example of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the essential nature of an action is as follows:
"Of the wives of the enemies of the illustrious Kākatīya king..."
In the desert region where they dwell, the forest edges— with their interiors suddenly made resonant by waves of breath— seem to offer replies to those who have made their pleas.
An example of a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) regarding the non-existence of the very nature of an action is as follows:

"When the Lord of the Kākatīyas turned his face away [in battle], even the forest border, with its tips of hard thorns, seemed to drag the enemies' hair toward itself, as if it were granting them entry into its own interior. (ViPrud 8.88)
Here, in the phrase "not taking," there is an absence of the essential nature of the action.
An example of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the cause of the action is as follows: "The sprouts of pride among kings wither day by day."
As if overcome by the intense heat of the sun of the Kākatiya lord’s majesty.
In this context, [the phrase] "as if by overcoming, etc. indicates the causality of an action.
An example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the absence of a cause for an action is as follows: "How could her two cheek-plates have become such as they are..."
As if not seeing one another, they both had reached such a state of emaciation.
An example of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the fruit of an action (*kriyāphalotprekṣā*) is as follows:

"The roar of the march of the Lord of Andhra—acting as a great protector against the fury of the thunderbolt—plunges into the interiors of mountain caves, as if to search for the hosts of enemies who have hidden therein. (ViPrud 8.91)
An example of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the fruit of an action is as follows:

"In the groves of the boundary mountains, the wives of the *siddhas*, having fashioned half-moons of moonlight, sing of the playful glories of the fame of Śrī Vīrarudra, as if unable to touch the darkness. (ViPrud 8.92)
In this case, "as if not to be touched" constitutes the fruit of an action.
An example of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the nature of a quality is as follows: "The playful glance of the compassionate Lord of the Kākatīs shines forth."
Even among all the constituent elements, he was like grace incarnate.
An example of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on the absence of a quality (*guṇābhāvasvarūpotprekṣā*) is as follows:

"With all her limbs cooled by the drops of water from the great coronation of Pratāparudra, the Earth shines as if the heat of the heavy sighs of the Lord of Serpents—his burden of pain now stilled—has been dispelled. (ViPrud 8.94)
In this case, there is an absence of the quality [of coolness] expressed as "one whose heat has been stilled.
An example of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on a cause for a quality is as follows: "Having approached those who have become the refuge of the glories of victory..."
In battle, the sword of the illustrious Vīrarudra was eager to seize the glory of victory from his enemy kings, as if out of envy.

In the phrase "as if out of envy," the excellence (*guṇa*) functions as the cause [of the poetic fancy]. An example of a poetic fancy where the absence of excellence serves as the cause is as follows:
"Having now become those whose feet are kissed by the heels of the profound majesty of King Vīrarudra..."
Thus, as if out of a lack of joy in their very existence, the oceans assume a state of turbidity.
In this case, "due to lack of joy and so forth" indicates that the absence of qualities serves as the cause [for the following].
An example of *guṇaphalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the fruit of a quality) is as follows: "As if eager for the sake of purifying their blessings, which are smoky with poison..."
The female serpents [sang] the virtues of the Lord of the Kākatīyas, emitting nectar to sing them.
In this case, the phrase "for the sake of purity" indicates that the quality (guṇa) functions as the fruit.
An example of a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the fruit of the absence of a quality is as follows:
"As if, for the sake of enmity-free coexistence with the female deer who have acquired kinship through dwelling in the forest, [the birds], themselves having no refuge..."
The women of the lord of the Trilinga country turned their faces away from the playful movements of his eyes.
Here, by the phrase "for the sake of non-enmity," the absence of a quality is shown to be the fruit [of the comparison].

An example of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the essential nature of a substance (dravyasvarūpa) is as follows: "Thinking, 'Perfection does not exist eternally in this [world],' the sky, having abandoned its state, descended to the surface of the earth."
Bringing joy like the moon, the new lord of the Kākatīs shines in the world with his own splendor.

An example of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the absence of the essential nature of a substance (*dravyasvarūpābhāvotprekṣā*): "While the illustrious Kākatīndra—who is uniquely eminent in his generosity and who instantly fulfills the multitude of supplicants—shines upon the earth, the heavens seem as if deprived of the Pārijāta tree. (ViPrud 8.100)
Here, the absence of the *pārijāta* tree from heaven is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*).
An example of the poetic fancy based on a material cause (*dravyahetūtprekṣā*) is as follows:
"By King Pratāparudra, the expansion of the wings of the mountains..."
It was uprooted from its very foundation, as if by another wielder of the thunderbolt.
An example of *utprekṣā* based on the absence of a material cause (*dravyahetvabhāva*) is as follows:
"Viriñci was thrown into confusion by Meru, whose limbs were melted by the heat of the Kākatīya’s prowess, as if by a mountain that was no longer made of gold. (ViPrud 8.102)
In this case, there is an absence of a logical reason (*hetu*) expressed by the phrase "by the mountain not made of gold.
An example of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding a substance as a fruit (*dravyaphala*) is as follows: "As if for a hundred oceans of milk, [he gave] the peak of Mount Kailāsa."
Surely Pratāparudra has spread his fame in all directions.
In this case, in the phrase "to [the ocean] of milk for hundreds of times," the substance itself constitutes the fruit.
An example of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) of a fruit arising from the absence of a substance is as follows:
"Arising from the King Vīrarudra’s departure for victory..."
The sphere of the directions was covered with dust, as if it had become devoid of space.

Here, "spaceless" (nirākāśam) means for the sake of the absence of space; in this manner, other varieties [of this figure] should be illustrated as far as possible. Thus concludes the analysis of the figures of speech containing comparison (aupamya).

The figure of speech *atiśayokti* (hyperbole): where the object [of comparison] is not mentioned and the correlate is instead described, that shall be *atiśayokti*, which has the poet’s bold assertion as its lifeblood. (ViPrud 8.105)
Where, through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a poet, the subject (*viṣaya*) is concealed and the superstratum (*viṣayin*) is described, that is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
It has four varieties: non-difference where there is difference, and difference where there is non-difference; [and so forth].
There is non-connection where there is connection, and connection where there is non-connection; however,
that which consists in the reversal of the sequence between cause and effect is indeed distinct [from these], because it is rooted in indecision (*anadhyavasāya*).
However, because it is rooted in bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*), it is called hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
Among these, an example of non-difference where there is actually difference is as follows:
"It is fitting that the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*) was born from the ocean of the Kākatiya dynasty."
This Lord of Lakṣmī is truly marvelous; he is a great festival for the world of mortals.
In this case, there is an identification (adhyavasāya) between Pratāparudra and the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
An example of difference within identity (*abhede bheda*) is as follows:
"His loftiness is truly unique; his majesty is some indescribable depth."
The path of his majesty and fame is quite another, and the renown of his arms is entirely different;
I know that everything about King Rudra is truly new. As for the materials and the sequence devised for his creation, how much and of what kind could even the Four-faced Creator have prepared?
Here, although there is no real difference between the two heights and so forth, a difference is imagined.

Consequently, despite the difference between the height established by nature and the height established by the poet’s bold assertion (*kaviprauḍhokti*), there is an identification (*adhyavasāya*) based on their non-difference.
An example of non-connection where there is a connection is as follows:
The stone is the wish-fulfilling gem,
the tree is the celestial kalpa-tree, and this beast is the cow of plenty.
The entire world is likewise free from defects;
therefore, this fourfold creation of the Creator cannot,
O Lord, touch Rudra, who is the abode of the sovereignty of all virtues.
Here, even though there is a connection with the creation of the Creator (Brahmā), a lack of connection is expressed.
There is an identification here [of the present] with the past creation of Brahmā by means of the Lord (Īśvara).
An example of a connection where there is no connection is as follows:
O Brahman! Even though Mount Meru has been fashioned, why do you not feel such joy as this, O Lord? It is true that my office has now borne fruit, since Vīrarudra has been appointed.
Why do you boast falsely? He was requested by me for the protection of the three worlds.
The conversation between Hari and Brahmā arose as to whether Śambhu had descended to the earth.

Here, although no such conversation between Hari and Brahmā actually occurred, a connection is asserted where none exists. Furthermore, there is an identification of the Lord of the Kākatīs with Śambhu.
An example of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consisting of the reversal of the sequence between cause and effect is as follows:
O Mother! How is it that the arrows of Kāma fall as precursors to the gaze of the Lord of Kākatīya? Surely even Smara, conquered by her beauty and grace, has become his servant.
Here, the prior occurrence of the fall of the arrows of Love—which is the effect—is stated relative to the glance of the beloved—which is the cause.
This is the figure of speech *sahokti* (simultaneity).
Now, in the investigation of the figure of speech *uktisāmya* (equality of expression), there is that which is caused by *atiśayokti* (poetic exaggeration).
Co-mention (sahokti) is now defined:
where there is a connection with the sense of "together" (saha) through hyperbole (atiśayokti), extending as far as imagined similitude (kalpitopamā), that is accepted as co-mention. (ViPrud 8.111)

Where, through a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) characterized by non-difference despite difference— consisting in the inversion of the temporal sequence of cause and effect— one thing is construed as the primary correlate while the other is connected with it as a companion (*sahārtha*), and the relationship of subject and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) is thus conceived, there exists *sahokti* (concomitance).

Since the relationship of subject and object of comparison pertains to both the contextual (*prākaraṇika*) and the non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*), and since both are equally contextualized by virtue of their connection through the sense of "together," this [relationship] does not possess the nature of that [standard comparison].
An example of *sahokti* (simultaneity) based on the poetic figure *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) consisting of a reversal of the temporal sequence between cause and effect is as follows:

"In battles, the sword-blades of the Andhra king’s warriors, possessing the luster of blue lotus petals, fall upon the throats of enemy monarchs simultaneously with the flower-garlands cast by the celestial women. (ViPrud 8.112)

In this instance, the simultaneous occurrence of the falling of the divine garland with the moment following the fall of the sword is stated; thus, there is a reversal of temporal sequence (*paurvāparyaviparyaya*).

This is a case of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) consisting of non-difference where there is difference, which contains a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and takes the form of an identification (*adhyavasāya*) of non-difference, serving as the cause for an excellence of beauty.
An example based on that [non-difference] is as follows:
Day by day, the glory of King Rudra’s majesty rises,
illuminating the entire expanse of the quarters along with the sun of irreproachable luster.
Here, by means of paronomasia (*śleṣa*), there is an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) between the mountain of sunrise and spiritual exaltation, based on the [shared] expression "is rising.
This is the figure of speech *vinokti*. Now, *vinokti*, which is the opposite of *sahokti* (concomitance), is defined.
When, in the absence of some related thing, there occurs either the lack of delight or the presence of delight in another, that is known as *vinokti* (the figure of "without"). 8.114.
Where a thing becomes either pleasant or unpleasant due to the absence of someone, that is *vinokti* (description by separation).
It is of two kinds: unpleasantness and pleasantness.
O lords of poets, listen: what kind of poetic composition can there be without a description of the virtues of King Pratāparudradeva? (ViPrud 8.115)
Here, by means of the description of the virtues of Pratāparudra, it is stated that the splendor of poetry (*kāvyasri*) would be unlovely without them.
By this, the very injunction—that poets desiring the beauty of poetry must describe the virtues of Pratāparudra—is revealed. An example of loveliness (*ramyatā*) is as follows:
While King Rudra— whose pure majesty is the embodied bliss of the three worlds— reigned eternally victorious like the moon that fills its digits,
he attained a body that was full every day even without a spot.
If the moon were in the sky, it too would be beautiful.
In this passage concerning Pratāparudra, the moon's beauty is described as being without a spot;
for in the presence of an adversary endowed with every excellence, loveliness consists precisely in possessing such qualities oneself,
and not otherwise.
The figure of speech *samāsokti* (brief expression):
where, through the similarity of the adjectives, there occurs [an implication] regarding that which is under discussion.
When that which is not the subject at hand is understood [through implication], that is considered *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation).
Where the unmentioned (the *aprastuta*) is understood through the similarity of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the subject at hand (*prakṛta*), that is *samāsokti* (synecdoche).
It is of three kinds: [that based on] the similarity of double-meaning (*śliṣṭa*) qualifiers, and [that based on] common [qualifiers].
And [the type] containing a simile (*aupamyagarbha*).
An example of the identity of shared epithets (*śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇasāmya*) is as follows:
"Bearing a body that was suddenly loosened from its girdle, thrilled with horripilation, and straightened..."
The creeper-like sword of King Andhra seizes the throats of his enemies; through that contact,
rendered helpless by their state of passion, they close their eyes and, with their inner faculties long made void, indeed attain a certain state of being.
Here, by the power of the double-entendre (*śliṣṭa*) in the adjectives "with loosened girdle" and "thrilled with horripilation," the sword-blade is perceived as a heroine;
and through the adjectives such as "helpless due to feelings of passion," the enemies are perceived as heroes.
An example by means of common adjectives (*sādhāraṇaviśeṣaṇa*) is as follows:
O Lord of the Fish-bannered God [Kāmadeva], the state of Kākatīmīnātha has become one where shame has vanished, pride cast aside, a change of voice arises,
perspiration manifests, violent trembling of the limbs occurs, fainting sets in, tears flow,
and total dissolution has taken place.
Agitated by the god of love,
kings flee to solitary mountain caves, embraced by fear.
In this case, by the power of the common attributes shared by the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the terrible (*bhayānaka*) sentiments, the kings are perceived as heroes because they are embraced by fear.
An example of this through an epithet containing a simile (*aupamya-garbha-viśeṣaṇa*) is as follows:
"Filled with a multitude of jewels of virtue, full of the water of goodness..."
King Pratāparudra bears the splendor of the entire earth.
In this figure of speech, *samāsokti* (brief expression), the superimposition (*samāropa*) of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is everywhere the very lifeblood.
It is fourfold:
the superimposition of a worldly convention upon a worldly object; [and so forth].

Superimposition (samāropa) is of two kinds: superimposition of the conventional usage of a scriptural entity upon a scriptural entity, and superimposition of the conventional usage of a worldly entity [upon a scriptural entity].
Thus, regarding a scriptural entity, there is both the superimposition of the conventional usage of a scriptural entity and the superimposition of the conventional usage of a worldly entity.
Thus it is fourfold;
the examples follow in order:
"He is resplendent with the glory of a magnificent and expansive gift that radiates through seven limbs."
The auspicious-souled Pratāparudra extends his sovereignty over the entire earth.

In this case, regarding the worldly subject at hand, there is the cognition of a worldly convention involving a world-encircling elephant (diggaja) named Sārvabhauma. Likewise: "In the sword of Pratāparudra, which is preeminent in battle and by its own great weight instantly overcomes the rising arguments of opponents, there resides a great mastery in refutation. (ViPrud 8.122)
In this case, there is a superimposition of the conventional usage of objects well-known in the treatises on logic onto an ordinary sword;
likewise:
"The path of excellence for a new subject matter, possessing the essence of the words spoken by a venerable master."
Triumphant is the poetic glory of the poets under King Vīra, which at every step conceives some reality graspable through sacred revelation;
in this glory, the assembly of the wise is able to skillfully exercise its authority.
In this matter concerning the science of poetics (*alaṃkāraśāstra*), there is the superimposition of the technical terminology of the *tantra* scriptures upon the subject at hand.
Likewise—
she is "possessed of ornaments" (*sālaṃkārā*).
The speech of the Lord of the Kākatīyas shines forth, possessing all colors, endowed with qualities, overflowing with aesthetic flavor,
and bound to the inner emotional state.
In this matter of the science of poetics, there is the superimposition of the behavior of a worldly heroine upon that which is called *bhāratī*.
In the figure of speech known as *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation), because there is no mention of both the qualifier and the qualified, it differs from *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
This is the figure of speech *vakrokti* (indirect expression).
Even when other ornaments share a similarity of expression, *vakrokti* (paronomastic speech) is distinguished by its inclusion of *śleṣa* (punning).

It is defined as follows: "Where there is an interpretation otherwise of a statement that has been spoken in one way—either through intonation (*kāku*) or through punning (*śleṣa*)—that is called *vakrokti*. (ViPrud 8.125)
*Vakrokti* (paronomasia or intentional deviation) is the application of a sentence uttered with a certain intended meaning to another intended meaning.
Although such a deviation of expression may occur incidentally even in other figures, *vakrokti* is distinguished from all other ornaments because it lacks that specific definition.
An example by means of intonation (*kāku*) is as follows: [Example omitted per instructions]
"O friend, the king is indeed deeply beloved; he is completely devoted to her splendor.
Surely you too, by your own splendor, ought not to consider yourself inferior. (ViPrud 8.126)
"O friend, the king indeed has many favorites; his attachment to riches is excessive. Even though you are inferior to those riches, why do you disparage yourself?
Herein, [the meaning is: "You also are not of inferior quality compared to riches."
Therefore, it is understood through an interrogative intonation (*kāku*) that "the king is indeed attached even to you; why do you disparage yourself?
For example, by means of *śleṣa* (paronomasia):
O beautiful one, what caste does he always abide in within your heart? Is he not the moon,
the ornament of the mountain?
Is Sumeru like this?
No, it is the all-pervading Lord Rudra.
Is he the Master, my friend?

"You have spoken the truth, O fortunate one; you are born from the very essence of the lineage"— at these words, which were indeed free from mockery, the young bride forgot her separation for a moment.
Now, the description of intrinsic nature (svabhāvokti): This charming description of a thing exactly as it is is called *svabhāvokti*. (ViPrud_8.128)
Svabhāvokti (Naturalistic Description) is that wherein the description of an object is composed with beauty according to its actual state,
as for example:
"With ichor flowing, ears flapping in dance, head tossed aloft, and standing on three legs..."
Kākativīrarudra became one for whom there was perpetual celebration, by means of the elephant whose trunk-tip was ever-playful.
The figure of speech *vyājokti* (dissembling).
Now, *vyājokti* is described because of its similarity to [the previous] *ukti* (statement):
*Vyājokti* is that where an arisen fact is concealed. (ViPrud 8.130)

*Vyājokti* (Concealment) is that figure of speech wherein a manifest object, because it is worthy of being hidden due to its inherent similarity [to something else], is covered over by some pretext. For example:
"At the time of taking the hand of the Earth, when horripilation spread over all his limbs out of joy, the moon of the Kākatiya lineage, the ornament of kings—"
Smiling gently, the noble and steadfast prince looked toward the elder ministers, wondering, "Should the royal consecration now be performed with cool waters?"

In this passage, King Pratāparudradeva, concealing through his dignified composure (*dhīrodātta*) the hair-raising thrill born of taking the hand of the earth (in marriage) under the pretext of the coolness of the waters of the great consecration (*mahābhiṣeka*), causes the ministers to be perceived [as if they were the very waters].
This is the figure of speech *mīlana* (concealment).
*Mīlana* is said to occur when, following a statement of concealment (*vyājokti*), something is perceived due to a certain similarity.
Concealment (*mīlana*) is where one object is hidden by another object.
The figure of speech known as *mīlanā* (concealment) occurs when one object is concealed by another object;
it is of two kinds: the concealment of the adventitious by the innate, and the concealment of the innate by the adventitious.
To provide examples in their respective order:
By the fierce flashes of the thunderbolt-like weapons of King Kākati Vīrarudra,
those who had fled from the battlefield and whose lives were extinguished somewhere else— [fell upon his enemies].
The great desert heat, though long transferred to the bodies of the wives of his enemies who suffer from the most intense fever of love, is no longer perceived on the road.
In this case, by means of the innate heat of the fire of love arising from the beloved of the enemy, the adventitious desert heat is concealed due to the circumstances of the path. Likewise:
"Because of the power of Pratāparudra’s arm, the kings constantly dwell within fear;
thus, even when perspiration, tears, trembling, and the like arise, the women do not trust in love during their amorous conversations. (ViPrud 8.134)
In this case, there is the concealment of the innate trembling born of love by the adventitious trembling born of fear;
this is the figure of speech known as *sāmānya*.
*Sāmānya* is that where, due to the equality of qualities, there is the identity of one thing with another. (ViPrud 8.135)
The figure of speech known as *sāmānya* (commonality) occurs when this very object, through the equality of its qualities, attains identity with another object; for example:
"When the fame of the Andhra king was unobserved among Kailāsa, the Ocean of Milk, and the swans of [Viṣṇu’s] vehicle..."
In the first [yuga], three types of men smile upon seeing their own servants looking on with agitation.
Here, as the fame of Pratāparudra spreads throughout the worlds, there is an identification (*aikātmya*) with pure objects such as Mount Kailāsa and others;
this is the figure of speech *Tadguṇa*.
It is called *Tadguṇa* because of the excellence resulting from the proximity of the qualities of another, due to their extreme similarity.
That quality consists in the acquisition of another's superior qualities through the relinquishing of one's own qualities.
The figure of speech *tadguṇa* occurs where, having abandoned one's own inferior quality, an excellence belonging to a proximate object is adopted. For example:
"By the expansions of the moonlight from the toenails of King Pratāparudradeva..."
The kings, their jeweled crowns bowed down, were rendered pure.
Here, the ruby crowns of the kings bowing down abandoned their own crimson luster and bore instead the whiteness inherent in the moonlight of the toe-nails of Kākati Vīrarudra.
This is the ornament *atadguṇa* (non-attribution of quality).
*Atadguṇa* is defined as the opposite of that [the *tadguṇa* ornament].
When a cause exists, there would be the non-acceptance of other qualities; thus it would be "devoid of that quality."
The figure of speech *atadguṇa* occurs where there is no assumption of another's qualities (*guṇa*), even though the cause consisting of proximity exists. For example:
"He wanders about the world near the Lord [Śiva], who is radiant with the loud laughter of his sport;
he is illumined on all sides by the shining blue luster playing upon the body of the Enemy of the Daityas [Viṣṇu]."
And near Brahmā, whose body was radiant with the luster of gold,
the majesty of the fame of King Rudra nourished his own bright splendor.

Here, although the worlds surrounding Hari, Hara, and Viriñci are filled with their respective diverse splendors, the unrestrained whiteness of Pratāparudra’s fame alone expands as it wanders incessantly among them;
this is the figure of speech known as *virodhālaṅkāra* (apparent contradiction).
Since contradiction has been introduced [as a topic], the figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra* (contradiction) is now defined.
When a contradiction appears as a mere semblance (*ābhāsatva*), it is considered the poetic figure *virodhālaṅkṛti*. (ViPrud 8.141)
The figure of speech called *virodhālaṅkāra* (contradiction) is that in which a contradiction perceived initially as a mere appearance is resolved in the final conclusion.
Among these, when there is a contradiction of a genus (*jāti*) with a genus and so forth, there are four varieties;
when there is a contradiction of an action (*kriyā*) with an action, a quality (*guṇa*), or a substance (*dravya*), there are three varieties.
Regarding contradiction, there are two types of contradiction involving a quality (guṇa): contradiction with another quality and contradiction with a substance (dravya).
There is one type of contradiction involving a substance: contradiction with another substance.
Thus, there are ten types of contradiction.
An opposition between genus and genus, as well as with action, is as follows:
"O King, though he possesses a lotus-like origin (*padmākara*), this ruler is exceedingly non-insentient in his disposition (*ajaḍāśaya*);
though he possesses a stream of most pure water (*vimalataravāridhārā*), he causes distress to the enemy lords of the earth. (ViPrud 8.142)

In the first half of this verse, there is a contradiction between two universals (jāti), because there is a contradiction in the idea that "even Kamalākara is one whose disposition is not dull-witted.
In the second half, there is a contradiction between a universal and an action (kriyā).
Because a stream of extremely pure water is opposed to causing heat;
here, there is a contradiction based on *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
An example of the contradiction between a genus (*jāti*) and both a quality (*guṇa*) and a substance (*dravya*) is as follows:
This King Vīrarudra, though an emperor, is free from pride; though radiant, he is a treasury of arts; he is a playground for wonders.
Here, "even a universal monarch is free from pride" expresses a contradiction between genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*).
"Even the sun is a treasury of digits" expresses a contradiction between genus and substance (*dravya*);
for since a treasury of digits is singular, it possesses substantiality.
Here too, the basis is *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
An example of the contradiction between one action and another is as follows:
"Kākati Vīrarudra, while bringing about the destruction of those who hate righteousness and those who steal wealth..."
Although its range is common to all three aims of life, it makes the heart moist with affection even toward the enemy of desire.

In this context, for one whose conduct pertains to all three aims of life (*trivarga*), it is contradictory to cause the ruin of those who oppose virtue (*dharma*) and wealth (*artha*), and yet to show affection toward enemies of pleasure (*kāma*).
An example of contradiction between an action and its qualities or substances is as follows:
"Though this is the playground of the Conqueror (*jiṣṇu*), he is intensely devoted to his lineage."
Even the king, the lord of the Andhra people, brings about the blossoming of the lotus.
Here, in the phrase "the affection for his lineage (*gotravātsalya*) of Jiṣṇu’s vihāra," there is a contradiction between action and quality (*kriyāguṇavirodha*).
In the phrase "the king, even while causing the blossoming of lotuses (*kamalollāsaṃ kurvan*)," there is a contradiction between action and substance (*kriyādravyavirodha*).
In these cases as well, the basis is solely *śleṣa* (punning paronomasia).
An opposition between quality and quality is as follows:
"O King Rudra, you are praiseworthy in the world for protecting the earth through your sovereignty."
How is it that she, though red, has become pale?
"O Rudranarendra, since you are praiseworthy as a king who delights this world,
how is it that she, though once red, has become white?"
In this case, there is a contradiction between redness and paleness.
An example of the contradiction of a quality with a substance is as follows:
"The Lord of the Kākatiyas, though fierce with blazing majesty..."
Having become the life-giver, he shines eternally as the one who brings joy to the entire universe.
Here, there is a contradiction between a quality (*guṇa*) and a substance (*dravya*), namely that Pratāparaudra is also "Jaivātṛka" (the life-giver).
An example of the contradiction of one substance with another substance is as follows:
"This Lord of the Kākatīyas shines; though Rudra, he possesses four faces."
And thus this Supreme Person is called Jiṣṇu.
Thus, ten varieties have been shown.
This [type of figure] also occurs through non-connection (*aśleṣa*), as for example:
"The gaze of King Kākatīya is cool by its very nature, even though it is a look."
She became one who scorched all the limbs of the rival kings.
Here, there is the contradiction that she is "cooling by nature yet burning";
this is the figure of speech *viśeṣālaṅkāra*.
Now, the figures of speech containing contradiction (*virodha*) within them are being examined.

The ornament of distinction (*viśeṣālaṃkāra*) is of three kinds: that which consists of a substratumless superstratum, that which is both one and has multiple objects, and that which makes impossible things possible. (ViPrud 8.150)
Where the supported is fixed without a support, that is one particularity (*viśeṣa*). When a single thing has multiple objects of perception, that is the second particularity.
When something else that is impossible in the context at hand is produced, that is the third.
The illustrative examples in their respective order are as follows:

"The glory of fame once resting upon kings such as Nala, Nahuṣa, Dilīpa, and Dharmaputra now daily approaches and sports with the renown of Kākati Vīrarudra, having entered into friendship with it. (ViPrud 8.151)
In this case, even upon the disappearance of the former kings who served as its support, the glory that depended upon them remains; as it is said:
"Beholding the lord of the earth with his sword raised, the rival kings, overwhelmed by fear, look behind, ahead, to their sides, within and without, and in every direction."
With their arms and weapons fallen away due to the jolting of their chariots as they rush out from the gaps between the wheels,
they flee from mountain to mountain, the splendor of their gravity and heroism flashing amidst their trembling.
In this regard, although King Pratāparudra is but one, he is perceived as many by enemy kings who are terrified; and so it is said:
"Wherever the glance of Lord Vīrarudra—sweet in its course through his grace—falls upon a person in the assembly of that ocean of boundless compassion..."
Does he who is superior to all not preside over the three worlds— he who transcends Indra, Mātali, and the lord of the Kinnaras, and who is exalted above the entire universe?

"What extraordinary person, having been made a recipient of the grace of Pratāparudra’s glance, does not obtain [everything]? Thus is the figure of speech *aśakyavastvantarakaraṇa* (the production of another impossible thing).
This is the figure of speech *adhika* (excess).
The figure of speech *adhika* is defined based on the marvelousity of the relationship between the locus (*ādhāra*) and the located (*ādheya*).”
The absence of conformity between the container and the contained is considered "excessive" (adhika).
Where there is no correspondence between the locus and that which rests upon it, that is the figure of speech *adhika*.
It is of two kinds, according to whether the locus is small or large.
In a small portion of the cavity of the universe, the fame of the Lord of Kākatīya— becoming a single mass through its own effortless contraction as it wandered at will due to its vastness,
yet shining with the radiance of his body— [is surpassed] by these: the snowy mountain (Himālaya), the silver mountain (Kailāsa), the celestial river (Gaṅgā), and the moon.
Now, its state of being a mass [of light] has been manifested by the oceans whose primary waters are milk.
Here, there is the smallness of the abode—the hollow of heaven and earth—and the vastness of the glory of Pratāparudra, which is supported by it.
An example of the second [type] is as follows:
"Somewhere, somewhere are Kaliṅga, Mālava, Mahārāṣṭra, Aṅga, Vaṅga, and so forth..."

O wonder! Kings whose entire horizons were overwhelmed by the majesty of such military power have vanished into the shoreless ocean of the strength of King Kākati Vīrarudra’s vast array; they do not find even a corner for fulfillment, alas!

Here, there is the vastness of the ocean that is Pratāparudra’s army, which serves as the substratum (*āśraya*), and the smallness of the armies of the kings of Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, and others who depend upon it (*āśrita*). Now, [there are also] *vibhāvanā* and *viśeṣokti*.
The production of an effect without a cause is called *vibhāvanā* (manifestation);
the non-production [of an effect] despite the presence of its causal complex is declared to be *viśeṣokti* (peculiar statement).

Vibhāvanā is that wherein the production of an effect is described through the abandonment of its well-known causes. Viśeṣokti is that wherein there is a non-production of an effect even when all [its causes] are present. For example—
For the adversaries defeated by Pratāparudra and having fled into the caves of the Vindhya mountains,
darkness arises even during the day, and their splendors do not manifest even in the stars.
In this case, night is the well-known cause for the manifestation of darkness;
yet its arising is described as occurring even without it.
An unestablished cause, such as grief and the like, certainly exists;
likewise, although the rays of the sun are present during the days, the non-arising of heat exists here because of causes such as a lack of intensity.
This is the figure of speech *asaṃgati* (incongruity).
In the context of the discussion regarding the contradiction between cause and effect, non-connection (*asaṃgati*) is stated:
non-connection occurs when the cause and the effect exist in different locations. (ViPrud 8.159)
Where the cause and effect, though existing in the same location, are described as being situated in different places, that is the figure of speech *asaṃgati* (incongruity). For example:
"While the lord Vīrarudra bears the heavy burden of the earth, the crests of the subordinate chieftains remain perpetually and exceedingly bowed. (ViPrud 8.160)
In this case, [the figures are] "the burden of the earth upon the king" and "bowing down to enemies.
This is the figure *vicitra* (the marvellous).
Because it follows the discussion of *virodha* (contradiction), *vicitra* is now defined.
The exertion for the sake of attaining a fruit that is contrary to one's own nature is "vicitra" (the strange). // ViPrud_8.161 //
The figure of speech called *vicitra* (the marvelous) occurs where an effort is made for the sake of attaining a result that is contrary to one's own [interests].
For example:
"In the presence of King Pratāparudra, the lords of men from afar..."
They dismount from the elephants, for there is no restriction on their mounting them.
Here, the effort made to "ascend" and "descend" is for the sake of attaining a contrary result.
This is the figure of speech *anyonyālaṃkāra* (mutual ornamentation).
Now, *anyonya* (mutuality) is defined.
This too is rooted in contradiction, wherein there would be a mutual relationship of producer and produced between them. (ViPrud 8.163)
Where there is a mutual relationship of producer and produced by means of action, that is the figure of speech *anyonyālaṃkāra* (mutual ornament). For example:
"As King Rudra ascends the throne of the Kākati king, it shines resplendently."
Having ascended that [throne] which is a vessel of radiant jewels, the king too bears a greater measure of splendor.

In this instance, there is a mutual relationship of being the embellished (alaṃkārya) between Pratāparudra and the auspicious throne (bhadrasana); this is the figure of speech Viṣama (the Uneven). Now, the figure of speech Viṣama based on contradiction (virodha) is described.
Where there is the production of a contradictory effect, or where misfortune occurs, or where there is a union of incompatible things— that is the *viṣama* (incongruity) ornament, which is threefold.
The first *viṣama* occurs where a contrary effect arises from a cause;
the second is the arising of misfortune that was not an intended effect;
and the third is the conjunction of two dissimilar things.
In that regard, first, for example:
"Behold the glory of fame, white as the radiance of the autumnal moon, arising from the sword of King Kākati Vīrarudra, which is dark as the *tamāla* tree."
Having now heard that the celestial river was born from the lotus-feet of the Enemy of Mura, his mind, having attained its true nature, ceases from wonder.
Here, from a sword of blue color, there arises fame white as the moon.
An example of the second [type] is as follows:
"Let alone the hope for victory of the enemy kings who have reached the edge of the battlefield."
Upon the sight of Pratāparudra, weapons fall away along with the lives of his enemies.
In this case, there is not only the non-occurrence of victory—the fruit of the exertion for battle—but even the occurrence of misfortune in the form of the loss of life.
An example of the third [type] is as follows:
"Where are those kings whose natures were honored by such magnificent power?"
"Where is this dwelling in the wilderness, a sole abode of inauspicious conduct?"—
thus looking again and again at their enemies in the forest lands, the Śabara warriors of Rudra’s city praise the majesty of King Rudra in every direction.
Herein is the conjunction of forest regions that are inauspicious and unsightly, yet fit for kings who ought to dwell in great cities.
Thus have the ornaments containing contradiction (virodhagarbha) been determined.
Now, the ornament of similarity (samālaṅkāra):
Now, the figure of speech *samā* (simile) is defined by way of contrast with the *viṣama* (incongruity):
that is the *samā* ornament when there is a conjunction of two things that are mutually corresponding.

The figure of speech *samā* (concordance) occurs where a combination of mutually corresponding objects is effected. For example: "All sciences, together with Lakṣmī, have united in the son of Pradyumna; thus, Brahmā himself has become one who possesses a beautiful eye. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 8.170)

"Having united all the sciences with Lakṣmī in Pratāparudra, Brahmā himself becomes fulfilled, having achieved his purpose. Here, there is a conjunction of all the sciences and Lakṣmī in Pratāparudra.
This is the figure of speech *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing). Now begins the section on figures of speech where the comparison is implied (*gamyamānopamya*).
[It occurs] when there is a common attribute (*tulyadharmata*) between the subjects under discussion and others, exclusively.
Where a comparison is understood, that is considered *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing).

*Tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) is that figure where a comparison is understood through the connection of a common attribute between either exclusively relevant subjects (*prastuta*) or exclusively irrelevant subjects (*aprastuta*). An example of the former [relevant subjects] is as follows:
"When the god Rudra was seated upon his auspicious throne, both his glories and the wives of his enemies [were present]."
Those who possess various types of delusion constantly undergo a state of paleness at every moment.
In this case, both the glories and the wives of the enemies are the contextual subjects (*prakaraṇika*).
"Attaining whiteness" is the common attribute (*samāna-dharma*).
An example of non-contextual subjects (*aprākaraṇika*) is as follows:

When the lord of the Kākatiyas became the sovereign of the earth, the Tortoise, the Lord of Serpents, the Lord of Elephants, the Green One (Viṣṇu), the Moon, the Lineage, and the Mountains all attained mutual worthlessness.
In this instance, the Lord of Tortoises and the others are not relevant to the context;
their shared attribute is that they have become "pithless.
Here, the implied simile is not literal.
However, it is based on intention;
it is the figure of speech *dīpaka*.
When both the relevant (*prastuta*) and the irrelevant (*aprastuta*) are present together through a common attribute, [it is called *dīpaka*].
Where a comparison is understood [through implication], that is called *dīpaka*.

*Dīpaka* (the Illuminator) is that figure of speech where a comparison is understood between all the subjects—both the relevant (*prastuta*) and the irrelevant (*aprastuta*)—through their connection with a common attribute (*samānadharmasaṃbandha*).
This [attribute] is of three kinds according to whether it occurs at the beginning, middle, or end [of the sentence].
An example of *ādidīpaka* (the Illuminator at the beginning) is as follows:
The brother was joined with Nala by Śauri, the lamp of the Raghu dynasty;
the father-in-law was joined with Tapana by Kali, and the sister-in-law with Vīrudha.
"The Kṛta age shines through Nala; the Tretā through Śauri, the lamp of Raghu’s lineage; the Dvāpara through the son of Tapa; and the Kali age through Vīrarudra.
Here, just as the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages are resplendent through Nala, Rāma, and Dharmaputra respectively, [so too is this age resplendent through him].
Similarly, by means of Vīrarudra, the Kali age is understood to be "shining," thus providing a simile.
An example of *madhyadīpaka* (middle illumination) is as follows:
"The ocean [shines] with the Bhāgīrathī; the night with moonlight; and the full-moon day with the moon."
By his thread [of lineage] he was Kamalābhava, and by his fame he was Prabhākararudra.
The full-moon night shines with its moonlight upon the ocean of the Bhāgīrathī.
"By his sacred learning, he is like the lotus-born Brahmā; by his fame, he is Pratāparudra as well.
Here, just as the ocean and other bodies of water shine because of the Ganges and other rivers, so too does Pratāparudra shine because of his fame; thus, a simile is understood.
An example of *antadīpaka* (concluding illuminator) is as follows:
The Lord of the Gods protects the realm of the Asuras; the heroic and fierce Lord of Men protects the realm of men;
and the Lord of Serpents protects the realm of the Nagas—each keeping it free from affliction and secure.
The Lord of the Gods [ruled] the world of the Asuras, and the heroic Rudra, Lord of Men, [ruled] the world of men.
"The Lord of Serpents protects the world of serpents from harm and agitation.

Here, just as the world of gods and the world of serpents are protected by the Lord of Gods and the Lord of Serpents respectively, so too is the world of men protected by Vīrarudra; thus, a simile is understood.
Now, following the two figures of speech pertaining to word-meanings (*padārtha*), the two figures of speech pertaining to sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) are described.
First is the figure of speech *Prativastūpamā* (Parallelism):
where there is a general statement [of a common property] in two separate sentences.
That which relies on a comparison with something accessible is considered *prativastūpamā*.

Where a commonality is indicated through the relation of "thing and counter-thing" (*vastu-pratirastu-bhāva*) in two sentences, by that [means] there is the *prativastūpamā*, which implies a comparison.
It is of two kinds: by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) and by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). An example of the first is as follows:
The Mandara mountain alone is capable of churning the ocean;
Pratāparudra alone is powerful enough to churn his enemies.
Here, as the Mandara mountain is capable of churning the ocean, so Pratāparudra is able to churn his enemies; thus, a simile (*aupamya*) is understood.
An example of the second [type] is as follows:
"Pratāparudra alone is preeminent in delighting the people."
Apart from the moon, no other is capable of satisfying the cakora bird.
Here, just as the moon brings satisfaction to the *cakora* bird, so too does Vīrarudra bring delight to the people; thus, a comparison based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇaupamya*) is understood.
Now, the simile (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration):
where a common attribute is expressed through the relationship of image and reflection in two sentences, that is called *dṛṣṭānta* by those who know the nature of sentences. (ViPrud 8.181)

The figure of speech called *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration) occurs where a commonality (*sāmānya*) is indicated through the relationship of an original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) in two sentences.
It is also twofold, according to similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). An example of the first [type] is as follows:
Only a few mountains bear the earth, yet there is an incomparable majesty in the mountain of gold (Meru), whose forest-glories rival the capital cities of the world-protectors;
may the two kings who bring delight to the people [shine] alongside the illustrious Lord Vīrarudra.
What other greatness can there be for one whose arms are capable of bearing the burden of the three worlds?
Here, through the relationship of image and reflection between Pratāparudra and Mount Meru, a simile is implied.
An example by way of contrast (vaidharmyeṇa) is as follows:
"Prosperities awaken from the mere glance of the Kākati king’s eye of compassion."
The lotuses sleep for as long as the sun has not yet risen.

Here, just as lotuses blossom by the mere rising of the sun, so too do riches come into being by the mere glance of Pratāparudra’s compassion; thus, through contrast (*vaidharmya*), there is the figure of speech *nidarśanā*, which consists of the reflection of an image upon its counterpart.
Now, following the discussion of implied comparison (*gamyamāna-aupamya*), the figure of speech *nidarśanā* is examined.

Where the act of reflection between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison is understood through the connection with an impossible property, that should be considered *nidarśanā*. (ViPrud 8.184)

When the attribute of the standard of comparison (upamāna), having been established as residing in the object of comparison (upameya), cannot be logically connected [to it], and the process of creating a reflection (bimba-pratibimba-karaṇa) is implied for the sake of establishing that connection, that is one type of *nidarśanā*. When the reverse of that occurs, it is the second type of *nidarśanā*.
The first [example] is as follows:

The lord of the Kākatīyas, who dispels the darkness of his enemies, who sits upon a jeweled lion-throne, and who is honored by the three worlds— Please note: The provided text consists of a single verse fragment; the full example would typically include a second verse for comparison. However, I have translated the portion given. If you require the translation of the subsequent part of the verse or further examples, please provide them.
It bears the fame of the intense-rayed sun, which kisses the crest of the mountain of sunrise, as it performs its play that brings joy to the world honored by many.

In this case, since the "splendor" (*abhikhyā*) of the "fierce sun" is impossible in the context [of the subject], the phrase "bearing a splendor similar to splendor" implies the operation of the *bimba-pratibimba* (original and reflection) relationship.
An example where the attribute of the object of comparison (*upameya*) is impossible in the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is as follows:
"The excellence of the purity of the fame of King Vīrarudra..."
They are perceived within the circular mirror of the playful expanse of the ocean of milk.

In this case, since the clarity of fame is impossible in the ocean of milk and so forth, the relationship of original and reflection (*bimbapratibimbana*) is understood through the acceptance of similarity.
Sometimes, by means of an implied attainment resulting from a negation, there is an implication of the formation of the original and its reflection, as for example: [text omitted].
The wives of the enemies of the Lord of Kākatī, fleeing through every forest,
create on the ground the splendor of red lotuses with their feet stained by lac-dye.
Here, by the prohibition "they do not release [the rays]," the attainment of the splendor of the red lotus is implied prior to that;
this is the figure of speech *vyatireka* (contrast).
Now, regarding *vyatireka*:

When there is a similarity between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison characterized primarily by their difference, that is called *vyatireka* (contrast), due to the statement of superiority or inferiority. 8.188.

The figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction) occurs where a similarity characterized by difference is established through the representation of the object compared (*upameya*) as either superior or inferior to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). For example:
"The day-maker (the sun) does not possess passion (redness) in the lilies; the lotuses, moreover, turn their faces away from the moon.
Yet, Pratāparudra—the friend of the entire world—shines forth, his light being accepted by both the blue water-lilies and the lotuses. (ViPrud 8.189)

Here, because the sun and the moon are impossible [to exist] and because [the moon] is beloved by all, the superiority of Pratāparudra—who serves as the object of comparison—is stated in the phrase "the light accepted by the *kuvalaya* and the *kamala*"; thus, this is a figure of speech called *vyatireka* (distinction) brought forth by *śleṣa* (punning).
Now, the figure of speech *śleṣa* is defined.

If a similarity based on words alone is stated as pertaining to both the relevant (prakṛta) and the irrelevant (aprakṛta), this is *śleṣa* (paronomasia); it exists in all cases except for the first two types [of *sādharmya*].

Where *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is described as occurring between two purely contextual (*prakṛta*) elements or two purely non-contextual (*aprakṛta*) elements, there is the coalescence of both the adjectives and the substantives in those two types.
In the final variety concerning the contextual and non-contextual, there is the coalescence of the adjectives alone.
If the two qualificands (*viśeṣya*) were also based on word-pun (*śliṣṭa*), it would result in the undesirable consequence of *dhvani* rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*).
However, when there is a single-word denotation of either solely contextual (*prakṛta*) elements or solely non-contextual (*aprakṛta*) elements, there is no suspicion of *dhvani*.
In this case, since there is no disparity—whether the two meanings are conveyed as non-contextual or as contextual—the function of direct denotation (*abhidhā*) alone is sufficient.

Regarding the subject of the relevant and the irrelevant, however, because the primary denotative function (*abhidhā*) is dependent solely upon the relevant [meaning], the comprehension of the irrelevant meaning is entirely dependent upon the operation of suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
Thus it has been stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*:
"When the denotative capacity of a word with multiple meanings is restricted..."
"Coloration (*añjana*) is the operation that produces the cognition of an inexpressible meaning through [factors] such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Thus, *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is threefold.
Among these, an example of two purely contextual [meanings] is as follows:
The entire lunar day of Mādhava assumes the ritual of honoring the King [the Moon],
upon which the splendor of shimmering lotuses and gems rests, marked by the plumage of the blue-throated peacock.
In this instance, Hari and Hara are the contextual subjects by virtue of being the objects of worship.
An example of two non-contextual subjects is as follows:
"This Lord of the Kākatīyas is equal to the great mountain-like kings of noble lineage."
Those who bear the wealth of shimmering bracelets upon their heads, having grasped the true path.

In this case, the great families such as those of Hariścandra and so forth, as well as the principal mountain ranges, function as points of comparison and are therefore non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*).
An example of both the contextual (*prākaraṇika*) and the non-contextual is as follows: "Having conquered the cities of his enemies..."
In his physical form, he was the abode of all auspiciousness;
the crest-jewel of kings, he stood like Rudra himself, with valor as his sprout.
Here, Pratāparudra and Rudra possess the status of the contextual and the non-contextual respectively. This is the figure of speech *parikara*.
It is called *parikara* because it is rooted in the strikingness (*vaicitrya*) of the adjectives (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Where there is a succession of qualifiers pregnant with intention,
that is considered by those who know intention to be *parikara* (poetic elaboration).
The figure of speech called *parikara* occurs where epithets are employed with intentional significance (*sābhiprāya*). For example:
Of the king, that jewel among the monarchs of the Yādava lineage, whose glory of valor is renowned, who possesses a vast army of galloping, lofty steeds, and whose sole wealth is his honor...
That Gautamī knows the deeds of Sevaṇapati, who was suddenly insulted by a certain leader of the armies of Rudra, the lord of men.
Here, the qualifiers such as "of the king" and so forth contain a sense of irony;
this is the figure of speech *ākṣepa* (paralipsis).
Now, regarding the figure of speech *ākṣepa*:
The statement of a semblance of negation regarding that which has been said, or is about to be said, for the sake of conveying a specific distinction, is declared to be *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis). 8.196.

The figure of speech called *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) occurs where there is a semblance of negation regarding two relevant subjects— one already mentioned and one yet to be mentioned— for the purpose of conveying a specific distinction.
In this context, either a fact or its verbal expression is negated.
In the context to be explained hereafter, the very act of speaking is prohibited.
Even there, having made a general assertion, the prohibition is made in a specific form;
or, when one part has been stated, another part is prohibited.
Thus, this objection is fourfold; here follow their examples in sequence,
O Crown of Kings.
"We are not merely messengers of your message;
it is said that for the one who is the householder of the world, there is no enemy whatsoever."
In this context, when those who conduct peace and war negotiations say, "We are not merely messengers," there is a negation of the literal fact.
Since that [literal negation] is untenable, it results in the state of speaking the truth by avoiding deceptive speech appropriate for the occasions of peace and war;
[the implication being]: "O Protector of the entire world, kings should not be viewed as enemies by you."
However, this implies a specific distinction such as that they must be protected in the form of servants.
An example of a prohibition against speaking is as follows: "How can this statement, 'We are without refuge,' be consistent with the world?"
"To take refuge in the Three Jewels and cry out, 'Protect us!'— this is clearly ignorance on your part,
O King Pratāpa, who are worthy of homage from the three worlds and are capable of protecting all people, even as you are addressed with the words, 'We bow to You'."

From the negation of the statement of reasoning beginning with "In this matter we are without refuge," a specific distinction is understood, such as the necessity of its mandatory preservation, which takes the form of an appearance (*bhāsa*).
An example of the negation of stating after having made a general proposition regarding a subject to be discussed later is as follows:
O upholder of the Kākatīya lineage, what is it that you wish to inform us? Or rather, what need is there for anything to be informed when you, the omniscient one, are our protector?
Having made the general proposition, "We inform you on this matter," the specific point—that "we must be protected in every way"—is implied by the apparent prohibition of further speech.
This is an instance where, upon the statement of one part, another part is negated. For example:
Pratāparudra himself possesses kindled splendor, and fate has lent its hand to his prowess;
you, moreover, possess a core as soft as cotton—so this is indeed fitting, or rather, what need is there for further words?

Here, by the statement of one part—"Pratāparudra is great, while you are insignificant"—or by the apparent negation of another part—"What is the use of further words?"—a specific point is implied through the medium of the enemy's wife's speech: "In every way he must be propitiated with prostrations; you must not resort to hostility."
It is accepted that, by virtue of having a common purpose, even what appears to be an undesirable injunction is a form of *ākṣepa* (implication).
Just as the negation of what is desired is fallacious because it is untenable, so too the prescription of what is undesired is fallacious because it is untenable. For example:
"O Lord! If you abandon service to Pratāparudra, then abandon it;
I shall practice the way of life of a householder in the forest. (ViPrud 8.202)
Here, the abandonment of service at the feet of Pratāparudra—which is undesirable—is enjoined by the wife of his enemy;
that injunction, being untenable, results in a semblance (ābhāsa).
By the statement "the manner of a forest-housewife is being practiced," this very semblance of an injunction is further reinforced.
The figure of speech *vyājastuti* (feigned praise).
Now, following the discussion of what is implied (*gamyaprastāvāt*), *vyājastuti* is described:
that wherein praise alone is understood through a censure that is expressed.
When praise leads to censure, that is considered "Praise by Disguise" (vyājastuti).
Where praise is understood by means of speaking censure—that is the first. Where censure is understood by means of praise—that is the second type of *vyājastuti* (feigned praise). Examples in order:
Was it by the fame of the lord of the Kākatīyas that everything was whitened today, such that a great blackness is now seen upon the faces of his enemies? (ViPrud 8.204)
An example of censure through praise is as follows: "O, how reckless are the enemies of King Pratāparudra!
For they enter the oceans and climb the mountains on all sides. (ViPrud 8.205)
The figure of speech *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description).
Now, following the discussion on suggestiveness (*gamyatva*), *aprastutapraśaṃsā* is discussed:
"Where the relevant subject (*prastuta*) is understood from the mention of something irrelevant (*aprastuta*)."
This is Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Praise of the Irrelevant), constrained by similarity and other such factors.

Where, through the description of something irrelevant by way of similarity, the relation of universal and particular, or the relation of cause and effect, there arises the cognition of the relevant subject, that is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
By the phrase "the cognition of the relevant from the irrelevant," it is distinguished from *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression).
Nor should one suspect the emergence of inference (*anumāna*) when there is a cognition of the cause from the effect.
In the figure of speech *anumāna* (inference), it is accepted that both the object to be conveyed (*pratyāyya*) and the means of conveying (*pratyāyaka*) are contextual (*prākaraṇika*).
By this, the exclusion of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) is also established.
Furthermore, this is not *dhvani* (suggestion).
Because the suggested meaning serves as a factor for establishing the expressed meaning.
In that regard, an example by way of similarity (*sārūpya*) is as follows:
"What have the swarms of bees gained from these withered trees, whose sprouts have been extinguished in all directions?"
The Punnāga tree imparts fragrance with its blossoms of ever-fresh scent; begin your celebration!

Here, by means of the irrelevant account of the bees, the relevant matter is understood: that Pratāparudra alone—who is endowed with every excellence and brings joy to all people—is to be served by all the learned, having abandoned all other lords of the earth whose prosperity is incomplete.
An instance where a particular is understood from a general statement is as follows:
The illustrious creation of the Lotus-born, which produces the crowns of kings,
has after a long time become this middle world, worthy of the fortune of being cherished through its protection.
In this instance, while the greatness of the qualities of Pratāparudra is the subject under discussion, a general statement is expressed.
An example of the apprehension of the general from the particular is as follows:
"Though desiring to see, she does not look; though eager to speak, she does not speak."
Even in the assembly, the merchant’s wife does not appear; what kind of wealth is hers?
"Though desiring to see, she does not look; though eager to speak, she does not speak;
though longing for touch, she does not touch—what kind of creation is this woman?
Here, while the general state of great shame felt by innocent women at their first union is introduced, a specific instance is expressed.
The cognition of a cause from its effect is as follows:
"When this lord of the Kākatiya dynasty descends upon the earth, the oceans have become as if shallow, and the great mountains as if low. (ViPrud 8.210)
Here, by means of the effects such as depth—which are irrelevant to the context—the causes, namely the majesty and profundity of Pratāparudra, are perceived.
An example of the perception of an effect from a cause is as follows:
Of King Pratāparudra, who is a wish-fulfilling tree for the earth...
Compassionate vision has arisen within me; why, my friend, do you marvel?

In this instance, when a friend asks with wonder about the cause of his current state—asking, "How have you now become the recipient of such great prosperity?"—the causal factor, the glance of Pratāparudra’s grace, is expressed.
The various subdivisions of this figure should be understood by oneself as they occur, according to whether the expressed meaning (vācya) is possible, impossible, or both.
This is the figure of speech known as *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
Following the discussion on what is implied (*gamya*), *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) is now described:

where the cause is understood from the description of the effect, which is connected with the subject under discussion by virtue of being itself the topic at hand—that is called *paryāyokta*. (ViPrud 8.212)
Paryāyokta (periphrasis) occurs when, through the description of the effect itself, the cause—which is equally under discussion—is implied. For example:
"Greyed by the spray [of water] from the long ponds in the pure inner apartments of rival kings..."
The soldiers of the Kākatīya army wash their limbs.

Here, the cause is understood to be that the rival kings fled, abandoning their own cities at the very commencement of the battle, due to the activity— consisting of sporting in the waters of the moats of the enemy’s city— performed by the soldiers of Pratāparudra’s army;
this is the figure of speech *pratīpa* (the contrary).

Now, the *pratīpa* (counter-comparison) is described as the sublation of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) by means of its pointlessness; or rather, that which would constitute the state of being the object of comparison (*upameya*) is cited as *pratīpa*. (ViPrud 8.214)

Where, because the object of comparison (upameya) is transcendent, the negation of the standard of comparison (upamāna) is made, that is one kind of *pratīpa* (the inverse). Where the status of being the object of comparison is attributed to the standard of comparison, [that is another].
That is the second [type].
The first is as follows:
"While the fame of Pratāparudra shines forth to the ends of the quarters..."
For what purpose does this shameless moon rise?
The second is as follows:
"In the Kākatīya dynasty, he is the Lord of Fortune; of this there is no doubt.
How can he be compared to Mount Sumeru by those of meager knowledge? (ViPrud 8.216)
The Ornament of Inference:
Now, the ornaments rooted in the logic of reasoning (*tarka-nyāya*) are being defined.
When there is the presentation of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), it is called inference (*anumāna*). (ViPrud 8.217)
Its distinction from reasoning (*tarka*) and inference (*anumāna*) lies in its being caused by a visible form (*rūpa*). For example:
"That which spreads forth as dust and smoke arises from the clash of armies;
sparks are seen originating from the swords wielded by the soldiers."
Therefore, I believe that the abundant fire of King Rudra’s wrath, ignited by the time of his expedition for purification, is consuming the cities of the enemy kings.
The figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason).
Now, regarding *kāvyaliṅga*:
when a cause (*hetu*) constitutes the meaning of a sentence or a word, it is illustrated as *kāvyaliṅga*. (ViPrud 8.219)
*Kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) occurs where a cause is presented either as part of a sentence or as part of a word. For example:
"This auspicious five-syllabled mantra, 'Pratāparudra,' is something extraordinary."
By bearing her in their hearts, kings bring all riches under their control.
In this case, the cause pertains to the meaning of the sentence as a whole.
An example where it pertains to the meaning of individual words is as follows:
"The forehead-mark of the mountains, though faded, has blossomed once again."
Sprinkled with the nectar of the moonlight from the toenails of King Pratāparudra.
In this instance, the cause for the renewed respiration of the previously withered royal forehead-tilaka is the sprinkling of the moonlight from the toe-nails of King Pratāparudra.
Because this resides within a qualifying attribute (viśeṣaṇa), it is described as residing in the meaning of a word (padārthagata).
This constitutes the figure of speech known as Arthāntaranyāsa (Corroboration).
Now, the Arthāntaranyāsa [figure of speech]:
where there is a mutual support of cause and effect, or of general and particular, that is cited as Arthāntaranyāsa. (ViPrud_8.222)
That in which the subject at hand is supported by means of the relationship of cause and effect or the relationship of the general and the particular is *arthāntaranyāsa*.
By way of the relationship between cause and effect, for example:
"The kings bow down to Pratāparudra; they do not remain unbowed. He causes those who are high to bend, and he also causes those who are bowed to rise. (ViPrud 8.223)
Here, the cause of humility is supported by means of its result, which is loftiness.
An example of supporting a particular by means of a general is as follows:
"The rival kings were made to tremble by the martial exploits of King Rudra."
These [omens] bear a wondrous appearance; to one who is afraid, everything indeed causes fear for those lacking consciousness.
In this case, the general principle that "everything is a cause of fear to one who is afraid" is supported by the specific instance that "kings who are enemies fear even insentient things.
An example of supporting a general principle through a specific instance is as follows:
"Indeed, even a wicked person becomes a virtuous one through association with the great."
Having approached Pratāparudra, the Kali age acts like the Kṛta age.

Here, by means of the greatness of Pratāparudra’s association, the Kali age is shown to be like the Kṛta age; this is a specific instance supporting a general proposition (*viśeṣeṇa sāmānyasamarthanam*).
As for the support of an effect by its cause even within a relationship of cause and effect, that is included within *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) and has therefore not been mentioned here.
Thus, there are three varieties of *arthāntaranyāsa*.
This is the figure of speech *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence).
Following the figures of speech based on the logic of reasoning (*tarka*), those based on the logic of sentence structure (*vākya*) are now defined.
It consists of arranging enumerated items in their respective order, first and then later.
Where there is no specific enumeration, it is intended that the correspondence follows the order of the sequence.
When objects mentioned in a certain order are subsequently mentioned in that very same order, there is the figure of speech known as *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence). For example:
"Having observed depth, loftiness, and unimpededness in Pratāparudra, the Creator [bestowed these qualities upon him]."
He considered the creation of the oceans, the mountains, and the elephants of the quarters to be the sole fruit of his exertion.
The figure of speech *arthāpatti* (presumption):
When, from the existence of one thing, another thing follows by way of the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutya*), that shall be the poetic ornament of *arthāpatti*. (ViPrud 8.228)

When, upon the accomplishment of one matter, another matter follows by way of *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so") due to a similar logic, that is the figure of speech *Arthāpatti* (Presumption).
Nor should there be any suspicion of inference (*anumāna*) here, because it consists in a connection based on the principle of *kaimutya*. For example:

Even as he strode across the earth amidst the tumultuous clamor of various cavalry charges surging from all sides, Sevaṇapati became distressed when King Rudra’s brow was slightly furrowed with a frown of rising anger.
What need is there to mention other kings whose wrath has been rendered fruitless?

Moreover—Even the golden mountain, the essence of the three worlds, was unable to ascend to equality with King Pratāparudra upon the scale; what need is there to mention other mountains? (ViPrud 8.230)
Here, by comparison with Pratāparudra, the worthlessness of other mountain-kings follows as a matter of course (*kaimutya*), even though Mount Meru itself is [otherwise] worthless;
this is the figure of speech *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification).
Now, regarding *parisaṃkhyā*:
When, upon the attainment of one thing, there is a restriction to one [of several] at once, that is indeed called *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification). ViPrud_8.231 //
Where a single object, though possibly existing in multiple locations simultaneously, is restricted to one location alone, that is *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification). It is first of all twofold:
that preceded by a question (*praśnapūrvikā*), and...
"And otherwise than that":
since those two [types of] objects to be avoided are twofold—verbal and objective—there is a fourfold division.
Among these, the verbal object to be avoided preceded by a question is as follows:
What is the ornament of the three worlds? Not Mount Kāñcana, but the tilaka-mark on the forehead of Kākatīya. Who is to be praised by the wise? Not Mount Mandara, but King Rudra. (ViPrud 8.232)
The question-based *ārthavarjanīyā* is as follows:
"What is the canopy for the worlds? The glory of the Kākatīya dynasty."
What happiness is there for the earth, other than dwelling upon the arm of King Rudra?

An example of a verbal avoidance that is not preceded by a question is as follows: "Attachment should be directed toward the Dharma, not toward sensual pleasure; one's association should be with an assembly of the virtuous."
He took no pleasure in the company of women, nor did he find constant delight in the science of ethics, gambling,
or the accumulation of wealth; rather, his diversion was found in the constant pursuit of fame.
Nor did he [dwell] with King Rudradeva’s attendants during his practice of learning.
The *ārthavarjanīyā* (exclusion based on meaning) that does not precede a question is as follows:
"The earth itself is the world; the self-existent god himself is the king;
Pratāparudra alone is the auspicious city, [which is] nothing but a single rock. (ViPrud 8.235)
While King Rudra, the destroyer of his enemies, protected the earth,
the fear of serpents in the abode of Bali and the talk of Indra, the breaker of mountains, in heaven [vanished].
Through the employment of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is an excellence of beauty in the ornament;
this is the ornament of the "Reply" (*uttara*). Where the question is to be inferred from the reply, such is the ornament of "Question and Reply" (*praśnottara*).
And they are bound in many ways; that which follows is now declared.
Where a question is inferred from a subsequent answer being provided, that is the first type of answer.
For the sake of elegance, when an extraordinary answer is presented repeatedly following a series of questions, that is the second type of answer.
Examples in order:
What training have you had in the worldly conduct of virtuous people,
since that which must now be known has become manifest? For ever since King Rudra began, the pure glory of Dharma reigns supreme.
And the lords of the earth were delighted by the undertaking of various kinds of magnificent displays.
In this context, from the moment Pratāparudra came to power, the earth became firmly established in the complete practice of dharma,
and even the gods on earth (brāhmaṇas) attained such satisfaction.
From the reply, "What do you ask now?", the question is inferred as to whether there is the protection of dharma in the kingdom of Pratāparudra, and whether the brāhmaṇas are happy.
The second example is as follows:
"What indeed is wealth? Family lore. What is greed?"
Dwelling with a virtuous person—what city is it? Ayodhyā; what king is it?
King Vīrarudra. (ViPrud 8.239)
What indeed is wealth?
Family lore. What is gain?
Dwelling together with the virtuous.
What city?
Ekaśilā. What king?
Vīrarudra, lord of men.
The Ornament of Option (Vikalpālaṅkāra).
An option is discussed here because it follows the introduction to the ornaments based on the logic of sentences:
"When two [contradictory] factors of equal strength are in conflict, that is considered the ornament of option. (ViPrud 8.240)
Where two contradictory options, taught by equal authorities, are simultaneously applicable but cannot both exist at once, there is *vikalpa* (option).
Its beauty arises from its containing a comparison (*aupamya*). For example:
"O kings, let there be humility either with [your] heads or with [your] bows."
Let the shadow of the feet of the Lord of Andhra, the Vindhya mountain, be resorted to.
In this case, while Pratāparudra reigns, when both bowing the head and bending the bow— possessing equal force and measure through the acts of peace and war— arrive simultaneously for kings,
because those two are contradictory and simultaneous occurrence is impossible, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
This is the figure of speech *samuccaya* (accumulation).
The conjunction that serves as the antidote to conceptual construction is now examined;
