conjunction is defined as the simultaneity of qualities and actions. (ViPrud 8.242)
The figure of speech *samuccaya* (accumulation) occurs where there is the simultaneous presence of qualities—such as purity and the like—and actions—such as seeing and the like. For example:
"When King Pratāparudra ascended the throne of majesty, the hearts of the virtuous became clear, while the minds of the wicked became turbid. (ViPrud 8.243)
An example of the accumulation of actions (*kriyāsamuccaya*) is as follows:
"The king sees this; Love enters and pride fades; the mind is crushed and becomes empty. What is this? [Tell me], O friends. (ViPrud 8.244)
"The king gazes at her; Madana enters and pride melts away; the mind reels and becomes empty—what is this? Look, friends!
These two are examples where the objects [of the figures] are distinct.
An example of [similarity] in having the same object is as follows:

While the kings of Kākatīpura were lingering for a long time in order to serve the illustrious Lord Vīrarudra— whose fame was celebrated throughout the three worlds— the wives of those kings [did likewise].
They go to the door, they look ahead, they heave long sighs;
they wither away, they prattle, they become emaciated, and they faint and swoon.
By way of the totality of qualities and actions, for example:
When King Kākatīya Vīrarudra was intent on his victorious expedition, [the world was filled with] intoxicated elephants, moving infantry, galloping horses, and rushing chariots.
With pale faces and agitated eyes, manifesting wretchedness and trembling,
the host of rival kings wanders everywhere throughout every forest.
The second type of conjunction (*samuccaya*):
When many causes exert themselves together to accomplish a single effect, according to the maxim of the pigeons in a threshing-floor, that is the second conjunction. (ViPrud 8.247)
Where there is an exertion by many causes, each vying with the others (*ahamahamikayā*), to accomplish a single effect, that too is indeed *samuccaya* (cumulative conjunction).
Because many qualities exist simultaneously,
as in:
"Pure fame, great valor, excellent conduct, blameless learning, and a stainless lineage."
They manifest the extraordinary style of Pratāparudra, the lord of men.

Here, although fame and the other qualities each serve as a cause for the accomplishment of a supermundane style, they are connected simultaneously according to the maxim of the crows and the pigeon (*khalekapotanyāya*). This is the figure of speech *samādhi*. Now, *samādhi* is defined: *Samādhi* is said to be the conjunction of diverse causes with a single effect, even when there is no mutual dependence among those causes. It is like the case of a multitude of people carrying a heavy load together. For example: "By the power of his majesty, by the excellence of his learning, and by the force of his penance, the king has conquered the entire earth. In this instance, although majesty and the others are individually causes for the conquest of the earth, their simultaneous connection is expressed through the maxim of the crows and the pigeon; thus, it is the figure *samādhi*. Furthermore, it is not the case that there is a lack of mutual dependence among the causes, because the specific nature of each cause is intended to be conveyed. Therefore, this is distinct from the figure *sāra*, which consists in the predominance of one cause over others. Nor is it the figure *samuccaya*, because the causes are not presented as being mutually independent. Nor is it the figure *hetu*, because there is no mention of a single cause producing a single effect. Nor is it the figure *vibhāvanā*, because the effect is not produced without its [usual] causes. Nor is it the figure *viśeṣokti*, because the effect is not denied despite the presence of its causes. Nor is it the figure *vyatireka*, because there is no comparison with another. Nor is it the figure *atiśayokti*, because there is no sublation of the literal meaning. Nor is it the figure *asambandhe sambandharūpātiśayokti*, because there is no relation between the causes and the effect. Nor is it the figure *utprekṣā*, because there is no suggestion of a possibility. Nor is it the figure *svabhāvokti*, because the description is not merely of the natural state of things. Nor is it the figure *apahnuti*, because there is no concealment of the primary object. Nor is it the figure *ullekha*, because there is no perception of the object by multiple perceivers. Nor is it the figure *bhrāntimān*, because there is no delusion regarding the identity of the object. Nor is it the figure *sandeha*, because there is no doubt. Nor is it the figure *ullāsa*, because there is no manifestation of the latent. Nor is it the figure *udātta*, because there is no description of greatness. Nor is it the figure *bhāvika*, because there is no vivid presentation of past or future events. Nor is it the figure *yathāsaṃkhya*, because there is no correspondence between the order of causes and effects. Nor is it the figure *parivṛtti*, because there is no exchange of things. Nor is it the figure *pratyanīka*, because there is no counter-attack against an adversary. Nor is it the figure *tulyayogitā*, because there is no commonality of action among equals. Nor is it the figure *dīpaka*, because there is no illumination of a single attribute. Nor is it the figure *prativastūpamā*, because there is no parallelism of two distinct objects. Nor is it the figure *dṛṣṭānta*, because there is no illustration of a general principle. Nor is it the figure *nidarśanā*, because there is no depiction of a relationship between two things. Nor is it the figure *arthāntaranyāsa*, because there is no statement of a corroborating generalization. Nor is it the figure *kāvyārthāpatti*, because there is no implication of a fact from a stated one. Nor is it the figure *kāvyaliṅga*, because there is no causal indication. Nor is it the figure *paryāyokta*, because the matter is not expressed through a periphrasis. Nor is it the figure *vyājastuti*, because there is no praise or blame under a pretext. Nor is it the figure *ākṣepa*, because there is no prohibition of a stated intention. Nor is it the figure *virodha*, because there is no apparent contradiction. Nor is it the figure *vicitra*, because there is no doing of what is difficult. Nor is it the figure *adhibhāva*, because there is no assumption of a
When one cause is employed for the accomplishment of an effect,
and another [cause] happens to coincide by way of the "crow-and-palm" principle (coincidence), that is declared to be *samādhi*.

The figure of speech *samādhi* occurs when, while one cause is engaged in accomplishing an effect, another cause arrives by chance (*kākatālīyatas*) and makes that effect easy to achieve. "The falling of blades of grass upon the faces of kings—who were offering praises to pacify the wrath of King Rudra on the battlefield—by the force of the wind: that, O Lord, is Your partiality. (ViPrud 8.250)

In this context, the *bhāvika* ornament is employed: the effect characterized by the pacification of King Pratāparudra’s anger— brought about by the ease with which it was accomplished through blades of grass that happened to fall by chance (*kākatālīya*) upon the faces of kings who had advanced to the front of the battle to offer praise, driven by the force of the wind.
Now, the figures of speech based on worldly convention are being defined:
When the past and the future are perceived as if they were present, due to the description of an exceedingly wonderful matter, that is cited as *bhāvika*. (ViPrud 8.251)
The poetic figure *bhāvika* is that wherein, through the description of extraordinary deeds, past and future entities appear as if they were present before the eyes.
Nor is the appearance of past and future things as if they were perceptible contradictory;
for, by means of the description of such most marvelous objects, a state of contemplative realization (*bhāvanā*) arises in the hearts of sensitive readers.
And thus, because of the repeated mental visualization through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), its appearing as if directly perceived (*pratyakṣāyamāṇatva*) is indeed possible;
just as, for example, a traveler [experiences] the appearing as if directly perceived of a beloved woman through the power of his meditation upon her.
Nor is this a description of essential nature (*svabhāvokti*); for in that [figure], there is a state of appearing as if perceived through the accurate description of a thing's essential nature,
whereas here it is due to its extreme wonderfulness.
Nor is it an ornament such as *rasavat* and the like;
for in those cases, the state of being experienced (*bhāvyatva*) belongs to rasa and so forth only through the contemplation of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors,
and not by virtue of their being exceedingly wonderful.

Nor is this a case of poetic fancy (utprekṣā), because there is no determination [of the object] through direct perception regarding the past and the future; nor is it the figure of speech known as "the mistaken" (bhrāntimad).
Because meditation (*bhāvanā*) consists of non-erroneous cognition, this ornament is indeed transcendent to all others. For example:
"Upon the tip of the banner of the Lord of Kākatīya shines Hari in the form of a boar."
The earth appeared like a mere drop of mud upon the tip of his tusk.

Here, by means of this most marvelous description—how the earth, together with its eighteen islands, exists as a mere drop of clay upon the tip of [the Lord's] tusk—the possibility of a perception as if it were directly present arises when such a meditation is practiced.
This is the figure of speech *pratyanīka* (the counter-argument).
Now, the figure of speech *pratyanīka* is being explained.
When it is extremely difficult to counteract a powerful adversary, that which constitutes its humiliation is called *pratyanīka* (the hostile). (ViPrud 8.253)
*Pratyanīka* (counter-position) occurs where there is a disparagement of a powerful opponent due to the inability to counter it. For example:

"The submarine fire, its own majesty eclipsed by the great heat of the valor of the Lord of the Kākatīyas, incessantly assails the ocean—the repository of waters—which is its constant kinsman in depth, both outside and within. (ViPrud 8.254)
In this case, because the state of belonging to that [object] is caused by similarity, it constitutes a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*). It is the figure of speech known as *vyāghāta* (contradiction).
Now, regarding *vyāghāta*:
When an object established by one [means] is performed otherwise by that very same means, or by another, it is called the ornament "contradiction" (vyāghāta). ViPrud 8.255.

When an object that has been accomplished by a certain agent through a certain means is performed otherwise by another agent using that very same means, that is *vyāghāta* (contradiction). For example:
"This one born of the Kākatīya lineage does not possess a status superior to that of the noble-born."
With his two arms, he brought kings to the rise of prosperity, while from those same two arms he produced others who remained without such rise.
The Ornament of Synonyms (Paryāyālaṅkāra). Now, in the context of defining the ornaments based on worldly conventions, the ornament of synonyms is defined:
"If one [entity] occurs sequentially in many substrates..."
Furthermore, when one [subject] has many [attributes], it is considered the figure of speech *paryāya* (permutation).

Where a single thing to be contained (ādheya) exists sequentially in multiple loci (ādhāra), that is one type of *paryāya* (permutation). Nor is this the figure of speech *viśeṣa*, because in that [latter] case, a single thing exists in multiple places simultaneously.
In this sequence,
the second type of *paryāya* (succession) occurs when multiple substrata reside upon a single substrate;
nor is there the figure of speech known as *samuccaya* (accumulation) here.
In that regard as well, there is the simultaneous presence of many in one place, whereas here it is in succession; for example:
"Long ago, in the fang of the Lord God Śauri, who assumed the form of a boar..."

Now, the earth has bound its festive garland upon the arm of the great and illustrious Lord of the Kākatīyas— the crest-jewel of sovereigns— which bears the essential strength capable of bearing every burden, and which rests upon the circle of the head of the serpent-king, the lord of the netherworld.
In this regard, the first [type] is the successive presence of a single earth in many places. The second is as follows:

those kings in whose mouths, in the presence of their own wives, there arose declarations of valor filled with pride; [yet] when they saw the faces of their enemies in battle, those very words became the cause of their shame.
Terrified by the sight of those scorching kings,
distressed words arise from them right there.
The Subtle Ornament (Sūkṣmālaṅkāra). Now, the subtle ornament is defined: that which reveals a subtle meaning not immediately perceived is called "subtle. (ViPrud 8.260)
The figure of speech *sūkṣma* (the subtle) is that wherein a matter known only by its mother through her cleverness is revealed by means of facial expression and gesture;
for example:
"Seeing the messenger sent by the king in the presence of her elders, the young wife..."
She applies a paste of kṛtavedhana mixed with saffron over all her limbs.
(Seeing the messenger sent by the king in the presence of her elders, the bride applies musk-paste over all her limbs with a smile.
Here, by means of the musk-paste application, it is revealed that the time for the tryst is the hour of darkness.
The Ornament of the Exalted (Udāttālaṃkāra).
Now the ornament of the exalted is being described.
Its immediate cause for following [the previous topic] is likewise its foundation in worldly convention.
That is called *udātta* (the elevated) where a prosperous object is described.
Where a description is made of an object possessed of great prosperity, there is the figure of speech *udātta* (the Sublime).
For example:
The wise ones, having reached the beautiful city named Ekaśilā,
stood within golden houses whose doorways and arches were fashioned with jewels; there,
upon the courtyards, they took up young elephants, eager for play, along with their children.
They rejoice upon beholding that playful act of renunciation by King Rudra.
Now, by the same logic, *parivṛtti* (exchange) is defined:

when there is an exchange between things that are equal, inferior, or superior, occurring simultaneously with those that are equal, superior, or inferior, this is considered *parivṛtti*. (ViPrud 8.264)
*Parivṛtti* (exchange) is the bartering of equals, unequals, or more and less;
it consists of the exchange of equal for equal,
and the exchange of the less for the more.
And there is the exchange of the inferior for the superior.
An example of the exchange of the equal for the equal is as follows:
Having given words that were common to all, he gave [the kingdom] to King Kākatīya.
Therefore, poets obtain a thousand scent-elephants.
Herein lies the equality between words and scent-elephants (*gandhasindhura*).
An example of the exchange of the lesser for the greater is as follows:
"Having offered elephants, horses, and other such tributes, all the kings [attained their ends]."
They obtain the firm favor of King Pratāparudra.
In this case, there is a superiority of the very manifestation of Pratāparudra’s grace that is received over the gift and so forth that is being abandoned.
An example of the exchange of the superior for the inferior is as follows: "The rival kings were conquered in battle by Pratāparudra."

Having given ornaments to the Kirātas, they receive garments of bark and the like. Here, there is a deficiency of the bark-garments and so forth being received compared to the collection of ornaments being given away; this is the *kāraṇamālā* (garland of causes) ornament.
Now, the figures of speech based on the logic of a chain (śṛṅkhalā-nyāya) are defined.
When each subsequent element serves as the cause for each preceding one, then it is called the figure of speech known as "The Garland of Causes" (kāraṇamālā). (ViPrud 8.268)
When each preceding element in succession serves as the cause for each subsequent one, it is the figure of speech called *kāraṇamālā* (the garland of causes). For example:
"Through learning comes excellence of discipline; through discipline, the acquisition of virtues."
And the affection of the subjects for his virtues—this is the natural order in the Lord of Kākatīya.

The Ornament of the Single String (ekāvalyalaṅkāra): Where there is a sequential description of each preceding element as a qualifier for each succeeding element, that is considered the Single String ornament. (ViPrud 8.270)
Where each preceding element successively functions as a qualifier for each subsequent one, that is the *ekāvalī* (single-string) ornament.
For example:
The city of Pratāparudra is graced by virtuous men;
the virtuous are endowed with abundant wealth, and that wealth is characterized by stability.
This is an example by way of affirmation;
it also occurs by way of exclusion (*apohana*), as follows:
"That is no kingdom where subjects do not possess exalted glory."
The Lord of Kākatīya was not the master of those subjects over whom he did not himself rule.
The Ornament of the Garland-Lamp (Mālādīpaka):
When each subsequent element brings about an excellence in each preceding one, that is called the Ornament of the Garland-Lamp. (ViPrud 8.273)
Where each preceding element brings about a subsequent quality, that is the figure of speech *mālādīpaka* (the lamp-in-a-garland).
For example:
"The earth, having reached the arm of the Lord of Kākatīya, has attained an abundance of fortune."
The arm possesses incomparable majesty, and that majesty [pervades] the three worlds.
The Ornament of the Essence (sārālaṅkāra): The Ornament of the Essence is said to be a progressive excellence from one stage to the next. (ViPrud 8.275)
Just as the earth shines among the worlds, within it is the city of Ekaśilā;
therein is the lineage of the Kākatīyas, and within that, King Rudra.
Since this ornament finally takes as its object Pratāparudra, who is the very essence of the entire world, its name "Sāra" (the Essence) is truly significant.
Thus ends the section on figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*) in the *Pratāparudrayaśobhūṣaṇa*, a treatise on poetics composed by Śrī Vidyānātha.
Now begins the section on mixed figures (*miśrālaṅkāra*).
Now, *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) and *saṃkara* (fusion) are being defined.
Just as in the case of worldly ornaments made of gold or jewels, which are individually causes of beauty, an excellence of loveliness is observed through their mutual association;
likewise, an excellence of beauty is perceived in poetic ornaments such as *rūpaka* (metaphor) and others through their mutual connection.
And that relation is of two kinds: in the form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and in the form of inherence (*samavāya*).
Regarding conjunction...
The maxim of sesame and rice;
in the case of a mixture— the maxim of milk and water.
When there is a relationship according to the analogy of sesame seeds and rice, it is *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture);
when there is a relationship according to the analogy of milk and water, it is *saṃkara* (blending).
Because both serve as causes for an excellence of beauty when they exist separately, they bear the primary burden of being poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).
But it is not the state of being a supplement to the previously mentioned figures of speech;
that is *saṃsṛṣṭi*.
Among those, *saṃsṛṣṭi* is described first.
When figures of speech are mutually intertwined, like the manner of sesame seeds and rice grains being mixed together, that is called *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture). 9.1.
Where figures of speech such as *rūpaka* and others are mutually interconnected according to the analogy of sesame seeds and rice grains, that is *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture).
It is of three kinds: by virtue of residing in verbal ornaments, by virtue of residing in semantic ornaments, and [by virtue of residing in both].
And by virtue of being present in both [types of ornamentation]:
an instance of the commingling of verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṅkāra*) is as follows—[the verse beginning] "śumbhatsaṃbhramagandhasindhuradhurānirdāritorvītalā... [is an example].
With chariots swiftly rushing along due to the formidable speed of their tall,
well-limbed horses; with the horizons flashing with the arrogance of fierce soldiers rising in intense exertion—
the boundless military expeditions for victory of King Rudra spread forth.
Here, there is a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of *che kānuprāsa* (alliteration of single consonants) and *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration of consonant clusters).
An example of the combination of figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*) is as follows:
"The army of the Lord of Kākatīya bestows the majesty of the ocean."
which devours the enemy armies like rivers devouring the banks.
Here, there is a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of the figures of speech *nidarśanā* (poetic illustration) and *upamā* (simile).
An example of the combination of both is as follows:
"The staff-like arm of Pratāparudra is adorned with the tip of his sword."
He is seen in battle by the heroes like a hooded serpent with its expanded hood.

Here, there is a coexistence (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of alliteration (*vṛttyanuprāsa*) and simile (*upamā*). Now, commingling (*saṅkara*) is defined: where there is a mutual relationship according to the manner of milk and water, [that is commingling].
The commingling of these ornaments has thus been illustrated.

Where there is a mutual relationship between figures of speech (alaṅkāras) according to the analogy of milk and water, that is *saṅkara* (commixture). It is of three kinds: by the relation of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), by the entry into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*), and by doubt (*sandeha*). Among these, an example of *saṅkara* by the relation of principal and subordinate is as follows:

With the tumultuous thundering of their swelling roars, which caused panic among the clouds that were the herds of elephants, and which were capable of besieging the mountain-like enemy camps like the pastimes of the rainy season,
they brought an end to the rising heat upon the circle of the earth through the heavy rain of tears shed by the women of their enemies.
The expeditions of the beloved of the Kākatiyas spread joy throughout the worlds.

Here, by means of the poetic figure of simile (*upamā*) in the phrase "the expeditions were like pastimes during the rainy season," the simile in the expression "a mass of elephants like a bank of clouds" (*dvipaghaṭākādambinī*) is established; thus, there is a relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between two similes of the same kind, because the compound *dvipaghaṭākādambinī* relies on the underlying simile "like a bank of clouds. This is also the case in the phrase "obstructing the mountain ranges" (*kṣoṇībhṛtkaṭakoparodha*).
Hyperbole based on *śleṣa* (pun).
An example of the commingling of different types [of hyperbole] is as follows:
"The edge of Pratāparudra’s sword falls incessantly upon the foreheads of his enemies."
As if for the very purpose of washing away the stain of bad writing that had come to reside there, the Creator fashioned it.

Here, by means of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) "as if for the sake of washing," the metaphor (*rūpaka*) in the phrase "of the stain of bad writing" is established; thus, there is a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between two distinct figures.
An example of *saṅkara* (commingling) where [figures] enter into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraviṣṭa*) is as follows:
"Having conquered the cities of his enemies, with all auspiciousness shining upon his form..."
Upon this earth, the lord of the Kākatīyas shines like Śambhu himself.

Here, "one who has conquered the cities of his enemies" constitutes a simile (*upamā*) due to the similarity of meaning, while "one in whom all auspiciousness shines" constitutes a paronomasia (*śleṣa*) due to the similarity of sound; both enter into the single word *iva* in the phrase "like Śambhu.
An example of the commingling of doubt (*saṃdehasaṅkara*) is as follows:
The moon Pratāparudra has been born from the ocean of the Kākatīya lineage;
he bestows upon the cakora-birds that are the people the nectar of his gracious radiance.

In this instance, in the verse beginning with "kākatīyakulāmbudhau" (in the ocean of the Kākatīya dynasty), there is a commixture (*saṅkara*) based on doubt between metaphor (*rūpaka*) and simile (*upamā*).

This is because two types of compounds are possible: either "the Kākatīya lineage itself is an ocean" (*kākatīyānvaya evāmbudhiḥ*), or "the Kākatīya lineage is like an ocean" (*kākatīyānvayo 'mbudhir iva*).
And since there is no proof or refutation as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for either side here, it results in nothing but doubt.
However, when proof or refutation as a means of valid cognition is possible, doubt ceases.
An example of proof here is as follows:
The sweet clusters of fame arising from King Pratāparudra’s *Pārijāta* tree serve as ear-ornaments for the women of the quarters.

In this case, regarding the poetic figure of *rūpaka* (metaphor) expressed as "the very fame is the clusters of blossoms," the phrase "they act as ear-ornaments" (*vataṃsayanti*) serves as the corroborating evidence (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*),
because through the act of being made into an ear-ornament, there is the cognition of identity [between the fame and the blossoms].
An example of subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) is as follows:
When the sound of the Kākatiya lord’s army’s march resounded throughout the quarters,
the ocean-like host of the enemy became agitated with its living beings thrown into turmoil.
In this context, the phrase "ocean of the power of the antidote" (*pratipakṣabalārṇava*) is sublated by the expression "one who has agitated the sentient beings" (*vyākulīkṛtasattva*),

because according to the grammatical rule— "that which is compared [is compounded] with *vyāghra* and so forth when a common quality is not employed"— the employment of a common quality constitutes a sublation of the simile.
Therefore, by the principle of elimination, this is the figure of speech *rūpaka*.
In this manner, the coexistence (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) and commingling (*saṅkara*) of other figures of speech should be understood as they occur in various compositions, according to their possibility.
Thus ends the section on Mixed Figures of Speech in the *Pratāparudrayaśobhūṣaṇa*, a treatise on poetics composed by the great preceptor Śrī Vidyānātha. [End of] the *Pratāparudrīya*.
The treatise on the ornaments of names is completed.
